p.h: Kerch and Yenikale for Russia, a fortress on a non-existent island for the Ottomans
p.g: The memoir lists Russia's peace terms as the Ottomans understood them: the fortresses and places on the Crimean, Taman and Kuban side would be handed to the Tatars, while Yenikale and the port of Kerch, with their districts, would go to Russia. At most, it says with open sarcasm, the Ottomans would be allowed to build a fortress 'on an imaginary island, whose name and body do not exist' between Yenikale and Taman. The Tatar towns of the strait are real fortresses bargained over by two empires.
p.q: قريم وطمان وقوبان جانبنده اولان قلاع وبقاع بالجمله … تاتاره ترك وتسليم اولنه وثانيا یکی قلعه وکرش ليمانی الکا وناحيه‌لريله روسيه دولتنه تمليك اولنوب نهايه یکی قلعه ايله طمان بيننده اسم وجسمی معدوم بر اطه موهومه ده دولت عليه بر قلعه بنا ايتمك جايز اوله
p.s: Ottoman memoir on Russia's demands, 1773 (item II in the library catalogue, apparently translated from a French memoir), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
p.t: All the fortresses and places on the side of Crimea, Taman and Kuban … shall be left and handed over to the Tatars; and secondly Yenikale and the port of Kerch, with their districts and territories, shall be made over to Russia; and at most the Sublime State may build a fortress on an imaginary island, whose name and body do not exist, between Yenikale and Taman.
p.c: A hostile Ottoman summary of Russian demands, perhaps translated from French; the sarcasm about the island is the memoir's own. Russia did gain Kerch and Yenikale by the treaty of 1774.
p.n: Transcribed from the manuscript image (corpus OCR of this manuscript is garbled); one unclear word omitted.

p.h: Bukhara: eleven gates and 360 mosques
p.g: Wolff gives a thumbnail sketch of Bukhara: a walled city of fifteen miles' circuit with eleven gates, hundreds of mosques, caravanserais, baths and about a hundred colleges, and the old citadel (the Ark), which he says was built a thousand years earlier by Arslan Khan.
p.q: It has eleven gates, and a circumference of fifteen English miles; three hundred and sixty mosques, twenty-two caravanserays, many baths and bazaars, and the old palace called Ark, built by Arslan Khan one thousand years ago, and has about one hundred splendid colleges. The houses have neither roofs nor windows.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.c: The number 360 is a traditional round figure, and the date and builder of the Ark are local tradition. 'Neither roofs nor windows' probably means flat roofs and no outward-facing windows.

p.h: Gushri Khan's Tartars take Shigatse fortress
p.g: Das summarises Sumpa's account of how the Khoshut Mongol ruler Gushri Khan invaded Tibet, besieged the fortress of Samdruptse (Shigatse), took thirteen district forts and captured the king of Tsang, who was thrown into the Tsangpo river. Gushri was then proclaimed king of all Tibet and handed religious authority to the Dalai Lama's church. The 'Tartars' here are Oirat Mongols from Kokonor.
p.q: The seige of Sam-dub-tse (now fort Shi-ga-tse) by the Tartars and the capture of thirteen Jong by them under the lead of Gucri Khan … The king of Tsang surrendered himself. He was thrown into the river Tsang-po
p.s: Sarat Chandra Das, English analytical contents to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo's Tibetan text (Calcutta, 1908)
p.c: Das adds that the king was packed into something before being drowned, but that word is garbled in the OCR.
p.tg: gushri khan khoshut shigatse fortress conquest

p.h: Karakorum: worse than Saint-Denis, with two quarters and many temples
p.g: Rubruck's famous verdict on the Mongol capital: apart from the Khan's palace, it is not as good as the French town of Saint-Denis, whose abbey is worth ten Mongol palaces. It has a Saracen quarter with markets and a Cathayan (Chinese) quarter of craftsmen, twelve idol temples, two mosques and a church. On the next page (n221) he adds earthen walls with four gates, each with its own market for grain, sheep, oxen and carts, or horses.
p.q: excepté le Palais du Cham, elle n'est pas si bonne que la ville de S. Denis en France, dont le Monastere vaut dix fois mieux que tout le Palais mesme de Mangu. Il y a deux grandes ruës, l'vne dite des Sarrasins, où se tiennent les marchez & la foire … Là sont douze temples d'Idolatres de diuerses nations; & deux mosquées de Sarrasins
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: except for the Khan's palace, it is not as good as the town of Saint-Denis in France, whose monastery is worth ten times more than the whole palace of Möngke itself. There are two main streets, one called the Saracens', where the markets and fair are held … There are twelve temples of idolaters of various nations, and two mosques of the Saracens

p.h: Who built the lost cities of Mongolia
p.g: Reflecting on the Old Town, Huc says such ruined cities are common in Mongolia and that their story is unknown locally. His best guess, from Chinese annals, is that the Mongols built many large cities in 'Northern Tartary' while they ruled China, and that after their expulsion the Ming emperor Yongle burned their towns in three campaigns deep into the desert.
p.q: the probabilities are, that they date no earlier back than the 13th century, the period when the Mongols rendered themselves masters of the Chinese empire … During their domination, say the Chinese annals, they erected in Northern Tartary many large and powerful cities. … the Emperor Young-Lo, who desired to exterminate the Tartars, invaded their country, and burned their towns
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.c: Huc's explanation is an educated guess from Chinese histories, not local tradition.

p.h: The Dasht of Berke: 'a land of the Tatars alone'
p.g: Describing the steppe that Timur coveted, Ibn Arabshah calls it the Dasht of Berke (after the Golden Horde khan) and says it was a country belonging to the Tatars alone, teeming with herds and Turkish tribes, well guarded, well peopled and healthy in water and air. He had lived there himself in the 1410s and 1420s.
p.q: دشت بركه وكانت بلادا بالتتار خاصه وبانواع المواشي وقبائل الترك غاصه محفوظة الاطراف معمورة الاكناف فسيحة الارجاء صحيحة الماء والهواء
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde (Dasht-i Qipchaq)
p.t: the Dasht of Berke. It was a country belonging to the Tatars alone, and teeming with every kind of livestock and with the tribes of the Turks; its borders guarded, its sides well peopled, its reaches wide, its water and air wholesome.
p.c: Rhymed, flattering prose. One word (al-mawashi, livestock) is blurred in the print.

p.h: Riazan: through the forest in winter
p.g: The Tatars came 'through the forest' in winter, ravaged the Riazan land as far as Pronsk, burned Riazan and killed its prince. The chronicler describes what they did to captives: some were impaled or stretched, others shot with arrows, others tied with their hands behind their backs. Then the army moved on to Kolomna.
p.q: придоша отъ всточныя страны на Рязаньскую землю, лѣсомъ, безбожніи Татари, и почаша воевати Рязаньскую землю, и плѣноваху и до Проньска; поплѣнивше Рязань весь и пожгоша, и князя ихъ убиша, ихже емше овы растинахуть, другыя же стрѣлами растрѣляху въ ня, а ини опакы руцѣ связывахуть
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.t: the godless Tatars came from the eastern lands onto the Riazan land, through the forest, and began to make war on the Riazan land, and captured as far as Pronsk; having captured all Riazan they burned it, and killed their prince; of those they seized, some they stretched out, others they shot through with arrows, and others they bound with their hands behind them

p.h: Moscow shrunk after the Tartar fire of 1571
p.g: Possevino, who saw Moscow himself, says it had been larger and more crowded under the same tsar until the Tartars burned it 'in the seventieth year of this century', killing most of the inhabitants. Traces of the old, larger circuit were still visible, and the city now filled barely five miles round. He means the Crimean Tatar sack of Moscow in 1571.
p.q: Et erat sanè eodem hoc Principe augustior, ac numerosior Moscua, sed anno præsentis seculi septuagesimo à Tartaris cõcremata, incolis plerisq; incendio absumptis, res omnis in angustiores terminos adducta est. Extant vestigia maioris circuitus; vt qui octo, vel nouem fortasse fuisset, iam vix quinq; millia passuum impleat
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars (the raid of Khan Devlet Giray)
p.t: And Moscow was indeed grander and more populous under this same prince, but in the seventieth year of the present century it was burned down by the Tartars, most of its inhabitants consumed by the fire, and everything was reduced to narrower bounds. Traces of a larger circuit remain, so that what was perhaps eight or nine miles round now scarcely fills five thousand paces.
p.c: He gives the year as 1570; the raid was in May 1571. The damage and population figures are his estimates.

p.h: Bukhara: 'They came, they dug, they burned, they killed, they plundered, they left'
p.g: After telling how Bukhara's citadel was stormed and its walls levelled, Juvaini says a man who escaped reached Khorasan and was asked what had happened. His answer was six verbs. The clever men who heard it agreed that nothing more concise could be said in Persian, and Juvaini says his whole chapter is only a commentary on those few words.
p.q: گفت آمدند و کندند و سوختند و کشتند و بردند و رفتند جماعت زیرکان که این تقریر شنیدند اتفاق کردند که در پارسی موجزتر ازین سخن نتواند بود
p.s: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
p.t: He said: 'They came, they dug, they burned, they killed, they plundered, and they left.' The shrewd people who heard this account agreed that nothing could be said more concisely in Persian.
p.c: Juvaini reports what a survivor said; he was not at Bukhara in 1220. One stray OCR token has been dropped.

p.h: Moscow boasts of its stone walls and iron gates
p.g: When Tokhtamysh marched on Moscow, the townspeople burned their own suburbs so no timber or fence was left for the attackers. Some broke into the boyars' cellars, got drunk on mead and jeered from the walls that the Tatars could not stay long before 'a stone city with iron gates'. The Kremlin walls of white stone had been built in 1367. Four days later the Tatars took the city by a false peace.
p.q: И изношаху ис погребовъ меды господскія и упивахуся до пьяна, и шатающеся пьяни, глаголюще: «не устрашимся нахоженіа Татарьскаго, имѣемъ бо градъ каменъ твердъ и врата желѣзна; и не терпятъ Татарове стояти подъ градомъ нашимъ долго
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)
p.pe: Tokhtamysh's Tatars; the besieged people of Moscow
p.t: And they carried the lords' mead out of the cellars and drank themselves drunk, and reeling about drunk they said: 'We shall not fear the Tatar invasion, for we have a strong stone city and iron gates; and the Tatars will not bear to stand long under our city
p.tg: moscow kremlin stone walls siege tokhtamysh

p.h: Khanbaliq, with a cathedral beside the palace
p.g: Marignolli refuses even to try to describe the size, population and military order of the Khan's capital, the seat of the 'Empire of the East'. What he does describe is the Christian presence: a Franciscan cathedral right next to the imperial palace, an archbishopric, several other churches with bells, all supported from the Emperor's table. The city is the Yuan capital (Dadu) on the site of modern Beijing.
p.q: pervenimus in Cambalec, ubi est summa Sedes Imperii Orientis, de cujus magnitudine incredibili, & populo, ordine militum sileatur. … Habent etiam fratres Minores in Cambalec Ecclesiam Cathedralem immediate juxta pallacium, & solempnem Archiepiscopatum, & alias Ecclesias plures in civitate, & campanas, & omnes vivunt de mensa Imperatoris honorifice valde.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: The Tartar (Yuan) capital and its Franciscan community
p.t: We came to Khanbaliq, the chief seat of the Empire of the East; of its incredible size, its people and the order of its soldiers, let nothing be said. … The Friars Minor also have in Khanbaliq a cathedral church right next to the palace, and a solemn archbishopric, and several other churches in the city, with bells, and they all live very honourably at the Emperor's expense.

p.h: Batu's camp looked like a great city
p.g: Arriving at Batu's camp on the Volga, Rubruck was amazed: the ordu spread out like a city for three or four leagues, with every family knowing its place. He explains that orda means 'middle', because the court stands in the middle of the people, with its doors opening south. This is the moving 'city' of the steppe, the ancestor of the word 'horde'.
p.q: When I saw the ordu of Baatu, I was astonished, for it seemed like a great city stretched out about his dwelling, with people scattered all about for three or four leagues.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.tg: ordu horde batu camp golden horde

p.h: Kozelsk, the 'evil city'
p.g: Batu turned back from the road to Novgorod and besieged the small town of Kozelsk, whose prince was a boy. The townsmen held out for seven weeks, sallied out, cut up the siege engines and killed three sons of a 'temnik' (commander of ten thousand). The chronicle says that afterwards the Tatars would not call it Kozelsk but 'the evil city'.
p.q: Оттолѣ же въ Татарѣхъ не смѣяху его нарещи Козелескъ, но зваху его градъ злый, понеже бяше билися у города того по семъ недѣль, и убиша три сыны темничи, Татарове же искаша ихъ, и не обрѣтоша ихъ во множествѣ трупа мертвыхъ.
p.s: Continuation printed as the 'Troitskaia letopis' in PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols under Batu); townspeople of Kozelsk
p.t: From then on among the Tatars they did not dare to call it Kozelsk, but called it the evil city, because they had fought at that town for seven weeks, and three sons of a temnik were killed; the Tatars searched for them and did not find them among the multitude of dead bodies.
p.c: Not in the Laurentian codex itself but in the parallel text the 1846 editors printed after it. The 'evil city' name is a report of what the Tatars supposedly said.

p.h: Ak-Mechet: a Russian new town beside a walled Tatar town
p.g: Webster found Simferopol, 'called by the Tartars, Ak-Metchet', split in two: the part built by the Russians since the conquest, and what remained of the old Tatar town. In the Tatar quarter every house and yard was surrounded by a wall with no window facing the street, and women rarely appeared, always veiled.
p.q: Symferapol, called by the Tartars, Ak-Metchet … consists of two parts, that which has been erected by the Russians, since their possession of the Crimea, and that which remains from the ancient Tartar town. This latter part is dull, dirty, and disgusting: every Tartar house and yard being surrounded by a wall, and not having a single window looking into
p.s: James Webster
p.c: The sentence ends '... into the streets' on the next page. 'Disgusting' is Webster's own prejudice.
p.n: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma.
p.tg: simferopol ak-mechet walled courtyards town plan

p.h: Kholm: a new town that craftsmen fled to from the Tatars
p.g: Daniil founded Kholm on a wooded hill he spotted while hunting, and the chronicler notes that the Tatars could not take it when Batu conquered Rus. Daniil invited Germans, Rus, Poles and other foreigners, and young men and master craftsmen of every kind 'fled from the Tatars' to it: saddlers, bowyers, quiver makers, and smiths of iron, copper and silver. Here the arrow runs the other way: craftsmen leave Tatar-held lands to build a Rus prince's town.
p.q: нача призывати прихожаѣ Нѣмцѣ и Русь, иноязычникы и Ляхы; идяху день и во день, и уноты и мастеръ всяціи бѣжаху изъ Татаръ, сѣдлници, и лучници, и тулници, и кузници желѣзу и мѣди и сребру, и бѣ жизнь, и наполниша дворы окрестъ града поле и села
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Prince Daniil of Galicia; craftsmen fleeing the Tatars
p.t: he began to invite newcomers, Germans and Rus, foreigners and Poles; they came day after day, and young men and masters of every kind fled from the Tatars, saddlers and bowyers and quiver makers and smiths of iron and copper and silver, and there was life, and they filled the courtyards around the town, the fields and the villages

p.h: Sarai, the Horde's capital, and its ruins on the Akhtuba
p.g: In his survey of the towns of Kipchak, Hammer places Sarai, capital and residence of the khans, on the Akhtuba channel of the Volga, where ruins stretched forty versts into the steppe and at least ten versts along the river. He takes from the Persian historian Wassaf that Batu founded it, and from coins that there were several Sarais: the old and the new (the second only an extension of the first), with Gülistan apparently a suburb, and a third called Sali Serai. Elsewhere (p. 140 to 141) he says Batu built Sarai in his last years, as he had earlier built Kazan.
p.q: Serai, die Hauptstadt von Kiptschak und die Residenz der Chane der goldenen Horde, deren Ruinen vierzig Werste in der Steppe vom Ufer der Wolga, und wenigstens zehn Werste längs der Achtuba … Serai gab es, wie die Gepräge ausweisen, drey, das alte und neue, welches letzte nur ein Zubau des alten, so wie das auf Münzen häufig vorkommende Gülistan nur eine Vorstadt der Residenz Serai gewesen zu seyn scheint
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), drawing on Wassaf, coin evidence and Russian travellers (Lepechin, Wojeikof)
p.pl: Sarai, lower Volga (Akhtuba channel), Astrakhan and Volgograd regions, Russia
p.pe: Golden Horde (Jochid Mongols and their Kipchak subjects)
p.w: 13th to 14th centuries (ruins described by 18th and 19th century travellers)
p.t: Sarai, the capital of Kipchak and residence of the khans of the Golden Horde, whose ruins [lie] forty versts into the steppe from the bank of the Volga and at least ten versts along the Akhtuba … There were, as the coins show, three Sarais: the old and the new, the latter being only an extension of the old, just as Gülistan, which often appears on coins, seems to have been only a suburb of the residence Sarai
p.c: Hammer's scheme of several Sarais, and his claim of a Batu-built 'Sarai in the Crimea', were disputed by Fraehn, whose objections he prints in his notes.
p.tg: sarai capital ruins akhtuba batu coins

p.h: Arriving at Ayuki Khan's camp by Lake Manuto
p.g: After ten days' ride from Saratov the envoys reached the headquarters of Ayuki Khan, not a town but a camp 'at present' on the shore of a lake. The Torghut nobles, priests and chiefs lined the road with their followers, displayed their flocks and herds, set out tables of food, and knelt to offer provisions. The next day the envoys were received in the khan's 'great tent of ceremony'.
p.q: we at length arrived at the head-quarters of A-yu-ke, the Khan of the Tourgouth nation, which are situated at present upon the banks of the lake Ma-nu-to. … Their flocks and herds were also collected and displayed, and tables, covered with provisions, laid out before us. All the people had come out to a very considerable distance to meet us
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
p.pl: Lower Volga steppe (Kalmyk lands east of the Volga)
p.tg: ayuki khan kalmyks horde camp volga

p.h: Sultaniyeh, a royal city founded by Hulagu's descendants
p.g: Passing Sultaniyeh, Chardin saw fine public buildings, about 3,000 houses and vast ruins of churches, mosques and towers stretching west. Some said no one knew its founder; others said Arghun Khan, grandson of Hulagu, laid its foundations and his son finished it and named it 'the Royal City'. He adds on the same page that it was later wrecked by Tamerlane and by other Turkish and Tartar princes.
p.q: Others on the other side affirm, that the foundations of it were laid when the Sun was in Leo, by the order, and in the Reign of Ergon Can, the Son of Abkei-Can, and Grand-child of Halacou-Can; and that because it could not be finish'd in his days, his Son Jangou-Sultan compleated the work and call'd it Sultania, or the Royal City.
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.c: Chardin gives competing traditions about the founder; he saw the ruins himself.

p.h: The fall and sack of Canton, 1650
p.g: Nieuhof tells how the Tartar army took Canton after a siege that, he says, lasted a whole year, helped by a bribed Chinese governor who opened a gate. Two Dutch gunners married to Chinese women had helped the defenders. The sack that followed lasted weeks. He arrived five years later, so this is what the townspeople told him.
p.q: It was upon the 24. of November, in the year 1650. when the Tartars upon this advantage rushed with their whole Army into the City … The whole Tartar Army being got into the City, the place was soon turned to a Map of misery … there was heard no other cry in the Streets, but Strike, Kill, and Destroy the Rebellious Barbarians
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

p.h: Sarai: a new city of merchants and the Turkish slave trade
p.g: Abu'l-Fida's entry on Seray (Sarai), capital of 'the states of Berke', says the present ruler is Uzbek, that the city lies in a plain on the Volga north-west of the Caspian, and that merchants crowd there and do a great trade in Turkish slaves. He calls it a modern city, founded by a descendant of Chinggis Khan named Sain Batu, and adds day-length information from a man of the city.
p.q: Le prince qui règne en ce moment s'appelle Uzbek. La situation de Seray est en plaine, au nord-ouest de la mer Caspienne … C'est un lieu très-fréquenté des marchands, et il s'y fait un grand commerce d'esclaves turks. La ville est d'origine moderne. On en attribue la fondation à un descendant de Djenguiz-Khan, appelé Saïn-Batou.
p.s: Abu'l-Fida (French translation by J. T. Reinaud, 1848)
p.t: The prince now reigning is called Uzbek. Sarai lies in a plain, north-west of the Caspian Sea … It is a place much visited by merchants, and there is a great trade there in Turkish slaves. The town is of recent origin; its founding is attributed to a descendant of Chinggis Khan called Sain Batu.
p.c: The entry opens on the previous page ('Seray, capitale des états de Berké'). Abu'l-Fida never went there; he cites a man from Sarai.
p.tg: sarai batu uzbek khan slave trade golden horde

p.h: The Crimean Tatars burn Moscow, 1571
p.g: Writing to Lord Burghley from Kholmogory in August 1571, Jenkinson lists Russia's woes: famine, the Tsar's executions, plague, and then the Crimean Tatars, who in late May routed the Tsar's army and set Moscow on fire. He reports that not one house was left standing and that more than 300,000 were said to have been burned or carried off as captives. The figures are hearsay, but the event is real.
p.q: a valyante natyon of Tartars, in the latter ende of May laste, inuadid this realme, gaue the Prynce an ouerthrowe in the feildes, cawsed him to retyre, burnte and consumed all the countrye before theim, and came to the cyttye of Musko, sett fyer one the same, not leauinge one house standinge
p.s: Anthony Jenkinson, letter to Lord Burghley, 8 August 1571 (ed. E. Delmar Morgan and C. H. Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars under Khan Devlet Giray
p.c: Jenkinson arrived after the fire and repeats reported numbers; he calls it 'a juste punyshment of God for such a wycked natyon' (the Russians).

p.h: Kazan: remains of the Tatar khanate in the Kremlin
p.g: Rose describes Kazan's fortress as still holding many remains of Tatar rule, which flourished there for three centuries until Ivan IV took the city in 1552, destroyed it and built a new one. A tower was still named after the wife of the last khan. On the same page he says the Russians lived in the city proper and the Tatars in the suburbs (slobody), making up about a third of Kazan's people.
p.q: In der Festung sieht man noch viele Ueberreste der Tatarischen Herrschaft, die in Kasan in einem besonderen unabhängigen Chanate drei Jahrhunderte lang geblüht hat, bis sie durch den Grossfürsten Joann Wassiljewitsch gestürzt ward, der die Stadt im Jahre 1552 einnahm, sie von Grund aus zerstörte, und eine neue an ihrer Stelle aufbaute. Ein alter Thurm heisst noch die Sunibeka nach der Gemahlin des letzten Tatarischen Chans.
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.t: In the fortress one still sees many remains of Tatar rule, which flourished in Kazan for three centuries in a separate, independent khanate, until it was overthrown by Grand Prince Ivan Vasilyevich, who took the city in 1552, destroyed it from the ground up and built a new one in its place. An old tower is still called the Sunibeka after the wife of the last Tatar khan.
p.c: The Söyembikä tower's date is disputed; many historians think it was built after the Russian conquest.

p.h: Bakhchysarai, the Tartar capital in its valley
p.g: Riding south past Tatar cottages with minaret-shaped chimneys and the domed tombs of the khans, Alexander looked down on Bakhchysarai, the old capital of the Crimean khans. He describes flat-roofed, tiled houses filling a narrow valley and climbing its sides, with the palace in the middle. On the next page he walks streets lined with workshops where Tatar tailors, smiths, shoemakers and saddlers sat cross-legged, smoking as they worked.
p.q: we saw beneath us the singular and romantic Tartar capital of the Crimea. Buckteserai, the Palatium of Strabo, is seated in a narrow valley, through which runs the stream of the Tchuruksu. The flat-roofed and tile-covered houses are built in the bottom of the valley, and up the sides of the hills : in the midst of them is a most interesting object, viz. the Tartar Palace.
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: Identifying the town with Strabo's 'Palatium' is a scholarly guess of his time.

p.h: The ruins of 'Saroff Gorod'
p.g: About forty Russian miles below Tsaritsyn Perry notes the ruins of a large city called 'Saroff Gorod', said to have been the ancient seat of a 'Scythian King'. The name points to Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde on the Akhtuba, though Perry does not connect it with the Tartars at all. Pallas (W005) describes the same brick ruins in detail.
p.q: …there is to be seen the Ruins of a large City, call'd Saroff Gorod, in a very pleasant Situation, and which is said to have been the ancient Residence of a Scythian King.
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.pe: unnamed builders; Perry reports 'a Scythian King'
p.c: He gives only a report ('is said'); the identification with Sarai is ours, not his.

p.h: The 'Tartar town' of Peking was first built by the Mongols
p.g: As the mission reached the walls of Peking, Klaproth added a note on the history of the 'Tartar town', the northern inner city where the Manchu garrison lived. It was first walled by the Mongols in 1267 with eleven gates; the Ming cut it down to nine gates, which is why its governor was called governor of the nine gates. So the 'Tartar' city of Beijing was a Mongol Yuan foundation reshaped by the Chinese Ming.
p.q: the Mongols, in 1267; it was then sixty li in circumference, and had eleven gates. The first emperor of the dynasty of Ming took off five li from its northern side, and took away two of the gates, so that only nine remained. It is for this reason that the governor of the Tartar town bears the title of governor of the nine gates.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (editor's footnote in the 1827 English translation)
p.c: An editor's footnote drawn from Chinese sources; the first words of the sentence are on the previous page (n337).
p.tg: beijing khanbaliq city walls yuan ming

p.h: Kublai builds Taidu (Beijing) beside the old city
p.g: Polo explains that Kublai, warned by astrologers that the old city of Cambaluc would rebel, built a new, square city called Taidu (Dadu, the core of later Beijing) right beside it and moved the people there. He gives its walls as 24 miles round, of rammed earth ten paces thick. Yule's notes compare the plan with the Beijing of his own day and adjust the figures.
p.q: So he caused the present city to be built close beside the old one, with only a river between them. And he caused the people of the old city to be removed to the new town that he had founded ; and this is called Taidu. … it is all walled round with walls of earth which have a thickness of full ten paces at bottom
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.c: Polo's measurements are too large; Yule's survey-based estimate is about 18 miles round. The city was designed and built by Chinese and other craftsmen for the Mongol court.
p.tg: beijing dadu taidu khanbaliq earthen walls planned city

p.h: Peking's walls under the Khitan, Jin and Mongols
p.g: Answering a French author who claimed Peking was founded by Khubilai in 1267, a Peking missionary traces its walls through Chinese annals: 36 li round with eight gates as the Khitan southern capital, 75 li under the Jin, then six leagues and eleven gates when the Mongol Yuan 'repaired its ruins' in 1274. Here the northern conquerors rebuild an old Chinese city rather than create one.
p.q: Pe-king n'avoit alors que trente-six li de tour … & huit portes. Sous les Kin, dont il fut aussi la Capitale, il eut soixante-quinze li de tour, ou sept lieues & demie. Les Yuen, qui le nommerent d'abord la Capitale du milieu puis la grande Capitale, ne lui donnerent que six lieues de tour & onze portes, lorsqu'ils en reparerent les ruines en 1274.
p.s: Anonymous Peking missionary writing in the voice of a Chinese scholar (Remarques sur un écrit de M. P**, Mémoires vol. 2, 1777)
p.t: Peking was then only thirty-six li round … with eight gates. Under the Kin, whose capital it also was, it was seventy-five li round, or seven and a half leagues. The Yuan, who first named it the Middle Capital and then the Great Capital, gave it only six leagues round and eleven gates when they repaired its ruins in 1274.
p.c: The figures come from Chinese geographical annals as the writer reads them; the Yuan in fact built a largely new city (Dadu) beside the old site.

p.h: Chen-hai's town of Chinese craftsmen
p.g: North of the snowy mountains lay T'ien Chen-hai ba-la-ho-sun (balgasun, the diarist explains, means city), a granary town nicknamed 'the head of the magazines', where Chinese artisans and two concubines of the Jin emperor Zhangzong turned out to greet the sage, and Changchun was surprised to see farming in the desert. Bretschneider's note, from the Yuan shi, says Chinggis had founded a military colony and built a city here, settling over 300 families from Western Asia to weave gold brocade and 300 from Kaifeng to make woollen cloth, under Chen-hai, the chancellor Chinqai whom Carpini later met. Before moving on, the sage's followers built a monastery there in under a month, 'the rich with money and the workmen with their labour' (p.61).
p.q: a number of Chinamen, artisans and workmen, who lived there … came in procession to see the master. They were all ravished; met him with exclamations of joy, bowed before him, and accompanied him with variegated umbrellas and fragrant flowers. There were also two concubines of the Kin emperor, Chang tsung, and the mother of a Chinese princess, who met the master with exclamations and tears.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pl: Western Mongolia (between the Khangai and the Altai)
p.pe: Chinese artisans and captives under Chinqai, Chinggis's official
p.c: The numbers of brocade weavers and cloth makers come from Bretschneider's note citing the Yuan shi, not from the diary. The town's site is uncertain.
p.tg: captives artisans military colony granary chinqai

p.h: Kazan's Tatar suburbs and their stone mosques
p.g: Georgi describes the Tatars as a large part of Kazan's population, living in two suburbs (slobodas). The first had two fine stone mosques whose minarets, he says, were built in the same style as those among the ruins of Bolghar; the second had two wooden mosques and was founded about a century earlier by Tatars who preferred leaving Kazan to suffering restrictions on their worship.
p.q: Die Stadttataren wohnen in zwey Vorstädten oder Sloboden … Die erste hat zwey schöne steinerne Metscheden, deren Thürme (Mesgir) von der Bauart der unter den Ruinen von Bolghari befindlichen sind. … Die zweyte Slobode hat 2 hölzerne Metscheds. Sie entstand fast vor 100 Jahren, da sich die Tataren in ihren Religionsübungen beeinträchtigt glaubten und lieber aus Kasan ziehen, als leiden wollten.
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: The town Tatars live in two suburbs or slobodas … The first has two fine stone mosques, whose towers (minarets) are of the same style as those found among the ruins of Bolghar. … The second sloboda has two wooden mosques. It arose almost 100 years ago, when the Tatars felt their religious practice was being restricted and preferred to move out of Kazan rather than suffer it.

p.h: New Russian towns on Tatar land
p.g: After Yermak's death the Russians returned, built the fort of Tyumen and then the fortresses of Tobolsk, Tara and others (previous page). Coxe sums up the following century bluntly: the Tartars were subdued or wiped out, and new towns and colonies went up everywhere. In his account the Siberian towns were new Russian foundations, not inherited 'Tartar' cities.
p.q: The Russians pushed their conquest far and wide: wherever they appeared, the Tartars were either reduced or exterminated. New towns were built and colonies were planted on all sides. Before a century had well elapsed, all that vast tract of country now called Siberia … was annexed to the Russian dominions.
p.s: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars and other native peoples
p.c: The previous page lists the forts as Tumen, Tobolsk, 'Sungur' (probably a scan error for Surgut) and Tara.

p.h: Sarai, 'the new town that Baatu is making'
p.g: On his way home Rubruck asked about his lost books and vestments. Coiac, an official of Batu's son Sartach, said he had left them near Sarai, a town Batu was then building on the Volga. It is a rare contemporary glimpse of the founding of the Golden Horde's capital, and Rubruck later travelled south toward it.
p.q: I left your things at my father's, who stays near Sarai, the new town that Baatu is making on the Etilia
p.s: Coiac, an official of Sartach, as reported by William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.tg: sarai golden horde batu new town volga

p.h: The Dzungar 'Tartars' storm Lhasa, 1717
p.g: Wessels summarises Desideri's eyewitness chapters on the Dzungar invasion. Invited by the discontented great monasteries, 'the Tartar king' of Independent Tartary sent 6,000 men under Tsering Dondup, who reached Lhasa in late 1717; on the night of 30 November the gates were opened to them by allies inside. Lhazang Khan ('Ginghes Khang') fled to the Potala, and the same page says the city was then plundered for two days. Desideri was at Sera monastery and lost only a few things left with the Capuchins.
p.q: At their instance the Tartar king crossed into Tibet in 1717 with an army of 6,000 men under the command of General Zze-ring-ton-drup … in the night of November 30 a general assault on Lhasa was delivered the gates were thrown open by their confederates. In a couple of hours there was nothing left for Ginghes Khang but to seek safety in the Potala Palace.
p.s: C. Wessels (1924), summarising Ippolito Desideri's eyewitness account
p.pe: Dzungar Mongols ('the Tartar king' and his army)
p.c: A summary, not Desideri's own words; Wessels notes that other histories (Waddell) tell the story differently.

p.h: A ruined city of the Tartar king 'Utai-chan'
p.g: On 10 October 1693 the caravan reached a large, old, deserted city called Taimingzinz, with two sealed towers, fallen masonry, and life-size stone statues of people and idols and huge stone lions, all carved so true to life that, Brand says, few such are found in Europe. The Chinese told him a Tartar king named Utai-chan had ruled there centuries before, until a Chinese king took it and drove the Tartar out; stone towers on the hills, they said, marked Tartar graves.
p.q: Den 10 Octobris kamen wir an eine grosse, alte und verwüstete Stadt Taimingzinz genannt, in derselben stehen 2. Thürme … Die Chineser erzehlten, daß dieser Ort vor viel 100. Jahren, als zur selben Zeit ein Tartarischer König, Utaichan genannt, allda regieret, durch einen Chinesischen König erobert, und der Tartar vertrieben worden
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (between the Nen River and the Great Wall)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols) as remembered by Chinese informants
p.t: On 10 October we came to a great, old and ruined city called Taimingzinz, in which stand two towers … The Chinese told us that this place, many hundreds of years ago, when a Tartar king called Utaichan reigned there, was conquered by a Chinese king and the Tartar driven out
p.c: Brand saw the ruins; the story of Utai-chan is what his Chinese guides told him.
p.tg: ruined city towers statues tartar king

p.h: No towns on the Ili until the emperor built one for exiles
p.g: The next note says the banks of the Ili had long been the favourite home of the Eleuth kings, but 'there were no towns': they camped in tents, moving from place to place. After the conquest the emperor had a town built there that grew daily, and it had become the place of exile for Chinese and Tartars convicted of crimes.
p.q: Les bords de la riviere d'Ily ont été depuis long-temps le séjour de prédilection des Rois des Eleuths. Il n'y avoit point de villes. Ils y campoient sous des tentes, tantôt dans un endroit & tantôt dans un autre. L'Empereur y a fait bâtir une ville qui devient chaque jour plus peuplée. C'est-là qu'on envoie aujourd'hui & les Chinois & les Tartares qui ont mérité la peine de l'exil.
p.s: Joseph-Marie Amiot (note to the Eleuth monument)
p.t: The banks of the Ili river had long been the favourite residence of the Eleuth kings. There were no towns. They camped there in tents, now in one place, now in another. The Emperor has had a town built there which grows more populous every day. It is there that Chinese and Tartars who have deserved the penalty of exile are now sent.
p.tg: ili new town exile qing dzungars

p.h: Ögedei puts walls round the camp at Karakorum, 1235
p.g: The Chinese annals record that in spring 1235 Ögedei ordered walls built around the encampment of Holin (Karakorum) and a palace called Wan'an five li round. Gaubil elsewhere in the book says Holin is the Caracoram of other writers. It is a precise date for when the Mongol camp-capital became a walled town.
p.q: Au Printemps de l'an 1235 L'Empereur Ogotay ordonna de revêtir de murailles le campement de Holin, & de faire de cinq lis de tour le palais appellé Ouangan.
p.s: Antoine Gaubil, translating the Chinese annals
p.t: In the spring of the year 1235 the Emperor Ögedei ordered the camp of Holin to be enclosed with walls, and the palace called Ouangan to be made five li in circumference.

p.h: Ruins of a Mongol city on the Kerulen: 'the City of the Tyger'
p.g: In Khalkha country Grosier places 'Karakum', seat of Chinggis Khan's empire, and describes ruins on the north bank of the Kerulen: a square city about two leagues round, built by the Mongol successors of Kublai Khan, with foundations, bits of wall and two half-ruined 'pyramids' (probably stupas or towers) still standing. The locals called it Para-hotun. Ruined cities here are credited to the Yuan emperors.
p.q: On the northern side of it are seen the ruins of a large city, built by the Mogul successors of the famous Coblai-kan ; this city was square, and about two leagues in circumference; its foundations, some pieces of the walls, and two pyramids
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols; ruins left by the Yuan (Kublai's successors)
p.c: Taken from Jesuit survey reports. The sentence ends on the next page: 'half in ruins, still subsist; it was called Para-hotun, or The City of the Tyger' (n198).

p.h: Mud-walled towns that last because it rarely rains
p.g: Muraviev lists the five towns of the khanate, with New Urgench larger and busier than Khiva itself. All were walled, but their buildings were mean and made almost entirely of mud, with walls faced with stone only here and there. They survived for years only because so little rain fell.
p.q: The buildings in all the above towns are very mean (the only ones approaching to anything like size being a few mosques), and mud is the almost universal material of the houses, as it may also be said to be that of the town walls … In spite of this perishable material, the buildings stand for many years, owing to the very scanty rain fall.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.pl: Khiva khanate (New Urgench, Shavat, Kat, Gurlen)
p.pe: Sarts, Uzbeks and Turkmens of Khiva

p.h: When the Crimean Tartars burned Moscow
p.g: Perry recalls that the Crimean Tartars once penetrated to the heart of Russia and burned Moscow, and that the tsars had been forced to pay tribute and even to agree to hold the khan's stirrup if they met. Perry's date is wrong by a century: Khan Devlet Giray burned Moscow in 1571. The tribute to the Crimean khans was indeed paid until the 1680s to 1700.
p.q: The said Tartars were formerly victorious against the Russes. They have often penetrated into the Heart of Russia, and in Anno 1671, they burnt the City of Mosco, and by the Articles of Peace … the Russes were obliged to submit to very scandalous Terms; not only to be tributary to the said Tartars, but even … that the Czar's of Russia should hold the Stirrup to the Great Cham,
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.c: Perry's year 1671 is a mistake for 1571. The stirrup clause is what he was told.

p.h: Why part of Beijing was called the Tartar city
p.g: Staunton describes Beijing as two walled cities side by side. The northern and larger one, with the imperial palace at its centre, was called the Tartar city; he explains the name by its being laid out anew under the first Tartar (Mongol) dynasty in the thirteenth century. The page after describes the 'Chinese city' adjoining its southern wall, half empty and partly under cultivation.
p.q: The principal part of it is called the Tartar city, from the circumstance of having been laid out anew in the thirteenth century in the time of the first Tartar dynasty. It is in the form of a parallelogram … in the centre of which is the imperial palace, occupying within the yellow wall at least one square mile.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.c: The origin of the name is Staunton's explanation; other European writers tied 'Tartar city' to the Manchu banner garrison that lived there under the Qing.
p.tg: beijing tartar city walls yuan palace

p.h: Karakorum: an earthen rampart, for stone is scarce
p.g: Polo calls Karakorum a city about three miles round, enclosed by an earthen rampart because stone was scarce, with a citadel and a governor's palace, and 'the first city that the Tartars possessed'. Yule's note adds that Ögedei built its walls and palace in 1234, and quotes Rubruck's famous verdict that apart from the palace it was no better than the village of St Denis.
p.q: Caracoron is a city of some three miles in compass. [It is surrounded by a strong earthen rampart, for stone is scarce there. And beside it there is a great citadel wherein is a fine palace in which the Governor resides.] 'Tis the first city that the Tartars possessed after they issued from
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871; square brackets mark Yule's additions from other manuscripts)
p.c: Polo may never have visited Karakorum himself; the bracketed description comes from the Ramusio version only.
p.n: Sentence continues on p.204 ('their own country').

p.h: Turkistan after the Tatars: nothing but ruins
p.g: The editor quotes the fourteenth-century Arab geographer Shihab al-Din (al-Umari), who was told by a traveller that the land had been ruined 'by the arms of the Tatars'. From a distance a village looks well built, but up close its houses are empty, and the people are now all herders. Elias adds that the towns had been built by earlier settled peoples such as the Uighurs and Kara-Khitai, before the Mongol nomads made it their home.
p.q: Since the region has been devastated by the arms of the Tatars," he writes, "it is inhabited only by a scanty population. According to what I have been assured by a man who has travelled through the country, there is nothing to be seen in Turkistan but ruins, and more or less obliterated remains.
p.s: Shihab al-Din (al-Umari), Masalik al-Absar, quoted in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols) and the nomads who followed them
p.c: Hearsay at two removes, quoted from Quatremère's French translation.

p.h: Kasimov, the old seat of Tatar khans
p.g: Pallas notes that the Russian town of Kasimov is built entirely of logs, even its streets are paved with timber, although good building stone lies all along the Oka. The Tatar rulers who once lived here did use the stone, and he found the remains of their court: a gate with Arabic inscriptions, a long stone residence and a mausoleum. The descendants of the old Tatar townspeople still lived in their own quarter as prosperous fur traders.
p.q: Zu denen Zeiten, da Kasimof noch der Wohnplatz Tatarischer Beherrscher gewesen, hat man diesen Vorrath von Steinen nicht völlig so ungebraucht gelassen, und die Stadt hat noch izt schöne Ueberbleibsel tatarischer Gebäude aufzuweisen, welche erhalten zu werden verdienten. … Dieser Platz scheint würklich das Hoflager der hiesigen Chane gewesen zu seyn
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Tatars of Kasimov (the Kasimov khanate on the Oka)
p.t: In the days when Kasimov was still the residence of Tatar rulers, this store of stone was not left so wholly unused, and the town still has fine remains of Tatar buildings which deserve to be preserved. … This place really seems to have been the court of the local khans.

p.h: Ogedei throws open the treasury of his new capital
p.g: Among the anecdotes of Ogedei's generosity, Rashid says that while Karakorum (Qara Qorum) was being founded the khan found about twenty thousand silver ingots (balish) piled in the treasury and saw no point in hoarding them. He had it announced that anyone who wanted balish could come and take it. The story assumes a real city with a population of rich and poor, nobles and commoners.
p.q: دیکر بوقت آنك قرا قوروم‌را بنیاد فرموده بود روزی بخزانه در آمد و قرب دو تومان بالش دید فرمود که از اذخار این مارا چه فایده … اهل شهر از شریف و وضیع توانکر و درویش روی بخزانه آوردند و هر کسی نصیبی وافر یافتند
p.s: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
p.t: Another story: at the time when he had ordered Qara Qorum to be founded, one day he went into the treasury and saw nearly two tumans [some twenty thousand] of balish [silver ingots]. He said: 'What use to us is hoarding this?' … The people of the city, noble and humble, rich and poor, made for the treasury, and every one of them found a generous share.
p.c: A moralising anecdote about the khan's generosity, taken over from Juvaini, not an eyewitness report.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled).

p.h: Baghdad forty years on: mostly ruined, still crowded, ruled by Tartars
p.g: Riccoldo lived in Baghdad and describes it after the Mongol conquest: the city is 'for the most part destroyed' yet still full of people, with many thousands of Christians and Jews and over two hundred thousand Muslims, all under Tartar lordship. He also found its Muslim colleges and Sufi houses thriving and admired their scholars.
p.q: In ipsa quidem ciuitate, licet sit pro maiori parte destructa, est tamen maxima multitudo populi in ea. Nam preter Christianos et Iudeos, qui sunt ibi multa milia, sunt ibi vltra ducenta milia Sarracenorum, vt probabiliter creditur; omnes tamen sunt sub dominio Tartarorum.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.pe: Tartars (Ilkhanid rulers); Muslims, Christians and Jews of Baghdad
p.t: In that city, although it is for the most part destroyed, there is nevertheless a very great multitude of people. For besides Christians and Jews, who are many thousands there, there are more than two hundred thousand Saracens, as is plausibly believed; yet all are under the lordship of the Tartars.
p.c: Population figures are his estimate ('as is plausibly believed').

p.h: The fall of Várad: stone-throwers, a new wall, a burning cathedral
p.g: Roger was a canon at Várad and had just had the damaged castle repaired with a broad new wall; he himself fled to the woods. He describes the castle's ditches and wooden towers on the walls. The Tartars set up seven stone-throwing machines against the new wall and battered it day and night until it fell. The noblewomen who had fled into the cathedral were burned inside it.
p.q: Nam magnis munitum erat fossatis, et turribus ligneis super muros, et multi loricati milites erant ibi … Et castrum illico circumdantes, ex opposito ad murum nouum septem machinas posuerunt, et die noctuque cum eis emittere lapides, quousque nouus murus dirutus est ex toto, nullatenus cessauerunt. … Et quia kathedralem ecclesiam subito intrare nequiuerunt, igne apposito ecclesiam et dominas, et quidquid erat in ecclesia combusserunt.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: For it was fortified with great ditches and wooden towers on the walls, and many knights in mail were there … And at once surrounding the castle, they set up seven machines facing the new wall, and did not stop hurling stones with them day and night until the new wall was completely thrown down. … And because they could not quickly get into the cathedral church, they set fire to it and burned the church, the ladies and whatever was in the church.
p.c: Roger saw the defences, having had the new wall built himself, but fled to the woods before the final assault; the fall of the castle and the burning of the cathedral are reported from survivors.

p.h: Batu at Kiev: creaking carts, bellowing camels, walls battered day and night
p.g: In his introduction Sreznevsky quotes the Hypatian (Galician-Volhynian) Chronicle's famous account of Batu's siege of Kiev to show the old Russian epic style. The Tatar host was so large that nothing could be heard in the city for the creaking of carts, the bellowing of camels and the neighing of horses. Batu set up siege engines by the Polish Gate and battered the walls day and night until they fell. It shows the Horde as a besieger of cities, with engineers and machines.
p.q: Приде Батый Кыеву въ силѣ тяжьцѣ... И бѣ Батый у города, и отроци его обсѣдяху градъ, и не бѣ слышати отъ гласа скрипанія телѣгъ его, множества ревѣнія вельблудъ его, и рьжанія отъ гласа стадъ конь его... Постави же Батый порокы городу подлѣ вратъ Лядьскыхъ … Порокомъ же беспрестани бьющимъ день и нощь, выбиша стѣны.
p.s: Hypatian (Galician-Volhynian) Chronicle, quoted by I. I. Sreznevsky in his 1858 introduction
p.t: Batu came to Kiev in heavy force... And Batu was at the city, and his warriors besieged the city, and nothing could be heard for the creaking of his carts, the bellowing of his many camels and the neighing of his herds of horses... Batu set up siege engines against the city by the Polish Gate … The engines battering without cease day and night broke down the walls.
p.c: The chronicle was compiled in Galicia-Volhynia some decades after 1240; Sreznevsky quotes it only as a stylistic parallel.

p.h: Samarkand, 'Ornament of the Face of the Earth'
p.g: Wolff describes Samarkand, Timur's old capital, as a clay-walled town of 40,000 people with a palace, marble houses, mosques, colleges and Timur's tomb. He adds stories that Chinese once lived there making paper from silk, and that the city took its name from a conqueror called Samar.
p.q: It has a wall of clay, and forty thousand inhabitants; a beautiful palace, and many houses of marble; many mosques and colleges. It was formerly inhabited by Chinese, who manufactured paper of silk; and it once had the name of Bokhara-Tsheen, but received the present name from the conqueror Samar, after Christ 643. Oologh Beyk erected there an observatory.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.c: Wolff did not describe visiting Samarkand on this journey; the name story and the Chinese paper-makers are traditions he repeats.
p.tg: samarkand timur clay walls marble paper

p.h: Bukhara, 'twice the size of Moscow', in Great Tartary
p.g: The Relation opens by noting that geographers count Bukharia as part of Great Tartary, because 'the Tartars, or rather the Kalmyks' had invaded part of it; the author insists it is a separate state, just as China remained China under its Tartar conquerors. Great Bukharia has several towns, each with its own khan, of which Bukhara is said to be twice as large as Moscow.
p.q: Les Géographes regardent ordinairement la Boucharie, comme faisant partie de la Grande Tartarie. En effet les Tartares, ou pour mieux dire les Calmuques, en ont envahi une partie … Il y a plusieurs Villes dans la Grande Boucharie, & elles ont chacune son Cham, ou Régent. Les principales sont: Bouchara, qu'on dit être deux fois plus grande que la ville de Moscou en Russie
p.s: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie' printed in the atlas
p.t: Geographers usually regard Bukharia as part of Great Tartary. Indeed the Tartars, or rather the Kalmyks, have invaded part of it … There are several towns in Great Bukharia, and each has its own khan or regent. The chief ones are Bukhara, which is said to be twice as large as the city of Moscow in Russia
p.c: The author says he knew Little Bukharia at first hand but reports Great Bukharia (Bukhara) from hearsay ('qu'on dit').

p.h: Khubilai 'built four great cities'
p.g: The chronicle credits Khubilai, who took the throne in 1260, with building four great cities: Daidu (Beijing), Chagan (Chagan Balgasun), Huriyetu and Lanfin (Kaiping, the later Shangdu), and with appointing able prefects. For this Mongol author, the khans were founders of cities, not tent-dwellers only.
p.q: Er erbaute vier grosse Städte: die Stadt Täitu, die Stadt C'agan, die Stadt Hnriyet'u und die Stadt Lanfin, er- nannte tüchtige Männer zu Präfekten
p.s: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
p.t: He built four great cities: the city of Daidu, the city of Chagan, the city of Huriyetu and the city of Lanfin, and appointed capable men as prefects.
p.c: Written more than five centuries later; the identification of all four cities is not certain.

p.h: Who built Kashlyk, the Tatar capital of Sibir
p.g: The chronicle credits a Tatar ruler, Mamet, with founding the town of Kashlyk at the mouth of the little Sibirka river after defeating a khan of Kazan. From this town, it says, the whole land took the name Sibir. The author says he took this from a 'Muslim history', meaning Tatar tradition.
p.q: Маметь царь казанскаго царя Алима побѣдилъ, и на усть рѣчки Сибирки градъ Кашлыкъ учинилъ, царство въ Сибири распространивъ и поддани учинилъ; и оттолѣ нача славнѣе зватися Сибирь и цари, ихъ же бусурманская исторія повѣдаетъ.
p.s: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 17 (1880 printed text)
p.t: Tsar Mamet defeated Alim, tsar of Kazan, and built the town of Kashlyk at the mouth of the little river Sibirka, spreading his realm in Siberia and making subjects; and from then Siberia and its tsars began to be more famous, as the Muslim history tells.
p.c: The chronicler reports Tatar tradition second-hand; Kashlyk is the town known in other sources as Isker or Sibir.
p.tg: kashlyk isker sibir founding siberian tatars

p.h: Nishapur levelled by the Tartars
p.g: Fraser retells, from Persian histories via Pétis de la Croix, how Genghis Khan's son Tolui took Nishapur after three days, plundered it, killed or enslaved the people, and levelled the site so that a horse could ride over it without stumbling. He openly doubts the historians' death toll of 1,747,000.
p.q: the Tartars having found means to enter the place after a siege of only three days, spent a day and night in plundering it, and in massacring and reducing to slavery its wretched and defenceless inhabitants; the city was razed, and the ground on which it stood levelled so completely, that it is said a horse might have ridden over the whole site without stumbling
p.s: James Baillie Fraser, following historians quoted by Pétis de la Croix
p.pe: Mongols (called Tartars) under Tolui, son of Genghis Khan
p.c: Based on later Persian histories; Fraser himself rejects the huge casualty figure.
p.tg: nishapur mongol conquest tolui massacre genghis khan

p.h: A city made of tents around a living Buddha
p.g: The Khalkha Mongols revered a lama called the Hutuktu, a 'living Fo' (Buddha), brother of one of their khans, who had built a costly temple of yellow glazed bricks on the Tula with workmen from Beijing; the Oirat ruler Galdan destroyed it in 1688. Now the Hutuktu lived in tents, and his camp drew Russian traders, monks from India, Pegu, Tibet and China, and lamas of every rank: 'a large City made of Tents'.
p.q: One may call it a large City made of Tents, the Hurry being much greater there than any where else in this Part of Tartary. The Russians of Selinghinskoy, which is not far distant, trade thither; there you meet also with Bonzas from Indostan, Pegu, Tibet, and China
p.s: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)
p.pl: Iben river, northern Mongolia (near the Selenga)
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols and their Hutuktu (Jebtsundamba Khutuktu)
p.c: The Jesuits boast of rebuking the lama to his face, and their account of Mongol Buddhism is hostile.
p.tg: ordu tent city hutuktu lamas trade

p.h: Who pulled down Madzhar
p.g: When Klaproth arrived only two burial chapels were left. He explains that nearby colonists tore the ruins down for bricks, and that Count Paul Potemkin had most of what remained demolished to build the fortress-town of Yekaterinograd; peasants carried off the rest, and inscribed stones ended up in their yards.
p.q: The destruction of these remains of antiquity has been occasioned chiefly by the settlement of several colonies, which have established themselves in this neighbourhood, and have pulled them down for the sake of the serviceable bricks. Their total demolition, however, is to be ascribed more particularly to Count Paul Ssergeitsch Potemkin, who ordered the greatest part of the buildings remaining in his time to be taken down
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
p.pe: Russian and Armenian settlers; Count P. S. Potemkin

p.h: Yermak enters an empty capital
p.g: After routing Kuchum's army on the Irtysh, Yermak marched on Sibir, 'the residence of the Tartar princes', expecting a hard fight. Instead the news of the defeat had emptied it; he rode in and sat on the Khan's throne unopposed, and neighbouring peoples came in to swear allegiance and pay tribute.
p.q: delay to Sibir, the residence of the Tartar princes … But the news of the late defeat had diffused universal consternation, and Sibir was entirely deserted … he himself soon after made his triumphant entry, and seated himself upon the throne without the least opposition.
p.s: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller and J. E. Fischer)
p.c: Based on Siberian chronicles written decades later from the conquerors' side.
p.n: OCR normalized; printed margin notes omitted.

p.h: Sarai, an Islamic city built by Khan Berke
p.g: Ibn Arabshah names Sarai as the throne city of the Dasht and calls it 'a city of Islamic building, of marvellous structure'. Khan Berke, he says, built it when he became a Muslim and made it his royal seat. Just before this he laments that today, from Khwarazm to Crimea, nothing stirs of those peoples, and only gazelles and camels are left.
p.q: وتحت الدشت سراي وهي مدينة اسلامية البنيان بديعة الاركان … وكان السلطان بركه رحمه الله لما اسلم بناها واتخذها دار الملك واصطفاها
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.t: The throne of the Dasht is Sarai, a city of Islamic building and marvellous structure … Sultan Berke, may God have mercy on him, built it when he became a Muslim, and took it as the seat of kingship and chose it.
p.c: Modern scholars credit Batu with founding the first Sarai; Ibn Arabshah gives it to his brother Berke, the first Muslim khan. The first word is printed tht, read as takht, 'throne, capital'.

p.h: The court is the 'orda', the queen is the 'khatun'
p.g: A page of ranks and offices shows how the Horde's court looked to Italian traders. Latin 'curia' (court) is Persian 'ordu' and Cuman 'orda', the word behind English 'horde'. An empress is 'khan khatun', a queen 'sultan khatun', a lord is 'bey' or 'khoja'. The khan's court, the orda, was the capital in the steppe.
p.q: dominus ghoya bey ul coia corona taz tagz curia ordu orda imperatris xen i padixa can catonj regina xen y patia soltan catonj
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
p.t: lord: (Persian) khwaja / (Cuman) bey or khoja; crown: taj / tagz; court: (Persian) ordu / (Cuman) orda; empress: (Persian) wife of the padishah / (Cuman) khan khatun; queen: (Persian) wife of the king / (Cuman) sultan khatun.
p.c: A word list, so it shows the vocabulary the compilers needed, not a description of the court.
p.n: Checked against the page image; 'ul' stands for Latin 'vel', 'or'.

p.h: Kazan in 1714: a wooden city of Russians and Tatars
p.g: Tulishen describes Kazan, the old Tatar khanate capital, as a Russian provincial seat: no stone walls but wooden palisades with eight gates, a ditch and wooden spikes, three public buildings of wood, five brick churches, and two-storey wooden houses for about 5000 families. The people were a mix of Russians, Tatars, Cheremis and Torghuts.
p.q: Instead of regular walls, Cazan is surrounded with wooden palisades. It has 8 gates … Within the city there is a market, three public edifices of wood, and five churches built of brick. The population consists of about 5000 families. The dwelling houses are all built of wood, and raised to the height of two stories. The inhabitants are a mixture of Russians, Tartars, Tzeremish, and Tourgouths.
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
p.tg: kazan wooden city palisade brick churches

p.h: Urga in 1821: a monastery town of wooden temples and giant yurts
p.g: The ancestor of Ulaanbaatar, as Bichurin saw it: a great monastery (Khüree) built on Tibetan lines, about 12 li round, with many irregular streets. At the centre was the court of the Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu. The temples were of wood, the main one with a gilded dome; the other buildings were huge yurts covered with canvas. The lamas lived in felt tents or mud-plaster huts. A Chinese trading town (Maimaicheng) stood nearby.
p.q: Курень, обширный монастырь, построенный по Тибетскимъ правиламъ. … Въ окружности содержитъ около 12 ли, и состоитъ изъ многихъ неправильныхъ улицъ. Въ средоточіи стоитъ обширный дворъ, въ которомъ Чжебцзунь-дамба-хутухта имѣетъ пребываніе. Здѣсь храмы построены изъ дерева и главный съ позолоченымъ куполомъ. Прочія строенія состоятъ изъ огромныхъ юртъ, обтянутыхъ парусиною.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.t: Khüree, a vast monastery built according to Tibetan rules. … Its circuit is about 12 li, and it consists of many irregular streets. In the centre stands a large courtyard in which the Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu resides. Here the temples are built of wood, and the main one has a gilded dome. The other buildings consist of huge yurts covered with canvas.

p.h: Baghdad razed, except mosques, colleges and hospitals
p.g: After Baghdad fell by storm, each Tartar soldier was ordered to bring a head, and towers of heads were built as a warning. Timur then ordered every house razed but the mosques, colleges and hospitals spared. A footnote from the translator adds Ibn Arabshah's figures: 90,000 killed and 120 towers of heads.
p.q: Afterwards Timur gave orders that there shou'd not remain one single house in the city unraz'd ; but that the mosques, colleges and hospitals shou'd be spar'd. Accordingly they ruin'd the markets, caravanseras, hermitages, cells, monasterys, palaces, and other edifices.
p.s: Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi (English of 1723, via Pétis de la Croix)
p.c: The official history presents the massacre as justified; the casualty figures in the footnote come from Ibn Arabshah, a hostile writer.

p.h: Beijing burned by a rebel, rebuilt by the Tartars in four years
p.g: Explaining that Chinese houses and palaces are almost all of wood and burn easily, Kircher cites Beijing: at the start of the Tartar invasion a rebel and tyrant (Li Zicheng) set it on fire for four days, but the Tartars, meaning the conquering Manchus, restored it to its former dignity with four years of building. Here the 'Tartars' are the rebuilders of a capital.
p.q: ut quemadmodum omnia ex ligno ferè constructa sunt, ita quoque incendio alicubi exorto nisi obstetur, integræ sæpè urbes exiguo temporis spatio in cineres rediguntur; uti Pekino accidit, quæ urbs post Nankingum omnium vastissima à Rebelle & Tyranno ad initium irruptionis Tartarorum quadriduano incendio consumpta fuit, à Tartaris tamen quadriennali fabricatione in pristinum dignitatis statum restituta.
p.s: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), compiling Jesuit reports (Martini and others)
p.t: since almost everything is built of wood, if a fire breaks out somewhere and is not checked, whole cities are often reduced to ashes in a short time; as happened to Peking, the vastest of all cities after Nanking, which at the beginning of the invasion of the Tartars was consumed in a four-day fire by a rebel and tyrant, but was restored by the Tartars to its former dignity by four years of building.
p.c: Second-hand; the palace fire of 1644 was real, but 'four years' is a round figure from Kircher's sources.
