p.h: Walls of ice at Astrakhan, and Timur's razing of Sarai
p.g: After defeating Tokhtamysh, Timur resolved to level Astrakhan. Its people used the hard winter to build walls of ice blocks cemented by pouring water over them, but Timur marched through the deep snow, emptied the town, razed it and had its headman (kelanter) Mahmudi drowned under the ice that was meant to protect him. He then went on to Sarai, capital and residence of the khans, and laid it waste, as revenge for the Horde's earlier destruction of a city of the Chagatai realm. The loot of both cities was divided among the army.
p.q: Trotz des strengen Winters, welcher den Bewohnern von Astrachan noch den Vortheil gewährte, sich mit Eismauern, welche, mit Wasser übergossen, zusammengefügt wurden, zu befestigen, und trotz des tiefen Schnees marschierte er auf Astrachan, leerte die Stadt von ihren Bewohnern, liess sie schleifen … Von Astrachan zog Timur nach Serai, der Hauptstadt von Kiptschak und der Residenz der Chane, und verheerte dieselbe
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), following Sharaf al-Din's history of Timur in Pétis de la Croix's French version
p.pl: Astrakhan and Sarai, lower Volga, Russia
p.pe: Timur's army; townspeople of the Golden Horde
p.t: In spite of the severe winter, which still gave the inhabitants of Astrakhan the advantage of fortifying themselves with walls of ice, joined together by pouring water over them, and in spite of the deep snow, he marched on Astrakhan, emptied the town of its inhabitants and had it razed … From Astrakhan Timur moved to Sarai, the capital of Kipchak and residence of the khans, and laid it waste
p.c: Told from the victor's side: Hammer follows Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's Zafarnama, written in the 1420s for Timur's grandson, through Pétis de la Croix's French version.
p.tg: timur astrakhan sarai ice walls destruction siege

p.h: New towns in eastern Tartary, none in the west
p.g: In a report on the China missions presented in Rome, François Noël says Eastern Tartary (Manchuria) is filling up: the emperor is building towns there and villages are well peopled. Western Tartary has neither towns nor villages except toward the Uzbeks and the Caspian; its peoples, recently subjected to the emperor, own nothing but herds, and move on every three months or so when the grass is eaten.
p.q: La Tartarie orientale se peuple tous les jours. L'Empereur y fait bâtir des villes, & l'on y voit des villages fort peuplés. Pour la Tartarie occidentale, il n'y a ni villes ni villages que du côté des Yousbecks, & de la mer Caspienne … Toutes les richesses de ces Peuples ne consistent qu'en de nombreux troupeaux, avec lesquels ils errent de côté & d'autre.
p.s: François Noël, Mémoire on the state of the China missions (presented in Latin at Rome, translated into French)
p.pe: Manchus (Eastern Tartary); Mongol and other nomads (Western Tartary)
p.t: Eastern Tartary is filling with people every day. The Emperor is having towns built there, and very populous villages can be seen. As for Western Tartary, there are neither towns nor villages except toward the Uzbeks and the Caspian Sea … All the wealth of these peoples consists only of numerous herds, with which they wander here and there.
p.c: A general survey written for Rome, not a travel report; the year on the title is garbled in the OCR.

p.h: The ruined city of Urgench and its gold
p.g: On the way to Khiva the factors passed the old city they call 'Jurgantz' (Urgench), once large but now all in ruins except a mosque. Their Tartar companions prayed there and then went looking for gold that, they said, rains often washed out of the ruins. Urgench had been the great capital of Khwarazm destroyed by the Mongols in 1221 and again by Tamerlane.
p.q: …we came to the city Jurgantz, which appeared to have been a large place; but now was entirely in ruins, no other building remaining than a mosque. Here our company were very devout: they offered their prayers to heaven for their safe journey, and then went in search of gold, which they said, they had frequently found washed out by the rains from amongst the ruins of this city.
p.s: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)

p.h: Ruined cities in Mongolia credited to Kublai's successors
p.g: The map-making Jesuits found ruins of a large city on the Kherlen and of cities 'in above 20 different places'. They argue these were not ancient: the Mongols preferred tents to the most convenient houses, but after Kublai conquered China they began to build cities in Tartary so as not to look inferior to the Chinese, and all were destroyed or abandoned within a century. They compare this to the Manchu emperor Kangxi building towns and summer palaces in their own day.
p.q: Rubraquis speaks of Kara koram as a Village; but it is the Genius of that Nation to prefer Tents to the most convenient Houses: However, when they took to the Chinese Customs … they begun to build Cities in Tartary, the Ruins of which are still to be seen in above 20 different Places.
p.s: Jesuit map-makers of 1709 to 1711 (Régis, Jartoux, Fridelli and others), compiled by Du Halde (English translation, 1738)
p.c: Their dating of the ruins is an argument, not a finding; the English editor's footnotes add material from Abu'l-Ghazi and Gaubil and disagree on details.

p.h: A walled town of Chinese captives taken by the Turks
p.g: A little south of the merchant city of Taraz stood a small walled town of some 300 households whose people were originally Chinese. They had been carried off by the Turks, then gathered their countrymen together and held this town. They had taken up Turkish dress and ways, though the next page adds that they still kept the speech and manners of their homeland. A glimpse of who actually lived in towns under steppe rule.
p.q: 南行十餘里有小孤城三百餘户本中國人也昔為突厥所掠後遂鳩集同國共保此城於中宅居衣服去就遂同突厥
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
p.pe: Chinese captives living under the Western Turks
p.t: Ten li or so to the south is a small isolated town of more than 300 households. They were originally people of China, carried off long ago by the Turks. Later they gathered together their fellow countrymen and jointly hold this town, living inside it. In clothing and bearing they have become like the Turks.

p.h: Every Horde has one chief city
p.g: An informant Possevino calls only 'N.' explains why Moscow could swallow Kazan and Astrakhan but not Crimea. The tsar's gunners fired from behind thick perforated planks fixed to carts, and each Tartar Horde had a single chief city or gathering place: take it and the rest submits. It is a neat description of the horde as a people centred on one capital.
p.q: Cum enim (dicebat) Moscus aduersùs illos, quos edomuit, Tartaros, maximis tormentis adductis, crassos etiam asseres perforatos curribus præfigi iussisset, per quos Pyxidarij bombardas suas exonerabant, certa hostium pernicie, ipsi à nemine læsi: facilè fuit nouo armorum genere circumuentos opprimere; præterquàm quòd cùm vniuscuiusque Tartarorum Hordæ primaria vna (vt dixi) ciuitas sit, seu conuentus, quo deuicto, reliqua omnia sine difficultate in potestatem veniant.
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
p.pe: Kazan and Astrakhan Tatars; Crimean ('Precop') Tatars
p.t: For (he said) the Muscovite, against those Tartars he subdued, brought up very large cannon and had thick planks with holes in them fixed to carts, through which the musketeers fired their guns, to the sure ruin of the enemy while they themselves were hurt by no one: so it was easy to overwhelm men caught by a new kind of arms; besides which, since each Horde of the Tartars has one chief city (as I said), or gathering place, once that is conquered everything else comes under his power without difficulty.
p.c: Hearsay from an unnamed adviser Possevino consulted before his journey.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.
p.tg: horde capital wagon fort guns kazan astrakhan

p.h: Almaliq: running water, fruit, Uighurs and Chinese settlers
p.g: Beyond the Iron Pass, guarded by Chinese soldiers, Chang De reached Almaliq, a Mongol-ruled city of the Chagatai realm. Its streets were crossed by running water and its melons, grapes and pomegranates were excellent. Muslim Turks lived mixed with Chinese and had picked up Chinese ways, and a town further south was full of settlers from Shanxi.
p.q: 出関至阿里麻里城市井皆流水交貫有諸菓唯瓜蒲萄石榴最佳囬紇與漢民雜居其俗漸染頗似中國又南有赤木児城居民多并汾人
p.s: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Uighurs/Muslims (Huihe) and Chinese under Mongol rule
p.t: Leaving the pass he reached the city of Alimali (Almaliq). Its streets and markets are all crossed by running water. There are all kinds of fruit; the melons, grapes and pomegranates are the best. The Huihe (Muslim Turks) live mixed with the Han Chinese, and their customs have gradually been coloured until they are rather like China's. Further south is the city of Chimur, whose inhabitants are mostly people from Bing and Fen (Shanxi).
p.tg: almaliq chinese settlers uighurs gardens chagatai

p.h: Sarai, Astrakhan, Bolgar and Kaffa: the cities of Great Tartary
p.g: Schiltberger lists the towns he visited 'that belong to Great Tartary': Urgench, Haitzicherchen (Hajji Tarkhan, old Astrakhan), Sarai 'the residence of the kings of the Tartars', Bolgar, Ibissibur, Tana on the Don, Solkhat in Crimea, and Kaffa with its double walls and its Italian, Greek, Armenian and Jewish quarters. So the Horde of his day had real cities as well as camps.
p.q: Item, a city called Haitzicherchen, which is a large city, and in a good country. Another city called Sarei ; there, is the residence of the kings of the Tartars. There is also a city called Bolar, in which are different kinds of beasts.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.pe: Golden Horde Tartars and their subject towns
p.c: He says he was in these places but gives almost no description of Sarai itself; editor Bruun's notes (p.173) add that its ruins lie on the Akhtuba.
p.tg: sarai astrakhan bolgar kaffa golden horde

p.h: Kazan: wooden walls, a stone castle, and no Tatars allowed inside
p.g: Struys walked through Kazan, capital of the former Tatar kingdom. The town wall is only timber but the castle is good stone. Russians and Tatars both live there under a Russian governor, but Tatars are barred from the castle on pain of death. A sharp picture of a conquered Tatar capital more than a century after the Russian conquest of 1552.
p.q: Ses murailles ne sont que de bois, mais celles du Château sont de bonne pierre & d'une épaisseur raisonnable … Ses habitans sont Moscovites & Tartares; lesquels obeïssent à un Gouverneur établi par le Grand Czar … Pour la garde du Château, les Tartares en sont exclus, & ils n'oseroient y entrer sur peine de la vie.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: Its walls are only of wood, but those of the castle are of good stone and reasonably thick … Its inhabitants are Muscovites and Tartars, who obey a governor appointed by the Great Tsar … From the guard of the castle the Tartars are excluded, and they would not dare enter it on pain of death.

p.h: Sarai, the lost capital of the Golden Horde
p.g: In Saratov a local official showed Haxthausen coins and ornaments dug from the 'supposed ruins' of Sarai. He then retells its history: Batu founded the city, the khans built magnificent palaces, and Russian grand dukes came to kneel there. On the next page he marvels that nobody could yet say for certain where this great capital had stood.
p.q: Batu Khan, the Grand Khan of the Golden Horde, who ruled over the half of two hemispheres, founded in the thirteenth century a powerful city, Sarai, and fixed his residence there. He and his successors built palaces of fabulous magnificence. Princes, among others the Grand Dukes of Russia, were obliged to come and bend the knee before their lord and swear fealty to him
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.pe: Khans of the Golden Horde (Mongols and Tatars)
p.c: The history is Haxthausen's summary of received accounts, not something he saw; 'palaces of fabulous magnificence' is his phrase, not a description of surviving remains.
p.tg: sarai golden horde batu capital coins

p.h: Baghdad taken, the caliph and his treasure
p.g: Hayton's account of the Mongol sack of Baghdad: Hulegu took the city by force, put men and women to the sword, and found such riches that it was a marvel to see. Asked why he had not spent his treasure on an army, the caliph answered that he thought old women alone were enough to defend his land. Hulegu then shut him in a room with his treasure to eat it, and 'never again was there a caliph in Baghdad'.
p.q: Le calif fu amenez vif devant Haloon, e tantes richesses furent trovées en la cité de Baldac que ce fut grant merveille à regarder. … E le calif respondi que il quidoit que veisles fammes soulement estoient soufisables à defendre la terre.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: The caliph was brought alive before Hulegu, and so much wealth was found in the city of Baghdad that it was a great marvel to behold. … And the caliph answered that he thought old women alone were enough to defend the land.
p.c: Hayton says his knowledge of Hulegu's reign came from his uncle King Het'um; the starving-among-treasure ending is a widely told story, not a verified fact.

p.h: The Tatars take Sudak, the Crimean trading port
p.g: In a note d'Ohsson translates the Arab historian Ibn al-Athir on the first Mongol raid into the western steppe. The 'Tatars' reached Sudak, a Qipchaq port on the Black ('Khazar') Sea where ships called and where Qipchaqs traded slaves and furs of fox, beaver and squirrel for cloth. They took the town; its people fled to the mountains or by sea to Seljuk Anatolia. The note then describes the Tatars' feigned retreat before crushing the Russians.
p.q: Les Tatares s'avancèrent jusqu'à la ville de Soudac, qui appartient aux Kiptchacs, et d'où ils tirent leurs grains; elle est située sur la Mer Khazarienne, et les vaisseaux y abordent. On y trouve des étoffes, que les Kiptchacs viennent acheter, donnant en échange des esclaves des deux sexes et des peaux de renard … Les Tatares s'emparèrent de Soudac, dont les habitants prirent la fuite
p.s: Ibn al-Athir, translated by Constantin d'Ohsson (Note VII)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai); Qipchaqs
p.t: The Tatars advanced as far as the town of Sudak, which belongs to the Qipchaqs and from which they draw their grain; it lies on the Khazar Sea and ships put in there. Cloth is found there, which the Qipchaqs come to buy, giving in exchange slaves of both sexes and fox skins … The Tatars took Sudak, whose inhabitants fled
p.c: Ibn al-Athir wrote in Mosul from reports; d'Ohsson's own footnote explains that Crimea was then called Khazaria.
p.tg: sudak crimea slave trade furs conquest

p.h: Perekop, Crim and the Khan's court at Bakhchysarai
p.g: A quick census of the Khan's towns in Crimea, counted in houses: Perekop (which the Tartars called Or) had about 400, and Bakhchysarai, where the Khan kept his court, about 2,000. The same page names a Black Sea trading town of about 2,000 houses belonging to the Khan (the name is garbled in the scan; probably Kozlov, today's Yevpatoria), and the next page adds the Khan's second palace at Almasaray, with a town of only 60 to 80 houses.
p.q: The Towns of this Peninsula are first Przecop, called Or by the Tartars, where there are about four hundred Houses … Crim, another Town of the Cham … inhabited by few but by the Tartars. Baciasary where the Cham ordinarily keepeth his Court … about two thousand Houses.
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.c: House counts are estimates; Chevalier does not say he visited Crimea.

p.h: A tent city with streets, butchers and bath-houses
p.g: When Timur called his army together for his festivals, some twenty thousand men pitched their tents in their assigned places without confusion. Clavijo describes the result as a moving town: streets of stalls selling cooked sheep, fruit, barley and bread, and even tents for hot baths with boilers. Compare Rubruck's description of Batu's ordu 150 years earlier (W043).
p.q: In this horde there are always butchers and cooks who sell cooked sheep, and others who sell fruit and barley, and bakers who sell bread. Every division of the horde is provided with all that the troops require, and they are arranged in streets. There are even baths and bath men in the horde
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

p.h: Bakhchysarai: a city shaped like a funnel
p.g: Maria Guthrie calls the former khans' capital a 'romantic city' hidden in a valley: Tatar houses stacked in rings up the slopes around the palace, like an amphitheatre, beneath overhanging rocks carved by wind and water into shapes like towers and obelisks. On the previous page she complains that the streets are dirty, badly paved and too narrow for anything but a horseman or a small cart.
p.q: Only figure to yourself, my good friend, in a deep valley, bounded by a huge chain of pendant rocks, an assemblage of Tartar houses of uncouth forms, stuck as it were against the sides of the mountains, and placed in circles one above another, round the palace of their Chan (situated at the bottom of the valley), so as to represent a large amphitheatre, or rather funnel
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

p.h: Samarkand: Timur's capital in ruins
p.g: Relying on the Indian traveller Mir Izzatullah and other reports, Fraser says Samarkand had been almost deserted until Shah Murad of Bukhara repopulated it. It had a mud wall and citadel but stone public buildings, and Timur's tomb still stood under a tall dome whose gold covering Shah Murad had removed.
p.q: This venerable city, often the seat of empire, once the favourite capital of the great Timoor, is now little better than a mass of ruins … In this place may yet be seen the Mausoleum of the Ameer Timoor ; it is a large building with a very lofty dome, which once was covered with gold ; but that was taken off by Shah Muraud.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser, drawing on Mir Izzatullah
p.c: Second-hand; Fraser never reached Samarkand.

p.h: Chingiden, the Tatar town where Tyumen stands
p.g: After conquering peoples along the Irtysh and Ob for Chingis, Taibuga asked leave to settle where he liked. He went with his household to the Tura river, 'built a town there and named it Chingiden; now on that place is the town of Tyumen'. Another page of the same volume says the Russian voevodas built Tyumen in 1586 'where before there was a Tatar town, Chingidi'. The Tatar builder and the later Russian town are named in sequence.
p.q: Изыде жъ князь Таибуга со всемъ домомъ своимъ на рѣку Туру и тамо созда градъ и нарече его Чингиденъ; нынѣ жъ на семъ мѣсте градъ Тюмень.
p.s: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
p.pe: Prince Taibuga of the Siberian Tatars
p.w: Legendary (Chingi-Tura existed by the 14th to 15th centuries)
p.t: Prince Taibuga went off with all his household to the river Tura, and there built a town and named it Chingiden; and now on this place is the town of Tyumen.
p.c: The founding by Taibuga is legend; Chingi-Tura is attested as a real Tatar town, capital of the Tyumen khanate.

p.h: Whose town was Madshar?
p.g: From inscriptions he could read, Güldenstädt dated the town to about 500 years before his visit. The mosques and Muslim tombs told him the people were Muslims, and the history of the region told him they were Nogais. So, he says, the older idea that the ruins belonged to the Magyars (Hungarians), prompted by the name, should be dropped: if Hungarians ever lived here, the Tatars must have driven them out earlier.
p.q: Aus einigen Inschrifften habe ich erkannt, daß der Ort … etwan vor 500 Jahren bewohnt gewesen, und die Bauart der Bethäuser und Mausoläen zeigt, daß die Einwohner Mohamedaner, und nach der Geschichte dieser Gegend Nogaier gewesen. Die heutigen Madscharen oder Ungarn verlieren also das Recht, welches man ihnen auf diese Trümmer zugestand
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1791)
p.t: From some inscriptions I recognised that the place … was inhabited about 500 years ago, and the style of the prayer-houses and mausolea shows that the inhabitants were Mohammedans and, according to the history of this region, Nogais. The present-day Madschars or Hungarians therefore lose the claim to these ruins that people had granted them
p.c: The Nogai attribution is Güldenstädt's inference. The town flourished under the Golden Horde in the 1300s (Ibn Battuta passed through it), before the Nogai Horde became the steppe power.
p.tg: ruins inscriptions nogais hungarians golden horde

p.h: 'He that is afraid builds towers'
p.g: Barbaro insists the horde was not a band of vagabonds: it carried clothiers, smiths and armourers, and its camps looked like great fair cities, only without walls. When he showed a Tatar merchant the fine tower over Tana's gate, the man smiled and said towers are built by the fearful. Barbaro thought he was right.
p.q: In this armie are many artisanes, as clothiers, smythes, armorers, and of all other craftes and things that they neede. … For (saving that they are not walled about) they seeme verie great and faire cities. … I saied vnto a Tartarien marchant … howe thinkest thou, is not this a faire thinge ? But he, smiling, againe answered, he that is afearde buyldeth towres
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

p.h: Isker, the real Tatar name of the town of Sibir
p.g: Müller says Khan Makhmet moved the princely seat from the Tura to a high headland on the Irtysh and fortified it, because the old capital Chimgi (Tyumen), though protected by ravines, a rampart and ditches, lay on flat ground. The ruins could still be seen above Tobolsk. He rejects the idea that 'Sibir' is a Tatar word for 'capital': the Tatars call the fortress Isker, and the name Kashlyk used in the Tobolsk chronicle was, he says, used by no people he knew.
p.q: Сіе мѣсто есть такъ именуемое старинной Татарской городъ и крѣпость Сибирь, котораго остатки повыше Тобольска … еще и теперь видны. … Подлинное Татарское имя сей старинной крѣпости есть Искеръ, которымъ именемъ Татаре еще и понынѣ оную называютъ.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars (khans of the Taibugid line)
p.t: This place is the so-called old Tatar town and fortress of Sibir, whose remains can still be seen upriver of Tobolsk … The true Tatar name of this old fortress is Isker, by which name the Tatars call it to this day.
p.c: The distance from Tobolsk is garbled in the OCR and has been left out.

p.h: Horsey's eyewitness of the great fire
p.g: Horsey describes the same disaster: the khan's men fired a church, a storm spread the flames, and the timber city burned in six hours. People drowned in the river with their valuables, and for a year afterwards survivors dredged for jewels. The khan watched from the Simonov monastery.
p.q: The enyme fiers St. Johns church high steple : at which instant happened a wounderfull stormye wynd, through which all the churches, howses and palaces, within the cittie and suberbs 30 miells compas, built most of firr and oak tymber, was sett one fier and burnt within six howers space
p.s: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: Horsey arrived in Russia in 1573, two years after the fire, so despite the vivid detail this is what he was told.

p.h: A capital made of black tents
p.g: The 'capital' of the Jamshidi tribe was mostly a spread of round black felt tents on a light wooden frame, darkened by smoke. Abbott notes only a few mud huts and a so-called fort that looked like a run-down farmyard.
p.q: The black tents which form the capital of the Jumsheedees are of thick felts, supported by a light and moveable framework of wood. Their shape is circular, and their dark hue is received from the smoke of fires lighted within : but sometimes from the colour of the wool. Khooshk however has a few mud huts and a fort, (so called) resembling a dilapidated farm yard.
p.s: James Abbott

p.h: A town on the khan's camping ground, for the tribute envoys
p.g: The author explains why a Horde ruler built a town near Rus: after the Rus princes bought him off with gifts, 'Tsar Sain' decided to build a town at his nomad camping ground, for his own glory and as a stopping place for his envoys who rode to Rus every year to collect tribute. The book adds that Kazan was long called 'Sain's yurt' and that the khan often came to live there from his capital, Sarai.
p.q: И отстави царь Саинъ плѣнити Рускія земля, и восхотѣ близъ ея на кочевищѣ своемъ … поставити градъ, на славу имени своему и на пріѣздъ и на опочиваніе посломъ его, по дань ходящимъ на Русь на всякое лѣто и на земскую управу людскую.
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: 'Tsar Sain' (Batu's epithet Sain Khan) of the Horde
p.t: And Tsar Sain gave up ravaging the Russian land, and wished to build a town near it at his nomad camping ground … for the glory of his name, and for the arrival and rest of his envoys going for tribute to Rus every year, and for the governing of the people of the land.
p.c: Legendary history; the author confuses Batu (Sain Khan) with a later ruler and elsewhere dates the founding to 1172. Archaeology dates Kazan's origins to Volga Bulgar times.
p.tg: kazan founding sain batu nomad camp sarai

p.h: Urga, the moving camp that became a walled town
p.g: In a footnote Pallas explains that on the Tola River stands the now fixed court of the Khutukhtu (the Mongol high lama) and the Mongol princes: a place enclosed by wooden walls with several temples and dwellings. It used to be a moving camp called Urga, he says, but is now called Küree, a word meaning a walled place, and Chinese governors live there to watch over the Mongol princes. This is the origin of today's Ulaanbaatar.
p.q: An demselben ist gegenwärtig das unveränderliche Hoflager des Kutuchta und der mongolischen Häupter, als ein fester, mit hölzernen Wänden umgebner Platz, mit verschiedenen Tempeln und Wohnungen angelegt. Man nennt daher dieses Hoflager, welches sonst, da es noch ein wandelbares Lager vorstellte, Urga oder Gergö hieß, nunmehr Kurö
p.s: P. S. Pallas (editor's footnote, 1781)
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols and their Jebtsundamba Khutukhtu
p.t: On it now stands the permanent court of the Khutukhtu and the Mongol chiefs, laid out as a fixed place surrounded by wooden walls, with various temples and dwellings. This court, which formerly, when it was still a moving camp, was called Urga or Gergö, is therefore now called Kurö
p.tg: urga ulaanbaatar temples wooden walls lamas

p.h: The 'town people' of the Tura and the old city of Tyumen
p.g: Georgi explains that one Tatar colony in western Siberia took to fixed dwellings and towns earlier than others, and so was called Turali, 'town people', from the Tatar word tura, a town. Their oldest seat was Chingi Tura, later called Tyumen, a name the Russians gave to the city they built in its place. He adds that when Yermak conquered them in 1580 their ruler lived in another town, Tura, rebuilt by the Russians in 1600 as Turinsk.
p.q: fand die tatarische Kolonie … mehr und früher Veranlassung als andere Kolonien, auf beständige und feste Wohnsitze oder Städte (T. Tura) zu denken, wovon sie Turali oder Turalinzi das ist Stad- oder seßhafte Leute genennet wurden. … Ihr ältester, fester Sitz war Tschingi Tura (die Stadt Tschingi,) die nachher von ihnen Tiumen genannt ward
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.pe: Turalinzy (Siberian Tatars of the Tura river)
p.t: the Tatar colony … had more and earlier reason than other colonies to think of permanent, fixed dwellings or towns (Tatar tura), from which they were called Turali or Turalinzy, that is, town or settled people. … Their oldest fixed seat was Chingi Tura (the town of Chingi), which they later named Tyumen

p.h: Crim, the old city that gave the Crimean Tatars their name
p.g: Crim had a very old, high wall and many ancient mosques inside and outside the town with Arabic ('Chaldaic') inscriptions carved in large stones. Tatar and Turkish residents told him their ancestors remembered that Persians had once lived there, and that it had been the leading workshop of the mechanical arts. The ruins showed a once famous city, and he notes that the Tatars are now commonly called 'Crimean' after it.
p.q: Nam templa seu delubra antiqua Mahometica non solùm in Ciuitate ipsa, verùm & vltra ciuitatem plurima admodũ cum Characteribus Chaldaicis in grãdioribus saxis excisis conspiciuntur. Turcę seu Tartari nõ pauci admodũ incolę, Gręci tamen rariores hoc referũt, quod maiores sui constanter meminerint, eã ciuitatem à Persarum olim gente inhabitatam, præstantem ac primariam ferè officinam Mechanicarum artium quondam eam extitisse. … Tartari ab eo loco Crimenses vulgò nunc appellantur.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.t: For very many ancient Muslim temples or shrines, with Chaldaic characters cut into rather large stones, are seen not only in the city itself but beyond it. Quite a few Turkish or Tartar inhabitants, though fewer Greeks, report that their forefathers constantly remembered that the city was once inhabited by a people of Persians, and was once an outstanding and almost the chief workshop of the mechanical arts. ... From this place the Tartars are now commonly called Crimean.
p.c: The 'Persian' founders are local oral tradition; 'Chaldaic' is Broniewski's word for Arabic script.

p.h: Bahcesaray: a city of red-tiled houses in a gorge
p.g: Evliya describes the Crimean khans' capital as a great city lying in a wide gorge between two cliffs, about eight thousand paces long. The Churuk Su stream runs through the middle, crossed by forty-three stone and timber bridges. On both sides, storey above storey, stand masonry houses roofed with red tiles and set in gardens, climbing to the foot of the cliffs.
p.q: بوشهرك تا اورتاسنده کی جریان ایدن صلاجق نهرندن ... و بو چوروك صو اوزرنده شهرك ایچنده قرق اوچ یرده طاش واغاج جسرلرله شهرك بریاندن بریانته کچیلوب بوشهرك یمین ویسارنده قات اندرقات تحتانی وفوقانی جمله کارکیر بنالی وسراپا لعل کون قرمزی کیره‌مت اورتولی
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.t: Through the very middle of the city runs the Salachik stream … and over this Churuk Su, inside the city, one crosses from one side to the other at forty-three places by stone and timber bridges; and to right and left of the city, storey upon storey, lower and upper, all are masonry buildings roofed from end to end with ruby-red tiles.
p.c: Evliya visited in 1666; his figures (bridges, houses) are typically inflated. Crimean Tatars here are settled townspeople, not nomads.

p.h: A khan's palace with golden doors in the city of 'Homah'
p.g: Julian reports that the son of the first Tartar duke, 'Chayn', rules from a great city called Homah, in a palace so large that a thousand horsemen ride in through one door and out again without dismounting, with golden doors and a high golden bed on golden columns. Anyone who touches the threshold with his foot is struck with a sword. It is a vivid second-hand picture of a steppe court, filtered through frontier rumour.
p.q: residet in civitate magna Homah … palatium habet ita magnum, quod mille equites intrant per unum hostium et eidem inclinantes equites exeunt nichilominus insidentes.
p.s: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
p.t: he resides in the great city of Homah … he has a palace so large that a thousand horsemen enter by one door and, bowing to him, go out again still mounted.
p.c: Hearsay; 'Homah' is not identified (Julian also mentions a 'sultan of Homach'), and the golden palace may blend tales of the khan's great tent with rumours of Near Eastern cities. The threshold taboo matches what Carpini and Rubruck saw.

p.h: An abandoned city half buried in the soil
p.g: On the road to the Blue Town (Hohhot) the priests came upon a large abandoned walled city with towers and four gates facing the cardinal points. It was three-quarters buried by wind-blown soil and covered in turf, so that streets and buildings showed only as bumps in the ground. The only person there, a young Mongol shepherd, knew nothing except that it was called the Old Town.
p.q: we came, in the solitude, upon an imposing and majestic monument of antiquity, … a large city utterly abandoned. Its turreted ramparts, its watch towers, its four great gates, facing the four cardinal points, were all there perfect, in preservation, except that, besides being three-fourths buried in the soil, they were covered with a thick coating of turf.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (between Tolon-Noor and the Blue Town)
p.c: Huc blames 'gradual accumulations of wind-borne soil' for the burial; he does not suggest any flood or catastrophe.
p.tg: ruins buried city walls wind-blown soil

p.h: Kublai founds in Cathay 'a city greater than Rome'
p.g: Summing up the khans, Sanudo says Möngke drowned trying to take an island in the sea of Cathay (a garbled report), and his brother 'Cobila Chaam' held the Tartar empire forty-two years, 'was a Christian', and founded in the kingdom of Cathay a city greater than Rome called 'Iong', where he always lived. This is Kublai's new capital, Dadu or Khanbaliq, now Beijing.
p.q: & successit illi frater Cobila Chaam, qui annis XLII. tenuit imperium Tartarorum: hic Christianus fuit, & fundauit in regno Catay, Româ ciuitatem maiorem, vocatam Iong, vbi continuè immoratus est.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: and his brother Kublai Khan succeeded him, who held the empire of the Tartars for 42 years: he was a Christian, and founded in the kingdom of Cathay a city greater than Rome, called Iong, where he stayed continually.
p.c: From Hayton's history; Kublai was not a Christian, and Möngke actually died besieging a Chinese fortress.

p.h: 'No abiding city': entering another world
p.g: Three days after leaving the Crimean port of Soldaia (Sudak), Rubruck met the first Tartars and felt he was entering another world. His opening line about them turns a verse from the Letter to the Hebrews ('here we have no abiding city, but we seek one to come'): the Tartars have no abiding city anywhere, and know nothing of the city to come.
p.q: Postquam ergo recessimus de Soldaia tertia die invenimus Tartaros, inter quos cum intravi visum fuit michi recte quod ingrederer quoddam aliud seculum, quorum vitam et morem vobis describo prout possum. Nusquam habent manentem civitatem, sed futuram ignorant.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: So on the third day after we left Soldaia we came upon the Tartars, and when I went in among them it truly seemed to me that I was entering another world. I will describe their life and customs to you as best I can. Nowhere do they have an abiding city, and of the city to come they know nothing.
p.tg: no cities nomads hebrews 13:14 first contact

p.h: A capital of tents laid out like streets
p.g: Riding to his first audience, Unkovsky entered the ruler's urga, the moving headquarters camp. He describes rings of Kalmyk and Bukharan tent-camps (kuri) set out 'like streets', which he was led around for about a verst, and a bazaar in front of the ruler's own tent. This is what the capital of a powerful steppe state looked like: a planned city of portable dwellings.
p.q: Какъ въѣхали въ первые кури, которые яко улицами поставлены, калмыцкіе и бухарскіе, и вели насъ между оными около версты не прямо, но вкругъ Урги, и какъ пріѣхали съ лица контайшиной Урги, гдѣ базаръ бываетъ, около ста сажень не доѣхавъ, сказалъ Кашка, что тутъ надлежитъ съ лошадей слезть.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: When we rode into the first kuri (tent-rings), which are set out like streets, Kalmyk and Bukharan, they led us among them for about a verst, not straight but around the Urga; and when we came to the front of the Kontaisha's Urga, where the bazaar is held, about a hundred sazhens short of it, Kashka said we must get off our horses here.
p.tg: urga ordu tent city bazaar dzungars

p.h: Tyumen, the 'city of Chinggis'
p.g: Erman reports that the Tatars still called Tyumen 'Chingistora', the city of Chinggis, from the time followers of the Mongol khan settled on the Tura. Khan Kuchum later moved his capital to Isker, near today's Tobolsk, which Yermak attacked. The first Russian town in Asia, he says, was founded on the site of Chingistora in 1586.
p.q: This city is, to this day, called by the Tatars Chingistora, the city of Chingis, the name it was known by when some followers of the Mongolian Khan, Chingis, fixed their residence on the Tura. In 1571, Yermak, with 500 of his followers, marched against the Tatar city of Isker, eastward of this place, near where Tobolsk now stands
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.c: Yermak's campaign is usually dated 1581 to 1582, not 1571. Chingi-Tura was the old Tatar town on the site of Tyumen.

p.h: Hordes that deserve to be called portable cities
p.g: Crossing the desert beyond the Great Wall at Xining on the way to Lhasa, Grueber and Dorville found it inhabited at set seasons by 'Tartars whom they call Kalmuk', camped along rivers where pasture was best, in hordes 'which not unfittingly deserve to be called portable cities'. The same Tartars roamed the desert as raiders, so caravans needed a strong armed escort.
p.q: Hoc desertum quamtumvis squalidum sit, à Tartaris tamen, quos Kalmuk vocant, constitutis anni temporibus, ubi ad ripas fluminum major pascuorum copia est, per hordas quæ portatiles non incongruè civitates dici merentur, habitatur; Tartaris desertum hinc indè longè latéque latrocinandi causâ divagantibus; undè ad Tartarorum insultantium violentiam propulsandam valida manu Caravanam instructam esse oportet.
p.s: Athanasius Kircher, S.J. (China illustrata, Amsterdam 1667), from the oral report and drawings of Johann Grueber and Albert Dorville
p.t: This desert, however squalid it may be, is nevertheless inhabited at fixed times of the year by the Tartars whom they call Kalmuk, along the banks of the rivers where there is more pasture, in hordes which not unfittingly deserve to be called portable cities; the Tartars roam the desert far and wide here and there for the sake of robbery, so a caravan must be equipped with a strong force to repel the violence of the attacking Tartars.
p.c: Kircher never travelled; he writes up what Grueber told him and drew. 'Kalmuk' here means the Oirat Mongols then dominant around Kokonor.

p.h: Khiva: a turquoise dome and mud streets
p.g: Muraviev describes Khiva as a walled town between two canals whose chief buildings were the great mosque with its turquoise-blue dome, a rather insignificant palace and some smaller mosques. Most building was in mud, the streets were narrow, and a market was held twice a week. Locals said its old name was Khivak and that it existed before the Amu Darya changed course.
p.q: The principal buildings are the great mosque, with its dome of turquoise-blue (a colour revered by Mussulmans) ; the Khan's palace, which is, however, an insignificant structure, and several smaller mosques. Mud is the material in general use for building purposes. The streets are narrow.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: Dzungar 'Tatars' seize Lhasa, 1717
p.g: Della Penna records how the 'Gionkar Tatars' (Dzungars) invaded Tibet, plundered it and took Lhasa in November and December 1717, and how in 1720 a Qing army of 107,000 Chinese and 30,000 Tatars retook the city and installed a new Dalai Lama. Before this, he says, Tibet had a 'Tatar king' from the Kokonor chiefs as its protector. Here Tatars are the armies competing for Lhasa.
p.q: the Chinese army, composed of 107,000 Chinese soldiers and 30,000 Tatars, retook the metropolis of Lhasa, and made themselves masters of the whole of the kingdom of Tibet, on the 20th September, and overthrew completely the Gionkar Tatars, who had treacherously invaded Tibet, and with the connivance of a great part of its people, had plundered the country, and taken Lhasa, in November and December, 1717.
p.s: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)
p.pe: Dzungar (Oirat) Mongols; Qing army of Chinese and Tatars
p.c: Della Penna was in Tibet in these years; the troop figures are his and may be exaggerated.

p.h: Eski-Krim: from 'Cimmerium' to a wretched market town
p.g: Peyssonnel identifies the town the Tatars call Eski-Krim ('Old Crimea') with Ptolemy's Cimmerium and argues that its name, which the Tatars gave to the whole peninsula, is Cimmerium disfigured. Now only a miserable market town, it seemed to have once been large and flourishing, with monuments from remote antiquity, the Middle Ages and the Genoese period.
p.q: La Ville appellée aujourd'hui par les Tartares Eski-Krim, est certainement l'ancienne Cimmerium de Ptolémée … son nom de Krim, qui est aussi celui de la presqu'Isle de Crimée, est visiblement le mot Cimmerium … défiguré par les Tartares. Cette Ville qui n'est plus qu'un misérable Bourg, paroît avoir été autrefois vaste & florissante. Il y a encore plusieurs monumens des siècles reculés, du moyen âge & du temps des Génois.
p.s: Charles de Peyssonnel
p.t: The town that the Tartars today call Eski-Krim is certainly the ancient Cimmerium of Ptolemy … its name Krim, which is also that of the peninsula of Crimea, is plainly the word Cimmerium … disfigured by the Tartars. This town, now no more than a wretched market town, appears once to have been large and flourishing. There are still several monuments of remote ages, of the Middle Ages and of the Genoese period.
p.c: Peyssonnel lived in Crimea but does not say he saw these ruins. His Cimmerium etymology is a guess; Eski-Krim is the medieval Solkhat or Qirim, the Golden Horde's seat in Crimea, and Qirim is usually explained from Turkic.

p.h: Kazan's wall blown into the sky
p.g: A foreign engineer called 'Razmysl' had dug gunpowder mines under Kazan's walls. As the deacon in Ivan IV's camp church read the Gospel line 'there shall be one flock and one shepherd', the first mine went off 'like thunder': the tsar saw the wall torn out, earth and logs and people thrown high into the air. A second blast followed, and the army stormed the city.
p.q: и абіе якоже силный громъ грянулъ: и велми земля дрогну и потрясеся. Благочестивый же царь изъ церковныхъ дверей мало поступи и видѣ градскую стѣну подкопомъ вырвану, и страшна убо зрѣніемъ земля, яко тма, являшеся и на великую высоту въсходяще и многіе бревна и людей на высоту възметающе поганыхъ.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars under Khan Ediger-Mahmet; Ivan IV's army
p.t: and at once it was as though mighty thunder crashed: the earth shook greatly and trembled. The pious tsar stepped a little out of the church doors and saw the city wall torn out by the mine, and the earth, terrible to look upon, appeared like darkness and rose to a great height, flinging many logs and pagan people up into the air.
p.c: Court narrative written to glorify Ivan IV; the logs thrown up show Kazan's walls were timber.
p.tg: kazan 1552 gunpowder mine siege ivan iv

p.h: Astrakhan, great before Tamerlane
p.g: Barbaro calls Astrakhan ('Cithercan') a little town almost destroyed, but once great and famous: before Timur (Tamerlane) sacked it, spices and silk came up through it to Tana and were shipped to Venice. It is a clear statement that a Tatar trading city existed, flourished and was ruined by a known conqueror.
p.q: the ryver Ledil, whereon standeth Cithercan, which at this present is but a litle towne in maner destroied ; albeit, that in tyme passed it hath been great and of great fame. For, before it was destroied by Tamerlano, the spices and silke that passe nowe through Soria came to Cithercan, and from thense to Tana
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.tg: astrakhan timur trade silk road ruins

p.h: The scrap of paper that proved Cambalu was Peking
p.g: At Cialis, Goes met merchants coming back from a trade 'embassy' to Peking who had lodged in the same foreigners' palace as Ricci and his companions. They did not know the Jesuits' Chinese names, but they had rescued from a servant's sweepings a note written in Portuguese. That settled it: Cathay differed from China only in name, and the capital the Muslims called Cambalu was Peking. Cialis is usually identified with Karashahr in Xinjiang.
p.q: addiderunt etiam ad fidem acrius exigendam schedulam a Nostris scriptam sermone Lusitano, quam e famuli cubiculum verrentis sordibus eripuerant … his nunciis cum Socio Noster satis recreati sunt, nihilque deinde dubitarunt Cataium a Sinensi Regno solo nomine discrepare, ipsamque Regiam a Saracenis Cambalu appellatam Pechinum esse
p.s: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries, reporting Goes's journey (1615)
p.pe: Muslim merchants returning from Peking; Goes and Isaac
p.t: to make their story more certain they added a scrap of paper written by our men in Portuguese, which they had snatched from the rubbish of a servant sweeping out a room … with this news our Brother and his companion were much cheered, and from then on they had no doubt that Cathay differed from the kingdom of China in name only, and that the royal city the Saracens call Cambalu is Peking

p.h: Timur tears down Sarai, Saraichuk and Astrakhan
p.g: After defeating Toqtamish, Timur's raiders reached Azaq (Azov), and he destroyed Sarai, Saraichuk and Hajji Tarkhan (Astrakhan) and the surrounding lands. The line is short, but it records in plain words that the Golden Horde's cities were destroyed by Timur, not lost to any natural catastrophe.
p.q: من الاموال والاسرى والمتاع ووصلت طراشته الى ازاق وهدم سراي وسرايجوق وحاجي ترخان وتلك الآفاق
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.pl: Sarai, Saraichuk and Astrakhan (lower Volga and Ural)
p.t: … of wealth, captives and goods; his raiding parties reached Azaq, and he demolished Sarai, Saraichuk and Hajji Tarkhan and those regions.
p.c: Ibn Arabshah was a child in Damascus in 1395; he learned this from others, later.

p.h: A capital that grew from a garden palace
p.g: In a footnote de Tott explains that Bakhchysarai ('Palace of the Gardens') began as a country house of the khans; people settled round it and it eclipsed the old capital, Krim (Eski-Krym), which had shrunk to a village whose tombs alone showed its past importance.
p.q: This town, at present considered as the capital of the Crimea, was formerly nothing but a country house, called the Palace of the Gardens. The sovereigns by living there have drawn together a number of inhabitants; and this town… has successively usurped the pre-eminence over the ancient town of Crimea, which is now no more than a paltry village, where the tombs alone testify its ancient importance.
p.s: Baron de Tott (his own footnote, English translation, 1785)

p.h: The Mongol siege of the Jin capital: double walls, siege lines and 'cannon'
p.g: Translating the Chinese history 'word for word', Visdelou describes the Mongol siege of the southern Jin capital (called Nan-kim here, which he stresses is not our Nanking but Kaifeng). The city had a double wall, the outer 120 li round; Subutai battered it with every kind of engine 'and even cannon', and the defenders answered in kind, so he ringed it with siege lines 54,000 paces round. In twelve days of fighting, the dead were counted 'by millions'.
p.q: La Ville étoit ceinte d'une double muraille. L'extérieure avoit 120 Li, ou 43200 pas géometriques de tour … il fit battre les murailles avec toutes sortes de machines de guerre, & même des Canons; mais comme les assiegés resistoient avec les mêmes armes, le siège n'avançoit point.
p.s: Claude de Visdelou, translating a Chinese history
p.pe: Mongols (Moumgols) under Ögedei and Subutai; the Jin (Jurchen) court
p.t: The city was surrounded by a double wall. The outer one was 120 li, or 43,200 geometric paces, round … he had the walls battered with every sort of war machine, and even cannon; but as the besieged resisted with the same weapons, the siege made no progress.
p.c: 'Canons' is Visdelou's word for Chinese fire-weapons of 1232, which were not European-style cannon; the 'millions' of dead is annalistic exaggeration.

p.h: Kazan in 1761: well-built wooden houses and honoured Tatars
p.g: Chappe spent several days in Kazan fixing its position by the stars. He found a town that kept a remnant of its former wealth though its trade had nearly died, with houses mostly of wood but very well built. Tatars made up a large part of the population and, he says, far from being persecuted, were treated with great respect and were loyal to the empress.
p.q: Elle conserve encore un reste de son ancienne opulence, quoique son commerce soit presqu'éteint. Les maisons, quoiqu'en bois pour la plupart, y sont très bien bâties. … Les Tartares forment une grande partie des Habitants de Cazan; mais loin d'y être persécutés, ils y sont traités avec les plus grands égards; aussi sont-ils très attachés à leur Souverain. Ils ont conservé l'innocence de leurs mœurs, leur probité, leur bonne foi
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.t: It still keeps a remnant of its former opulence, although its trade is almost extinct. The houses, though mostly of wood, are very well built. … The Tartars make up a large part of the inhabitants of Kazan; but far from being persecuted there, they are treated with the greatest regard; and so they are very attached to their sovereign. They have kept the innocence of their manners, their probity, their good faith
p.c: Chappe stayed only a few days; his praise of Tatar honesty is a traveller's general impression.
p.tg: kazan wooden houses tatars russian rule

p.h: Qubilai's new city 'Jong', bigger than Rome
p.g: After Mongke's death the Tartars made his brother Qubilai lord. Hayton says Qubilai founded a city called Jong, 'bigger than Rome', and lived there to the end of his life. The editor identifies Jong with Khanbaliq (Marco Polo's Cambaluc), today's Beijing, the Mongol capital that Qubilai built beside the ruined Jurchen city of Zhongdu.
p.q: firent seignor son frere Cobila Can, qui tint la seignorie des Tartars XLII ans, e fu crestien e ferma une cité qui est appellée Jong, que est plus grant que Rome. E en cele cité demora Cobila Can
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: they made his brother Cobila Can lord, who held the lordship of the Tartars for forty-two years, and was a Christian, and built a city called Jong, which is bigger than Rome. And in that city Cobila Can lived
p.c: Qubilai was not a Christian and reigned 34 years (1260 to 1294); Hayton exaggerates Mongol Christian sympathies throughout.

p.h: Stone lions, giant tortoises and a vanished Tartar king
p.g: Inside the ruined city lay heaps of brick, life-size stone statues, gravestones, stone lions and huge stone tortoises, and hares ran in through the four empty gates. Ides guessed a khan had once lived there. His Chinese companions said that many centuries earlier a Tartar king called Utaichan ruled here until a Chinese king drove him out. In the hills nearby he saw brick turrets that he took for old Tartar tombs.
p.q: Several large heaps of Bricks lay in the City, besides a great many Stone Statues, as big as the Life, of Men, and Idols, Grave-Stones, great Stone Lions, and Tortoises of an uncommon largeness … The Chinese relate that many hundred Years past Utaichan, a Tartarian King, governed here, but was conquered and driven out of his Country by a Chinese King.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: The ruins are eyewitness; the story of King Utaichan is Chinese oral tradition relayed through interpreters and cannot be matched to a known ruler.

p.h: Hunters glimpse castles and minarets under the sand
p.g: Describing the deserts east and south of Kashgar and Khotan, Mirza Haidar says great towns once stood there, of which only the names Lob and Katak survive. Hunters of wild camels told of seeing foundations, castles, minarets, mosques and colleges that vanished under the sand again soon after. He does not say who built them.
p.q: In ancient times there were large towns in these [wastes] … all are buried under the sand. Hunters, who go there after wild camels, relate that sometimes the foundations of cities are visible, and that they have recognised noble buildings such as castles, minarets, mosques and colleges, but that when they returned a short time afterwards, no trace of these was to be found
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.pe: Unknown former townspeople of the Tarim basin
p.c: Hunters' reports; the buildings named (minarets, mosques, colleges) are Islamic types, so these towns were not prehistoric in Mirza Haidar's mind.
p.tg: buried cities sand ruins taklamakan lop

p.h: Balkh, empty but for barking dogs
p.g: Travelling by night after crossing the Amu Darya on the way to Chinggis's camp, the party passed Balkh, a very large city whose people had recently revolted and fled, and all they heard inside was the barking of dogs. Bretschneider's note adds, from Rashid al-Din, that Balkh fell to Chinggis in 1221 and most of its people were massacred.
p.q: travelling during the night, we passed Ban-li a very large city, the inhabitants of which had revolted not long ago, and fled. We heard the barking of the dogs in the city.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Inhabitants of Balkh under Mongol rule
p.c: The diarist's 'revolted and fled' and Rashid al-Din's massacre are two versions of the city's fate; the travellers only passed by in the dark.

p.h: Where was Karakorum? Between the Orkhon and the Tamir
p.g: In the Khalkha section's list of ancient sites, the gazetteer copies the Yuan history's account of Hening (Karakorum) and then adds its own finding: according to the 'Map of the Northern Desert', the old capital stood east of the Khangai mountains, between the Orkhon and Tamir rivers. A few pages earlier the same section places the Erdene Zuu monastery on the upper Orkhon. Karakorum here is a known Mongol capital with a location, not a mystery.
p.q: 朔漠圖和寕北有錫爾格河又北庫庫布哈渡口西有迷河哈刺和林河西南有温泉南有旺吉河按其地在今杭愛山東鄂爾坤塔米爾河之閒
p.s: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: According to the Map of the Northern Desert, north of Hening is the Xiluge (Selenge) river, and further north the Kokebuqa ferry; to the west are the Mi river and the Qara Qorum river; to the southwest is a hot spring; to the south the Wangji river. Note: the place lies east of the present Khangai mountains, between the Orkhon and the Tamir rivers.
p.c: Listed under 'ancient sites' in the Khalkha section; the ruins of Karakorum lie beside Erdene Zuu on the Orkhon.

p.h: Sarai: sixty-three years from building to ruin
p.g: Ibn Arabshah says Sarai drew so many scholars, men of letters and wits in a short time that no other city could match it, not even the great mosque of Cairo and its villages. He puts the whole life of the city, from its building to its ruin, at sixty-three years, and calls it one of the greatest and most populous of cities.
p.q: فصارت سراي بواسطة هؤلاء السادات مجمع العلم ومعدن السعادات … وبين بنيان سراي وخرابها من الامكنه ثلاث وستون سنه وكانت من اعظم المدن وضعا واكثرها للخلق جمعا
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.t: So Sarai, through these masters, became a gathering place of learning and a mine of good fortune … Between the building of Sarai and its ruin there were sixty-three years; and it was one of the greatest of cities in layout and the most crowded with people.
p.c: The sixty-three-year span is Ibn Arabshah's own reckoning; the city's history was longer and more complex.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.

p.h: Tamerlane takes the Bolghar capital and a prince founds Old Kazan
p.g: After visiting the ramparts of Old Kazan (Iske Kazan), where he saw rubble stone and the gravestones of Tatar princes, Georgi gives a Tatar written account translated for him. It says Tamerlane took the Bolghar capital after a seven-year siege and killed its khan, and that the surviving prince found the old city too large and splendid to restore, so he built a smaller town on the Kazanka instead.
p.q: Er eroberte auch nach einer 7jährigen Belagerung die Bolgharische Hauptstadt Brechimowa, wobey er den Bolgharischen Chan Abdulah gefangen bekam und ihn tödtete … weil aber Brechimowa zu groß und prächtig gewesen, wagte sich der älteste Prinz Altyn Bek nicht an deren Herstellung, sondern erbauete im Iska Kasan einen geringern Ort an der Kasanka.
p.s: A Tatar written tradition, translated for Georgi through a Mr Bardanes
p.w: late 14th century (as told in a Tatar written tradition); recorded 1774
p.t: He also took the Bolghar capital Brechimova after a seven-year siege, capturing and killing the Bolghar khan Abdullah … but because Brechimova had been too large and splendid, the eldest prince, Altyn Bek, did not dare to restore it, and instead built a lesser place at Iske Kazan on the Kazanka.
p.c: A local Tatar legend; Georgi himself notes the chronology only works if 'Temir Lan' is Tamerlane at the end of the 14th century.
p.tg: bolghar iske kazan tamerlane foundation legend ruins

p.h: A town emptied by Turkish soldiers near Kucha
p.g: On Kucha's eastern border lay a town with no wells, whose people drank from a dragon pool. The story went that dragons had fathered a race of strong, swift men there who defied the king, so the king called in the Turks, who killed everyone, young and old. The town was now waste, with no smoke of hearths. A dragon legend wraps what may be a real memory of a Turkish massacre.
p.q: 城中無井取汲池水龍變為人與諸婦㑹生子驍勇走及奔馬如是漸染人皆龍種恃力作威不恭王命王乃引搆突厥殺此城人少長俱戮畧無噍類城今荒蕪人煙㫁絶
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
p.pe: Turks, called in by the king of Kucha
p.t: There were no wells in the city; they drew water from the pool. The dragons turned into men and lay with the women, who bore sons brave and fierce, able to outrun a galloping horse. Gradually all the people became of dragon stock; trusting in their strength they defied the king's orders. So the king called in the Turks to slaughter the people of this city, young and old alike, leaving hardly a soul. The city is now a waste, with no smoke of hearths.
p.c: Told as a tradition from 'earlier records'; the dragon ancestry is legend, the ruined city was there to see.

p.h: Burundai: 'tear down all your town walls'
p.g: The Tatar general Burundai arrived in Volhynia during a princely wedding and told the princes: if you are at peace with me, raze your towns. Lev dismantled Danilov and Stozhek and then Lviv; Vasilko razed Kremenets and Lutsk. Vladimir-in-Volhynia was too big to pull down quickly, so Vasilko had it burned overnight, and next day Burundai came to see it burned 'with his own eyes' and dined with the prince.
p.q: «оже есте мои мирници, розмечѣте же городы своѣ всѣ.» Левъ розмета Даниловъ, и Стожекъ, оттолѣ же пославъ Лвовъ розмета, а Василко пославъ Кремянець розмета и Луческъ.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843), quoting Burundai
p.pe: Burundai, Tatar general; Princes Vasilko and Lev
p.t: 'If you are at peace with me, then tear down all your towns.' Lev tore down Danilov and Stozhek, and from there he sent and tore down Lviv, and Vasilko sent and tore down Kremenets and Lutsk.
p.c: 'Razing' here means pulling down fortifications (walls and ramparts), not whole towns.
p.tg: burundai fortifications razing lviv lutsk kremenets

p.h: Tatar waterworks and fountains, and who wrecked them
p.g: Reuilly finds Tatar-built towns narrow, unpaved and dirty, with houses hidden behind high courtyard walls. But he praises the Tatars highly for piping water by canals, sometimes over long distances, to public fountains and into houses, and blames the Russians for destroying the fountains or leaving them to decay.
p.q: Too much praise, however, cannot be given to the Tartars for their care in conducting the water by canals, sometimes from a very considerable distance, and the purposes to which they apply it; either by making public springs, or conveying it into their houses… Unfortunately, these fountains have been in a great degree destroyed by the Russians, and those which remain, decay daily for want of necessary repairs.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)
p.tg: water fountains canals towns russian rule

p.h: 'No fixed dwelling': why the Turks refused a walled capital
p.g: Heikel retells the Chinese annals: Bilge Qaghan wanted to build a wall round his residence and temples to Buddha and Laozi, but his old adviser Tonyukuk warned him off. The Turks, he said, were not a hundredth of China's population and survived only because they follow grass and water, hunt, have no fixed homes and practise war; Chinese armies live in towns and are captured when beaten, and Buddhism makes men weak. Heikel concludes the khan's camp probably stayed unfortified.
p.q: »Le peuple doulgase (c. a. d. les Toukioux) n'atteint pas en nombre la centième partie de la population de la Chine, et si, malgré son infériorité numérique, il a pu résister à cet empire, la raison en est que les Doulgases, ne recherchant que de l'herbe et de l'eau, n'ont d'autre intérêt que la chasse, et n'ont pas de demeure fixe, mais ne s'exercent qu'au métier de la guerre.
p.s: Chinese annals (Tang history) in Axel Heikel's French retelling, Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (1892)
p.t: 'The Turk people do not amount to a hundredth part of the population of China, and if, despite their small numbers, they have been able to resist that empire, it is because the Turks, seeking only grass and water, have no interest but hunting and have no fixed dwelling, but practise only the trade of war.'
p.c: A speech recorded by Chinese historians, retold second-hand from Father Hyacinth's Russian translations.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: tonyukuk walls no cities nomadism buddhism

p.h: Kazan's kremlin: Tatars not only may enter, they must
p.g: Gmelin describes Kazan's stone fortress with its cathedral, a monastery founded by Ivan IV, and a stone arsenal. Anyone could go in, Tatars included; indeed they often had to, because the government chancery was inside. Nobody he asked had heard that Tatars were ever barred, as Olearius had written a century before. The next page adds that Tatars had their own shops in the stone merchants' hall, selling Persian silks.
p.q: Es ist jedermann erlaubet, in die Festung zu gehen, auch den Tataren. Ja sie müssen zuweilen wider ihren Willen hinein, weil die Regierungskanzeley darin ist, vor welcher sie sich öfters zu stellen haben. Es wuste auch niemand, den wir darüber befragten, daß der Eingang in die Festung den Tataren jemahls verboten gewesen wäre, wie Olearius zu seiner Zeit vorgiebt.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: Everyone is allowed to go into the fortress, the Tatars too. Indeed they sometimes have to go in against their will, because the government chancery is inside, before which they often have to appear. Nor did anyone we asked know that entry into the fortress had ever been forbidden to the Tatars, as Olearius claims for his time.
p.c: A direct check on Olearius (W048, n154): the rule may have lapsed in the hundred years between them, or Olearius may have been misinformed.

p.h: A prince's camp of thousands of carts
p.g: The party reached the camp of the prince Otchigin, Chinggis's youngest brother, who governed Mongolia while the Khan was at war in the west. A wedding was under way and Mongol chiefs had come bringing mare's milk, and the diarist counted the prince's town of carts and felt tents in the thousands, set out in long rows. The prince's first question to the sage, like his brother's a year later, was how to prolong life.
p.q: At that time the ice was only beginning to melt, and the first green was seen on the ground. There was a wedding being celebrated, and many Mongol chiefs had arrived with mare's milk. We saw several thousands of black carts and felt tents standing in long rows. On the 7th (April 29) the master was presented to the prince, who asked him about the means of prolonging life.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pl: Eastern Mongolia (Khalkha river or Kerulun area)
p.pe: Mongols of Temuge Otchigin, Chinggis Khan's youngest brother
p.c: Palladius and Bretschneider disagree on where the camp stood (on the Khalkha river or farther north).
p.tg: ordo camp wedding mare's milk felt tents

p.h: Beijing's two cities: the Tartar City and the Chinese City
p.g: Careri describes Qing Beijing as two joined cities: the old walled 'City of the Tartars' around the palace, where the Manchu bannermen, officials and ministers lived, and the 'City of the Chinese', built later beside it for the overflow of inhabitants, about the same four leagues round and joined to the Tartar City by a single shared wall.
p.q: La Città de' Cinesi (che si fabbricò appresso per dar luogo alla moltitudine degli Abitanti) è dell'istessa grandezza, che la Città de'Tartari, tenendo quattro leghe di giro; ma la figura non è somigliante a quella … nel cui lato si unisce con la Città Tartara, con un sol muro, che le divide.
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.t: The City of the Chinese (which was built next to it to make room for the multitude of inhabitants) is of the same size as the City of the Tartars, being four leagues round; but its shape is not like that one ... on which side it joins the Tartar City by a single wall that divides them.
p.c: The division itself was Ming (Inner and Outer City); the name 'Tartar City' reflects Qing residential segregation.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: beijing tartar city manchus walls urban layout

p.h: Samarkand, 'a delicious place'
p.g: Yelü Chucai calls Samarkand 'Sün-sz'-kan', explains that the name means 'fat' because the land is so fertile, and describes gold and copper coins without holes. For miles around the city he saw orchards, flower gardens, aqueducts, springs and pools, melons as big as a horse's head, grape wine, and white cotton clothes, since white was lucky there and black the colour of mourning.
p.q: Around the city, to an extent of several tens of li, there are everywhere orchards, groves, flower gardens, aqueducts, running springs, square basins, and round ponds, in uninterrupted succession ; indeed, Sün-sz'-kan is a delicious place ! The water-melons there are as large as a horse's head.
p.s: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Khwarazmian subjects in Samarkand, reached by Chinggis Khan's army
p.c: An abridged text; Yelü Chucai lived in Samarkand for a time after its capture.
p.tg: samarkand gardens irrigation melons mongol conquest

p.h: Karakorum: smaller than the town of Saint-Denis
p.g: Rubruck's verdict on the Mongol capital, where he spent the spring of 1254: apart from the khan's palace it was not as good as the little town of Saint-Denis outside Paris, and the abbey of Saint-Denis was worth ten times more than that palace.
p.q: De civitate Caracaron noveritis quod, excluso palatio ipsius Chan, non est ita bona sicut burgus Sancti Dyonisii, et monasterium Sancti Dyonisii in decuplo valet plus illo palatio.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: As for the city of Karakorum, you should know that, leaving aside the Khan's own palace, it is not as good as the town of Saint-Denis, and the monastery of Saint-Denis is worth ten times more than that palace.

p.h: The Crimean khan's walled palaces with iron gates
p.g: De Luca says the Crimean khan has five palaces (serails) and his heir two, one in the town where he lives (Bakhchysarai, spelled 'Bach* serai' on the previous page). Each covers about a mile, with a high but weak wall, iron gates and gilded, painted rooms. On the same page he notes that Caffa, bigger than Messina, was built by the Genoese and is now held by a Turkish garrison.
p.q: Le Roy a cinq Serails, & le Sultan deux; l'vn en la Ville où il fait sa residence … Chacun de ces Serails a enuiron vn mille de circuit, & est entouré d'vne haute muraille, mais peu forte; les portes en sont de fer, les appartemens qu'elles ferment sont dorez & peints au dedans de belles couleurs.
p.s: Jean de Luca, Dominican (Relation des Tartares Percopites et Nogaies, printed by Thévenot)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars (the khan and the sultan, his heir)
p.t: The King has five palaces, and the Sultan two; one in the town where he resides … Each of these palaces is about a mile round and is surrounded by a high wall, but not a strong one; the gates are of iron, and the apartments they enclose are gilded and painted inside in fine colours.
p.c: The town name after 'residence' and the other palace sites are unreadable in the OCR and are left out.

p.h: Isker, the khan's capital: 'if one can call it a town'
p.g: Müller visited the remains of Isker, the capital Yermak's Cossacks entered in 1582, on a steep height of the Irtysh above Tobolsk. He describes a small round hill protected on the landward side by a triple rampart and ditches, the river and a ravine guarding the other sides, and an interior only a few dozen fathoms across, room for little more than the khan, his family and servants. Part of it had fallen into the river.
p.q: Die Ueberbleibsel dieser ehmahligen Haupt-Stadt des Landes, wenn man anders einen Ort, so wie dieser gewesen zu seyn scheinet, eine Stadt nennen kann, sind noch heut zu Tage zu sehen.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.t: The remains of this former capital of the land, if one can indeed call a place such as this seems to have been a town, can still be seen today.

p.h: A royal valley of tombs, not houses
p.g: Local tradition said the khan's palace had stood at Tsarevy Pody. Pallas disagreed: the mounds and brick vaults were, in his view, tombs of Mongol Tartar princes, mosques and walled cemeteries. A wandering people like the Golden Horde, he argues, would no more live in houses than the Kalmyk khans who refused the houses built for them at Yenotaevsk. (Most historians now identify Tsarev with New Sarai, a real city of the Horde, so here the naturalist's judgement went too far.)
p.q: In my opinion, the ruins are not the remains of dwelling-houses, but partly of mosques, and partly of vaulted chapels, … A wandering nation, such as were called the golden horde of these countries, could no more be induced to reside in houses, than the Khans and Princes of the Kalmuks along the banks of the Volga;
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.c: This is Pallas's interpretation; later excavation showed the Golden Horde capitals had real houses, workshops and streets.
p.tg: golden horde nomads new sarai houses kalmyks

p.h: Who destroyed Bulgary? Two stories
p.g: The ruins of Bulgary on the Volga below Kazan were visited and measured by a student of Lepekhin's party, whose description the journal prints. It calls Bulgary 'an old Tatar town', turned by war from a famous city into a wretched village inside an earth rampart a whole mile round. The account notes that Russian writers and Tatar historians disagree about who destroyed it: the Tatars blame 'the Tatar robber Aisak Timir' (probably Aksak Timur, 'Lame Timur', that is Tamerlane), the Russians a Russian prince Yuri Dmitrievich, and the writer declines to decide.
p.q: Was inzwischen die Verschiedenheit den Erzählungen unserer Schriftsteller und der tatarischen Geschichtschreiber, in Ansehung des Zerstörers von Bulgary, anlangt; (denn diese schreiben ihren Untergang dem tatarischen Räuber Aisak Timir, jene aber dem … Fürsten Jurjew Dmitrjewitsch' zu): so kann ich hier nichts entscheiden, indem ich nicht weiß, wem man von ihnen am meisten glauben soll.
p.s: Lepekhin's journal, printing the description by a student of his party (German translation, 1774)
p.pe: Volga Bulgars and Tatars (the old town Lepekhin calls Tatar)
p.t: As for the disagreement between the accounts of our writers and of the Tatar historians about the destroyer of Bulgary (for the latter ascribe its downfall to the Tatar robber Aisak Timir, the former to the [Russian] prince Yuri Dmitrievich), I can decide nothing here, since I do not know which of them is most to be believed.
p.c: The student's name is garbled in the scan. The two destroyer stories are reported from written histories, not checked.

p.h: The fall of Baghdad
p.g: Chang De's report describes Baghdad as two cities, east and west, divided by a great river, the western one without walls and the eastern one fortified with painted brick. The Mongol army broke the caliph's troops in one battle and slaughtered the people of the western city; the eastern city fell after a six-day siege (the page goes on). It is one of the very few Chinese accounts of the sack.
p.q: 丁巳歳取報逹國南北二千里其主曰合里法其城有東西城中有大河西城無壁壘東城固之以甓繪其上甚盛王師至城不一交戰破勝兵四十餘萬西城䧟皆尽屠其民
p.s: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Mongols of Hulegu; the Abbasid caliph
p.t: In the dingsi year they took the country of Baoda (Baghdad), two thousand li from north to south. Its ruler was called the Helifa (caliph). The city has an east city and a west city, with a great river between. The west city has no ramparts; the east city is fortified with brick, painted very splendidly on top. When the imperial army reached the city, in a single battle it broke picked troops more than 400,000 strong; the west city fell and all its people were slaughtered.
p.c: The dingsi year is 1257; Baghdad fell in February 1258. This text reads 城不 where the Siku copy has 城下 ('below the city'); the translation follows the Siku reading. The troop figure is an exaggeration.
p.tg: baghdad siege caliph massacre brick walls

p.h: Towns for Persians, open country for Turks
p.g: Erskine explains why the Turki language absorbed so many Persian words. The cities north of the Oxus were mostly lived in and farmed by the older Persian-speaking people, the Sarts or Tajiks, because the Turks long disliked town life and farming, mocking wheat as 'a weed'. The Turkish rulers held court in these cities, but the townspeople were largely not Turks.
p.q: The cities of Samarkand, Bokhara, Ahsi, Andejan, and Tashkend, as well as the other towns to the north of the Oxus and Jaxartes, were chiefly inhabited by Persians, the Turks long retaining their aversion to the life of a town, and refusing to submit to the drudgery of agriculture for the sake of supporting themselves on the top of a weed, as they call wheat in derision.
p.s: William Erskine, preface (1826)
p.c: Editorial generalisation; Babur himself says the people of Andijan were all Turks.

p.h: A Turkish king who will not stay in his own capital
p.g: Kunduz (Huo) had a walled chief town and farmland, but its king was a Turk who ruled all the small kingdoms south of the Iron Gates. He did not live in the town: he kept moving 'like a bird'. Chains of neighbouring states in the old Tukhara lands are each described as having a capital but 'no chief ruler', being dependent on the Turks.
p.q: The king is of the Turkish clan; he governs all the little kingdoms to the south of the Iron Gates. He constantly shifts his dwelling, like a bird (his bird-dwelling), not constantly occupying this town.
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
p.tg: kunduz turks nomadic king iron gates

p.h: A wooden frontier town with Tatar minarets
p.g: Meyer describes the town beside the Semipalatinsk fort: all its houses, its four mosques and even its trading hall were of wood, with Kazakh yurts on the edges. The Tatars' dress, veiled women and minarets with the call to prayer gave it an 'oriental' look. A good picture of what a 'Tatar' town on the Irtysh really looked like in the 1820s.
p.q: Sie ist ziemlich groß, hat nur hölzerne Häuser, von denen die meisten klein und unansehnlich sind, 4 hölzerne Metschets, einen gleichfalls hölzernen Kaufhof, die sehr verfallenen Zollgebäude und, besonders nach Norden hin, viele Kirgisenjurten. … Die fremde Tracht der vielen Tataren, die verschleierten Frauen, die schlanken Minarets, von denen so oft der monotone Ruf zum Gebet erschallt, geben der Stadt einen orientalischen Anstrich.
p.s: Carl Anton Meyer (diary printed in Ledebour's Reise, part 2, 1830)
p.pe: Tatars (Muslim Volga and Siberian Tatars), Tashkent merchants, Kazakhs, Russians
p.t: It is fairly large, has only wooden houses, most of them small and plain, 4 wooden mosques, a trading hall likewise of wood, the very dilapidated customs buildings and, especially towards the north, many Kirghiz yurts. … The foreign dress of the many Tatars, the veiled women, the slender minarets from which the monotonous call to prayer so often rings out, give the town an oriental air.

p.h: 'Whoever is afraid builds towers'
p.g: Giosafat Barbaro, a Venetian merchant who lived at Tana on the Don for sixteen years, watched a whole horde migrate past the town. Asked whether these people wander like gypsies, he says no: apart from having no walls, their camps look like very large and beautiful cities. When he asked a Tatar merchant if Tana's fine gate tower was not beautiful, the man laughed: 'Pah, whoever is afraid builds towers.'
p.q: Rispondo di nò: conciosia, ch'eccetto il nõ esser circondati di mura, tali alloggiamenti paiono grossissime, & bellissime città. Ritrouandomi, a questo proposito, vn giorno alla Tana, sopra la porta dellaquale era vna torre assai bella, & essendo appresso di me vn Tartaro mercante, ilquale guardaua la torre, gli domãdai: Ti pare vna bella cosa questa? Et egli, guardandomi, & sorridendo, disse: poh, c'ha paura, fa torre
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Viaggio alla Tana, written 1487), in Ramusio's Italian edition
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde (the horde of Küchük Muhammad)
p.t: I answer no: for, except that they are not surrounded by walls, such encampments look like very large and very beautiful cities. Being one day at Tana, speaking of this, over whose gate there was a rather fine tower, and having beside me a Tartar merchant who was looking at the tower, I asked him: Does this seem a fine thing to you? And he, looking at me and smiling, said: Pah, whoever is afraid builds a tower.
p.c: Barbaro wrote his memoir some fifty years after the events.
