p.h: A land with no towns except 'Cracurim'
p.g: Sanudo's chapter headed 'the sordid origin of the Tartars' describes the land 'called Mongal or Tartaria' where the East meets the North: mountainous in parts, mostly gravel and sand, short of water, so that there are no villages or cities 'except one called Cracurim', said to be fairly good, though the land is excellent for raising herds. Cracurim is Karakorum.
p.q: Terra quæ Mongal siue Tartaria dicitur, in ea parte describitur, vbi Oriens Aquiloni coniungitur … & aquarum copiâ caret: vndè nec villæ ibi sunt aut ciuitates, exceptâ vnâ quæ Cracurim vocatur, & satis bona esse dicitur. In alendis tamen pecoribus terra optima est.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: The land called Mongal or Tartaria is described as lying in that part where the East joins the North ... and it lacks plenty of water: hence there are no villages or cities there, except one which is called Cracurim, and is said to be fairly good. For raising herds, however, the land is excellent.
p.c: Copied almost word for word from John of Plano Carpini's report of 1247; Sanudo never went to Mongolia.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: Sibir, 'the chief town', built on the Irtysh
p.g: Esipov continues: Taibuga's descendant Mamet killed Upak (Ibak, khan of Tyumen, whom Esipov calls 'the Kazan tsar'), destroyed his own town of Chingiden, went deeper into Siberia and built a town on the Irtysh, naming it Sibir, 'that is, the chief one'. This is the Tatar capital also called Isker or Kashlyk, which Yermak took in 1582. The Russian name for the whole region comes from this Tatar town.
p.q: Маметъ Казанского царя уби Упака и градъ свой Чингиденъ разруши и отиде оттуду внутрь Сибирския земли и постави себѣ градъ на рѣке Иртише и назва его градъ Сибирь, сиречь началный; и живяше в немъ царь лѣта многа
p.s: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
p.pe: Mamet (Muhammad), Taibugid prince; Upak (Ibak), 'the Kazan tsar'
p.t: Mamet killed Upak, the Kazan tsar, and destroyed his own town Chingiden and went away from there into the interior of the Siberian land and built himself a town on the river Irtysh and named it the town of Sibir, that is, the chief one; and the tsar lived in it many years
p.c: Esipov's 'Kazan tsar' Upak is Ibak of the Shibanid dynasty; the meaning 'chief' for Sibir is Esipov's gloss, not a proven etymology.

p.h: Alak-tsin, a town where every pot is silver
p.g: In his chapter on the Tatar people, the Khivan khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi describes a great town and many villages on a 'Bitter Sea' fed by the Uighur river (Klaproth identifies it as the Yenisei). The people shift their dwellings often, own only dapple-grey horses, mine silver nearby and cook in silver pots. Klaproth gives his own new translation because the old French version garbled the passage.
p.q: Sur les bords de cette mer est située une grande ville et beaucoup de villages. Les habitans changent souvent de demeure; ils possèdent de nombreux troupeaux, et une quantité considérable de chevaux. … Tous sont pommelés … Le nom de la ville est Alak-tsin; dans son voisinage il y a des mines d'argent. Chez ce peuple toutes les marmites et les jattes sont d'argent.
p.s: Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur Khan (Genealogy of the Turks, 1660s), translated by Julius Klaproth
p.pe: a tribe of the 'Tatar people' in Abu'l-Ghazi's history
p.t: On the shores of this sea stands a great town and many villages. The inhabitants often change their dwellings; they own numerous herds and a considerable number of horses. … All are dapple-grey … The name of the town is Alak-tsin; near it there are silver mines. Among this people all the cooking pots and bowls are of silver.
p.c: Abu'l-Ghazi wrote four centuries after the events from Rashid al-Din and oral tradition; the silver pots are hearsay, and Klaproth is unsure where the 'Bitter Sea' was.

p.h: The Tartar embassy house inside the Kremlin
p.g: Even the mighty Ivan III, Herberstein says, had to go out and stand before seated Tartar envoys. The Tartars kept a house inside the Moscow citadel. His Byzantine wife Sophia, claiming a dream, persuaded the Tartar queen to give the plot for a church, and the Tartars were never given a house in the fortress again.
p.q: There was within the citadel of Moscow a house in which the Tartars lodged for the purpose of learning what was going on at Moscow, and as this also gave great offence to his wife, she sent messengers with liberal presents to the queen of the Tartars, begging her to give up that house to her
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.pe: Envoys of the Golden Horde; Ivan III and Sophia Palaiologina
p.c: A court story told to Herberstein decades after the event.
p.tg: moscow kremlin tribute embassy golden horde

p.h: The ruins of a great Tatar city on the Akhtuba
p.g: On the way home the missionaries stopped at the 'saltpetre town', a Russian cordon post among ruins that stretched far along the Akhtuba, a navigable arm of the Volga. Zwick could see the city had once been large and splendid but could not learn its old name. Just before, he says these Tartars were subdued by Russia 'in 1562' and their lands laid waste from Kazan to Astrakhan (Kazan actually fell in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556).
p.q: At noon we arrived at Selitrenoi Gorodok, (which the Tartars call Tschigit) where we stayed till noon the following day. This ancient Tartarian city must, as it is evident from the remains, have been remarkable for its size and splendour; its ancient name I have not been able to learn. … The ruins of the city extend far and wide along the shore of the river.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.c: Modern archaeologists identify the Selitrennoye ruins as Sarai (often called Sarai-Batu), a capital of the Golden Horde; Zwick did not know this.
p.tg: sarai golden horde ruins akhtuba volga

p.h: Old Sibir: a rampart and a name
p.g: Gmelin and Müller rode 18 versts up the Irtysh from Tobolsk to where, by common report, the old town of Sibir had stood, seat of Siberia's former rulers. Apart from traces of a rampart they saw nothing at all. Gmelin suggests that both the little Sibirka stream and the whole province of Siberia took their names from this vanished town.
p.q: wo der gemeinen Sage nach die alte Stadt Sibir gestanden hat, welche der Sitz der ehemahligen Sibirischen Beherrscher gewesen seyn soll. … Außer einigen Spuren von einem Walle, der daselbst aufgeworfen war, konnten wir nichts sehen.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pe: Former rulers of Siberia (the Siberian Tatar khanate)
p.t: where, according to common report, the old town of Sibir stood, which is said to have been the seat of the former rulers of Siberia... Apart from some traces of a rampart that had been thrown up there, we could see nothing.

p.h: Samarkand after the conquest: a quarter of its people left
p.g: Samarkand, taken by the Mongols in 1220, was laid out along canals that carried river water down every street to every house. The diarist says it had held over 100,000 families before the Sultan of Khwarazm fell but only a quarter remained, that Muslim landowners could not dispose of their fields and had to manage them jointly with Khitan, Chinese and Tangut (Ho si) men, and that Chinese workmen lived everywhere. Changchun lodged in the Sultan's new palace on a mound about a hundred feet high, which the governor (probably Yelu Chucai, says Bretschneider) had left because robbers made that quarter unsafe.
p.q: the city of Samarkand had a population of more than a hundred thousand families, but after the occupation only the fourth part remained behind. Most of the fields and gardens belong to the Mohammedans, but they are not allowed to dispose of them. They are obliged to manage their properties in conjunction with K'i-tan (i.e., Karakhitai), Chinese, and men from Ho si. Chinese workmen are living everywhere.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Muslim townspeople under Mongol rule, with Khitan, Chinese and Tangut overseers
p.c: The population figures are what the diarist was told. Bretschneider notes it cannot be proved that the city Chinggis took in 1220 stood on the site of modern Samarkand rather than the Afrasiab ruins to the north.

p.h: Carpini: no towns except Karakorum, which he never saw
p.g: Describing the Mongol homeland, Carpini says there is little wood, so everyone from the emperor down cooks on fires of cattle and horse dung, and hardly a hundredth of the land is fertile. With few streams and very rare rivers there are no villages and no towns, except one said to be fairly good, called Karakorum. The friars did not see it, though they were half a day's journey away at the Sira Ordo, the imperial camp.
p.q: Sed aquæ et rivi ibidem sunt pauci, flumina verò rarissima: undè ibidem villæ non sunt, nec aliquæ civitates, exceptà unà quæ dicitur satis bona, quæ Caracaron nominatur; nos autem non vidimus illam, sed fuimus propè ad dimidiam dietam cùm apud Syram ordam essemus
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (Latin text ed. d'Avezac, 1839)
p.t: But waters and streams there are few, and rivers very rare: so there are no villages there, nor any cities, except one which is said to be quite good, called Karakorum; we did not see it, but we were about half a day's journey from it when we were at the Sira Ordo
p.c: Carpini's statement about Karakorum itself is hearsay, as he says.
p.tg: karakorum no cities dung fires sira ordo

p.h: Kadan at Trogir: a muddy channel and a herald shouting in Slavonic
p.g: Here Thomas was close by. King Béla had taken refuge on an island off Trogir. Kadan rode round the town trying to get under the walls on horseback, but found the channel separating Trogir from the mainland too deep in mud to ford. He then sent a herald to the bridge who shouted in Slavonic, 'Kadan, prince of the unconquered army, says this to you': hand over our enemies. On the king's orders the guards gave no answer, and the army left.
p.q: Caeterum Dux Caydanus omnibus loci illius circumstantiis perlustratis tentabat, si posset sub moenibus equitando transire, sed cum cognovisset, quod aqua illa, per quam Civitas a terra dirimitur propter limi profunditatem invadabilis erat, retraxit se inde … exclamavit voce magna Sclavonice dicens: Haec dicit vobis D. Caydanus invictae militiae Princeps.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: Duke Kadan, having surveyed all the surroundings of the place, tried whether he could pass beneath the walls on horseback; but when he learned that the water by which the city is cut off from the land was unfordable because of the depth of the mud, he withdrew … [the messenger] cried out in a loud voice in Slavonic, saying: 'This says to you Lord Kadan, prince of the unconquered army.'
p.c: Thomas was in Split, a few miles away, so he may have learned details from Trogir; the herald's words are as reported.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Tomsk: a new Russian castle on a site named by the Tartars
p.g: Boris Godunov ordered a town built on the upper Ob, and 'a fine castle was built with some other houses'. The Russians later heard that many Tartars had lived there, that the Tartars had named the place for its pleasantness, and that they had a king called Altijn. So the source credits the Russians with the building and the Tartars only with the earlier settlement and the name.
p.q: a fine castle was built with some other houses, so that it is now a fine city, called Toom, for they heard afterwards, that many Tartars had lived there, and it was reported those Tartars had given the city that name on account of its pleasantness. These Tartars had a king over them called Altijn
p.s: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
p.pe: Tartars of the upper Ob (subjects of 'King Altijn')
p.c: 'Altijn' likely echoes the Altan Khan of western Mongolia; the name story is hearsay.

p.h: Fourteen towns in one February
p.g: After Vladimir the army split up: some went to Rostov, some to Iaroslavl, some along the Volga to Gorodets and Galich, others to Pereiaslavl and as far as Torzhok. The chronicler sums up: hardly a village was left untouched, and fourteen towns fell in the single month of February, not counting 'slobodas' (settlements) and 'pogosts' (parish centres).
p.q: и оттолѣ всю ту страну и грады многы все то плѣниша, доже и до Торжку, и нѣсть мѣста, ни вси, ни селъ тацѣхъ рѣдко, идѣже не воеваша на Суждальской земли; и взяша городовъ 14, опрочь свободъ и погостовъ, во одинъ мѣсяць февраль
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.t: and from there they captured all that country and many towns, as far as Torzhok, and there is no place, nor village, and few hamlets, where they did not make war in the Suzdal land; and they took 14 towns, besides slobodas and pogosts, in the one month of February

p.h: The Kalmak Tartars once occupied Leh
p.g: Moorcroft summarises Ladakh's history as he heard it: about 150 years earlier the 'Kalmak Tartars' invaded and occupied Leh, and the raja fled to Kashmir to ask the Mughal governor for help. The Mughals drove the Tartars out on condition the raja became a Muslim, and a mosque was built in Leh that still stood in Moorcroft's day (next page).
p.q: About a century and a half ago, the Kalmak Tartars invaded Ladakh, and occupied Lé, and the Raja flew to Kashmir, and implored the aid of Ibrahim Khan, the governor of that province in the reign of Aurangzeb.
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
p.c: Local history reported to Moorcroft; the invasion matches the Tibet-Mongol war with Ladakh of 1679 to 1684.

p.h: Caffa: 4,000 houses, all of earth
p.g: Chardin spent forty days at Caffa, the Ottoman port in Crimea. He counted about 4,000 houses, 3,200 of them Muslim (Turks and Tartars) and 800 Christian. Houses, markets, mosques and baths were all built of earth; the only stone buildings were eight decaying churches left by the Genoese. The strong walls and castles he describes were the Ottoman garrison's.
p.q: They reck'n about 4000 Houses to be in Caffa; of which 3200 are inhabited by Mahumetans, Turks and Tartars, and 800 by Christians, Greeks and Armenians
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.pe: Turks and Crimean Tatars (with Greek and Armenian Christians)

p.h: Bukhara burned: wood gone, brick left standing
p.g: In his history of Bukhara, Fraser writes that Genghis Khan ordered the city burned when he found enemy officers hidden there. Because most houses were of wood, he says, nothing survived except mosques and public buildings of brick. He adds that Genghis's son Ögedei rebuilt the city.
p.q: as the greater part of its habitations were constructed of wood, its destruction was complete ; the sun, which rose upon its rich and crowded bazars, and thickly inhabited edifices, went down at night upon a waste of smoking ashes, among which, there was not one house standing, except some mosques and public buildings, that being built of brick, remained unburned.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.c: A retelling from Persian histories, not an eyewitness account.
p.tg: bukhara genghis khan fire wood brick

p.h: Bakhchysarai: thirty-one mosques and seventy-five fountains
p.g: Reuilly describes the old khans' capital packed into a narrow valley, its main street lined with wooden shops. Because Catherine II left the town to the Tatars, no Russian townsmen lived there; the people were Tatars and Jews. He counts its mosques and fountains and describes the one-storey palace with its mosque, stables, terraced garden and cemetery of the khans.
p.q: The principal street, which is about a verst and a half in length, contains, almost the whole way along, two rows of miserable wooden shops. As the empress Catherine gave up this town to the Tartars, it contains no Russian burgesses, but is inhabited entirely by Tartars and Jews… Bachtchisarai contains thirty-one mosques, and seventy-five fountains.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

p.h: Old Urgench, a brick fort melted into mounds
p.g: Abbott paced out the ruins of the old capital of Khwarazm: a town about a mile long with a square brick citadel and round bastions on a raised platform. The town walls, which he guessed were of unbaked brick, had slumped into low mounds.
p.q: The extent of this city was perhaps one mile by half a mile, with extensive suburbs on the north. At the east angle is the citadel, a brick fort of square figure, flanked by eight circular, and projecting bastions. … but the whole is now a ruin, as is the ancient city ; the walls of the latter, which were probably of unbaked brick, having subsided into mere mounds.
p.s: James Abbott
p.pe: Khwarazm (former capital); Turkmens and Kazakhs at the market nearby

p.h: The Empress's moving palace
p.g: Beyond the Khangai forests the party reached the ordo of one of Chinggis Khan's principal wives, where more than a thousand carts and tents stood along a river and the captive Jin and Tangut princesses sent gifts of millet and silver. Flour was dear because 'Western barbarians' brought it by camel from beyond the Tian Shan, and the diarist notes that the Mongol word (wu-li-do, ordo) is rendered in Chinese as hing kung, which Bretschneider translates 'movable palace'. He found the carts and tents grander than anything the ancient Xiongnu rulers (shan yu) had possessed.
p.q: On the southern bank of the river there were more than a thousand carts and tents. … At this place eighty kin of flour cost fifty liang; for the flour is brought from beyond the Yin shan, a distance of more than 2000 li, on camels, by the Western barbarians. … Carts and tents had all a magnificent appearance, such as was unknown to the ancient Shan yü.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Mongol court of one of Chinggis Khan's chief wives, with captive Jin and Tangut princesses
p.c: Bretschneider (after Potanin) places this ordo on the Eter, a headwater of the Selenga; the site is a guess. He reckons a liang of silver at about six shillings.

p.h: Karakorum built on an old ruin, with craftsmen from China and Islam
p.g: Juvaini says Ögedei chose the Orkhon valley and the Qaraqorum mountains for his throne, though there was no town or village there, only the trace of a wall of the old Uighur city of Ordu-Baliq. An inscribed stone found there named its founder, Buqu Khan. On top of the ruin Ögedei ordered a new city built, 'known as the city of Qaraqorum', and craftsmen of every kind were brought from Khitai and from the Islamic lands, along with farmers.
p.q: در آن موضع شهری و دیهی نبودست مگر رسم دیواری که آن اردو بالیغ بودست … و بر بالای آن فرمود تا شهری بنا نهادند و اردو بالیغ نام … معروف بشهر قراقورم است و از ختای از هر نوع … آوردند و از بلاد اسلام همچنان صناع و زراع
p.s: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
p.pe: Ögedei Khan's Mongols; Chinese and Muslim craftsmen
p.t: In that place there had been neither town nor village, only the trace of a wall, which had been Ordu-Baliq … and on top of it he ordered that a city be built, and [it was] named Ordu-Baliq … known as the city of Qaraqorum. And from Khitai they brought [workers] of every kind, and likewise from the lands of Islam craftsmen and farmers.
p.c: Juvaini visited Karakorum around 1250, but the founding story comes from court tradition. Garbled words in the OCR are marked with ellipses, including the word for the people brought from Khitai.
p.tg: karakorum ordu-baliq ruins craftsmen chinese muslim

p.h: Craftsmen spared when a city surrenders
p.g: On their cunning in sieges: the Tartars promise much to a besieged town, and if it surrenders they say 'come out so we can count you after our custom'. When the people come out, the Tartars keep those they find to be craftsmen and those they want as slaves, and kill all the rest by smashing their heads with stones. This matches other sources on Mongol use of captive artisans.
p.q: Et siquidem illi se reddiderint eis dicunt illis. Exite ad nos, vt secundum morem nostrum numeremus vos, cumque ad eos exeunt, quos comperiunt esse artifices sibi reseruant, alios autem omnes præter illos quos sibi pro seruis retinere volunt, cum lapidibus super lapides excerebrant.
p.s: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
p.t: And if they surrender to them, they say to them: 'Come out to us, so that we may count you according to our custom.' And when they come out to them, those whom they find to be craftsmen they keep for themselves; all the others, except those they wish to keep as slaves, they kill by dashing out their brains with stones upon stones.
p.c: Hostile report written to warn Christians; the same chapter repeats cannibalism charges.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: Kuchum Khan's realm and his fortress of Sibir
p.g: On the eve of the Cossack invasion, Coxe says, Siberia was split between several princes and independent 'Tartar' tribes. The strongest ruler, Kuchum Khan, held the lands from the Irtysh and Ob to the Tobol and Tura, with his residence at Sibir, a small fortress on the Irtysh. The next page adds that it stood near today's Tobolsk and that some of its ruins could still be seen.
p.q: Siberia was at that time partly divided among a number of separate princes; and partly inhabited by the various tribes of independent Tartars. Of the former Kutchum Chan was the most powerful Sovereign … His principal residence was at Sibir, a small fortress upon the river Irtish
p.s: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)

p.h: Kaffa, 'a whirlpool of our blood'
p.g: Michalo describes the sale of captives from his own country in the Crimean markets: led in chained rows of ten, auctioned by criers who shout that they are fresh, 'royal' not Muscovite slaves, stripped and checked for flaws, dressed up to fetch a better price, and resold for profit. This happens in all the peninsula's towns, 'but above all in Kaffa', whose port sends the bought captives straight onto ships. He calls Kaffa an insatiable place, a 'whirlpool of our blood'.
p.q: Aguntur haec & in caeteris peninsulae illius urbibus, in Caffa vero praecipue, Contigitque ibi quod globi miserorum illorum coemptorum aguntur ex mercatu ad naves recta. … situ suo insatiabilis illa … urbs sed vorago sanguinis nostri.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and Ottoman merchants; Lithuanian and Ruthenian captives
p.t: These things go on in the other towns of that peninsula too, but above all in Kaffa, and there it happens that crowds of those wretches, once bought, are driven straight from the market to the ships. … by its site that insatiable … city, but a whirlpool of our blood.
p.c: Kaffa was an Ottoman-held port, not a Tatar town, by Michalo's time. One or two words before 'urbs' are illegible in the OCR (probably 'not a city but'), so they are left out.
p.tg: kaffa slave trade captives port ottomans

p.h: Astrakhan: Tatar nomads outside, reed houses inside
p.g: Evliya says thousands of Astrakhan Tatars live outside the city along the Volga in their oba (tent camps), moving like the Nogays, and adds the local legend that the name comes from a dragon (azhder) that ravaged the country until a khan killed it. Inside the walls he counts monasteries, churches and a thousand-odd reed-roofed houses, and in the outer town thirteen thousand houses roofed with reeds and earth and seven mosques.
p.q: نیجه بیکی شهر خارجنده نهر ادل کنارنده اوبالر ایله ساکن اولورلر بونلرك دخی اصلی تاتاردر همان نوغای کبی اوبالریله قنوب کوچرلر ... زمان قدیمده بوشهر خراب یاتوب بونده براژدرها توره‌یوب ... بعده برخان بهادر بواژدرهایی قتل ایدوب ولایت امن وامان اولدوغیچون بودیاره اژدرخان دیرلر
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pe: Astrakhan Tatars and Nogays under Muscovite rule
p.t: Many thousands of them live outside the city on the bank of the Volga in their tent-camps; these too are Tatars by origin, and like the Nogays they camp and move with their obas … In ancient times this city lay in ruins, and a dragon was born here … then a heroic khan killed this dragon, and because the land became safe they call this country Azhder-khan.
p.c: The dragon etymology is folk legend (the name comes from Hajji Tarkhan). Evliya's presence in Astrakhan is doubted by some scholars.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.
p.tg: astrakhan oba tents nogay dragon etymology

p.h: Ruins of a great 'Nogai city' on the Akhtuba
p.g: Near the old saltpetre works of Selitrennoi Gorodok on the Akhtuba, Pallas found a stretch of ten versts covered with brick rubble, building traces and walled graves of what he calls a large Nogai town. On the highest mound stood the ruins of a walled palace or castle and of a khan's mausoleum, from whose vaults treasure hunters were said to have dug riches and coffins covered in silver. Modern archaeology identifies this site with Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde.
p.q: in welcher man längst der Achtuba, ein auch wohl zwey Werste breit, nichts als Ziegelschutt und Spuren von Gebäuden oder ausgemauerten Gräbern einer hier sonst gestandnen ansehnlichen Nagaischen Stadt sieht.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Tatars (Pallas says Nogais); the Golden Horde
p.t: in which, along the Akhtuba, for a width of one or even two versts, one sees nothing but brick rubble and traces of buildings or of walled graves of a considerable Nogai town that once stood here.
p.c: Pallas calls the town Nogai; the silver coffins are hearsay about earlier treasure digging.
p.tg: sarai golden horde ruins brick treasure

p.h: A prince's camp laid out like a town
p.g: The horde's headquarters had a fixed plan. The prince's tent, a tent serving as the hall of justice and the princess's tent stood on one side of the wells, the temple tents and the Lama's huts on the other, with the lesser priests in a semicircle around them and the prince's officials and servants ringed outside. Zwick adds that every door faced the main temple. Erdeni's camp held about 100 tents.
p.q: To the north of these were the royal tents, viz. that of Erdeni himself, the hall of justice, and the tent of Princess Mingmer ; to the south, the Churulls (or temples) and the huts of the High Priest, or Lama. Round these, in a wide semicircle, were the tents of the inferior priests (or Gellongs,) and these again were enclosed by the ministers and servants of the Prince.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.tg: horde camp temple tents lama court

p.h: City, castle, palace: the merchants' town vocabulary
p.g: The glossary gives, column by column, Latin, Persian and Cuman words for places. A city (civitas) is 'saar' or 'chent' in Cuman, a castle is 'kalaa', a palace is 'saray', and a house is 'eu' (ev). The words for city, castle and palace are loans from Persian and Arabic (shahr, qal'a, saray), next to the Turkic 'kent' and 'ev'. The Italian merchants clearly needed these words for dealing with towns in the Horde's lands.
p.q: ciuitas ghachar saar ul chent castrum kala kalaa casale de gala palacium saray saray domus ghana eu
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
p.t: city: (Persian) shahr / (Cuman) shahr or kent; castle: (Persian) qal'a / (Cuman) qal'a; village: (Persian) deh / (Cuman) qala; palace: saray / saray; house: (Persian) khana / (Cuman) ev.
p.c: The modern equivalents in the translation are the usual identifications of these spellings; the scribe's spellings are Italian.
p.n: Checked against the page image; 'ul' is the manuscript's abbreviation for Latin 'vel', 'or'.

p.h: Kazan: Tartars who farm, trade and live in houses
p.g: Herberstein sets the Kazan Tartars apart from the steppe herders: their kingdom has a city and fortress on the Volga, an army of 30,000 largely made up of Cheremis and Chuvash archers, and settled farming and trade. He says Moscow controlled their kings largely through the river routes and trade they depended on.
p.q: The kingdom of Kazan, with the city and fortress of the same name, is situated on the further bank of the river Volga, nearly seventy miles below Lower Novogorod. … These Tartars are more civilized than the rest, in as much as they cultivate their lands, live in houses, and carry on various branches of merchandize.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: 'Seventy miles' is in German miles (each roughly 7 km).

p.h: A Tatar history: 'The habitations of the Chans were stone buildings'
p.g: At Mozdok Klaproth bought a history of the Tartars in the Nogai dialect and translates its list of where the khans lived: Sarai, the Akhtuba, Madzhar, and vice-khans at Astrakhan and Kazan. He notes that the word he renders 'stone buildings' is 'Madshar' itself. The Nogais near the ruins also told him it had been the residence of Khan Mamai.
p.q: The habitations of the Chans were stone buildings. The residence of one Chan was Urisch, and the residence of another Chan was Churssan… Dshan Beg Chan's residence was at Ack Adil, with the name of Ssaray Aldy… Jaick Chan's was Madshar. There were three vice-chans; at Adshdruchan was the place of abode of Timur Ckutlu-Chan, Borki Chan's habitation was at Ckathatdr, and Sheich Aly Chan's residence at Ckasan.
p.s: Anonymous history of the Tartars in the Nogai dialect, as translated by Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
p.pl: Golden Horde lands (Sarai, Astrakhan, Kazan, Madzhar)
p.w: text acquired 1807; describing the 14th to 15th centuries
p.c: A late native chronicle of unknown date and author; place names are Klaproth's transcriptions.
p.tg: khans residences stone buildings sarai kazan astrakhan

p.h: Craftsmen carried off to build Samarkand
p.g: Clavijo explains how Timur filled Samarkand: he brought captives from every land he conquered, above all skilled workers. Silk weavers, bow-makers, glass and pottery makers came from Damascus; archers, masons and silversmiths from Turkey. So many arrived, some 150,000 of many nations, that many lived under trees and in caves outside the city. The page before says the villages around the city were peopled with captives too.
p.q: From Damascus he brought weavers of silk, and men who made bows, glass, and earthenware, so that, of those articles, Samarcand produces the best in the world. From Turkey he brought archers, masons, and silversmiths. He also brought men skilled in making engines of war
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Captives from Damascus, Turkey and elsewhere, under Timur
p.c: Clavijo saw the crowded city; where the craftsmen came from and the figure of 150,000 were told to him.
p.tg: captive craftsmen samarkand masons damascus builders

p.h: Aleppo, Hama and Damascus fall; Acre tears down its towers in fear
p.g: In his year-by-year chronicle Sanudo notes that in 1260 the Tartars broke in violently and took Aleppo, Harim, Hama, Homs and Damascus, killing every Saracen who met them, then entered the kingdom of Jerusalem and took Sidon, but not its sea castle. The people of Acre, afraid of them, cut down their orchards and threw down the orchard towers outside the walls, even carrying off cemetery stones. The Tartars were beaten by the Sultan of Egypt at Ain Jalut (the 'plain of Tiberias').
p.q: Tartari autem sequenti anno violenter irrumpentes ceperunt Alapiam, Harenc, Haman, Calamelam, & Damascum: occidentes cunctos factos sibi obuiam Saracenos. Intrant deindè regnum Ierusalem, capiuntq; Sydonem: sed castrum maris nullatenus capere potuerunt. Ptolomenses verò eorum timore præciderunt viridaria extra ciuitatem; & turres viridariorum ad terram proiecerunt, amouentes etiam lapides cimiterii cum lapidibus ædificiorum.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: The next year the Tartars, breaking in violently, took Aleppo, Harim, Hama, Homs and Damascus, killing all the Saracens who came against them. Then they entered the kingdom of Jerusalem and took Sidon, but could by no means take the sea castle. The people of Acre, for fear of them, cut down the orchards outside the city, and threw the orchard towers to the ground, removing even the stones of the cemetery along with the stones of the buildings.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: aleppo damascus sidon acre hulagu 1260 ain jalut

p.h: Towns wiped out by the Manchu war
p.g: Verbiest saw almost nothing left of the many towns and villages of Liaodong. He was told why: the 'petty King of the Tartars' who started the war, with only a small army, forced the local people to take up arms and then destroyed their homes so his soldiers had nothing to go back to. It is a clear case of a named cause for ruins, reported sixty years after the event.
p.q: There is now not the least footsteps remaining of a great number of Towns and Villages which were here before the Warr. Because the petty King of the Tartars, who began to kindle this Warr having but a very small Army, caused the Inhabitants of those places to take Armes, which places he forthwith destroyed
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: Verbiest saw the ruins; the explanation of how they came about is what he was told. The 'petty King' is presumably the Manchu founder Nurhaci, whose armies took Liaodong from 1618.

p.h: Karakorum: smaller than the village of Saint-Denis
p.g: Rubruck lived for weeks at Karakorum, the Mongol capital founded by Ogedei in 1235. His verdict is famously unimpressed: apart from the Khan's palace the town was smaller than the village of Saint-Denis outside Paris. Rockhill's note records that the ruins were located on the Orkhon river in 1889 by the Russian traveller Yadrintsev.
p.q: Of the city of Caracarum you must know that, exclusive of the palace of the Chan, it is not as big as the village of Saint Denis, and the monastery of Saint Denis is ten times larger than the palace.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

p.h: Kazan: a wooden town with a stone castle Tatars may not enter
p.g: Olearius stopped at Kazan on the way down the Volga. The town was large but built of wood, houses, towers and ramparts alike; only the castle was stone. Russians and Tatars lived in the town, but the castle was all Russian and Tatars were forbidden to enter it on pain of death. He goes on to tell how Ivan IV took the city by mining its walls in 1552.
p.q: It is of a considerable bigness, but all its Houses, as also the Towers and Rampiers, are of wood. Only the Castle and its Fortifications are of stone … the Inhabitants, who are Muscovites and Tartars: But in the Castle they are all Muscovites, and the Tartars are prohibited entring into it upon pain of death.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

p.h: Samarkand's marble and Timur's jasper tomb
p.g: Meyendorff was told that Samarkand's mosques and squares were finer than Bukhara's, built of white marble from nearby quarries, with fronts of glazed tiles, and that Timur's tomb of jasper still stood though Ulugh Beg's observatory had vanished. He adds that each new Khan of Bukhara was raised three times on a bluish stone called the Kok-tash.
p.q: The mosques and squares are handsomer than those at Bokhara, they are all built of white marble of which there are quarries at a trifling distance from this ancient residence of Timour. The fronts of the houses are covered with varnished tiles like those of Bokhara … The tomb of Timour, built of Jasper is still to be seen at Samercand, but the Observatory of Olong-Bey no longer exists
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.pe: Emirate of Bukhara; Timur and his descendants
p.c: Second-hand; the embassy did not visit Samarkand. Most of Samarkand's great buildings are actually of fired brick faced with tile, so 'all built of white marble' is an exaggeration.

p.h: Karakorum destroyed, then so forgotten no one knew where it was
p.g: After the Mongol emperors were driven out of China, Ritter says, Karakorum briefly became their capital again and a base for raids on China, until it was destroyed in the wars between the Oirats and the northern Mongols, which he places around 1415. After that the records fall silent so completely that even its location was forgotten, until the French sinologist Abel-Remusat fixed it again from Chinese texts; Ritter wishes physicists and antiquaries would go and examine the site. On the same page he summarises William of Rubruck's description of the khan's brick-walled enclosure, palace and the foreigners from every nation living there.
p.q: Es diente ihnen auch Karakorum nur kurze Zeit als Waffenplatz, um von da aus die Chinesischen Grenzen anzugreifen; denn in den Kriegen der Oirad und nordischen Mongolen wurde es zerstört, … Alle spätern Nachrichten hören hiermit so ganz auf, daß selbst die Lage des Ortes vergessen war, bis Ab. Remusats Critik demselben von neuem seine richtige Stelle anweisen konnte.
p.s: Carl Ritter (drawing on Abel-Remusat and Sanang Setsen's Mongol chronicle)
p.w: about 1368 to 1415; rediscovered in scholarship by the 1820s
p.t: Karakorum served them only for a short time as a stronghold from which to attack the Chinese frontier; for in the wars of the Oirats and the northern Mongols it was destroyed … All later reports cease so completely at this point that even the location of the place was forgotten, until Abel-Remusat's critical research could once again assign it its proper position.
p.c: The date of about 1415 is Ritter's own inference from a Mongol chronicle's mention of rebuilding the city.
p.tg: karakorum ruins oirats lost city abel-remusat

p.h: Chimgi-Tura, the old Tatar court at Tyumen
p.g: Müller identifies the first seat of the Siberian Tatar princes with Tyumen. The remains of the old Tatar court, a small entrenchment between two ravines of the Tyumenka stream, were still visible, and the local Tatars still called the fort and the Russian town Chimgi or Chimgi-Tura, without knowing why. Müller argues the name comes from 'Chingidin', given by the founder Taibuga in honour of Chinggis Khan.
p.q: Man siehet daselbst noch die Ueberbleibsel des ehmahligen Tatarischen Hoflagers, das in einer kleinen Verschanzung bestanden, und zwischen zwo Klüften des Baches Tümenka, welcher durch die Stadt in die Tura fällt, gelegen gewesen. Die dortigen Tataren nennen diese Festung, und hiernächst auch die dabey erbauete Stadt Tümen, noch heutzutage Tschimgi, oder Zimgitura. Warum? wissen sie nicht.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.t: There one still sees the remains of the former Tatar court, which consisted of a small entrenchment and lay between two ravines of the Tyumenka stream, which flows through the town into the Tura. The Tatars there still call this fortress, and after it the town of Tyumen built beside it, Chimgi or Chimgi-Tura. Why, they do not know.

p.h: The ruined city at Selitrennoye
p.g: On the Akhtuba, a branch of the lower Volga, Pallas found an abandoned saltpetre works standing among the ruins of a great city: rubbish heaps, traces of buildings and brick tombs spread over a strip one to two versts wide and more than ten versts long. He calls it 'an extensive city of the Nagays'. Historians today usually identify the site as Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde founded in the thirteenth century.
p.q: …here, along the banks of the Akhtouba, on a place from one to two versts broad, we discovered in every direction heaps of rubbish, traces of buildings, and tombs of brickwork, being the ruins of an extensive city of the Nagays. There had been a small fort erected on a hill, which unquestionably contained the principal and most elegant buildings of the place,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas, quoting his own earlier Travels (vol. 3), in the English translation (1812 edition)
p.pe: 'Nagays' in Pallas's words; the site is Sarai, capital of the Golden Horde
p.c: Pallas credits the city to 'Nagays'; the identification with Sarai is modern, not his.
p.tg: sarai golden horde ruins akhtuba brick

p.h: Tsarev: the ruined seat of the 'King of Great Tartary'
p.g: Some forty versts below the silk plantation near Tsaritsyn, on the edge of the steppe by the Akhtuba, Gmelin found the ruins of 'an ancient city' that had been the seat of Achmet, 'King of Great Tartary'. He describes many dug-over mounds built not of earth but of bricks covered with earth, traces of courtyards and walls, a 'house of a certain queen', and a high hill everyone took for the royal palace, all stretching 38 versts along the steppe. He adds that history says the place was taken under Grand Prince Ivan Vasilievich and razed a few years later by the Nogais, and that local people still carry off its bricks to build their houses and sometimes find small gold or silver coins, rings and earrings.
p.q: befinden sich die Ueberbleibsel einer uralten Stadt, welche der Sitz des Königes der großen Tatarey Achmets war, und die ein Zeugniß … wie wandelbar die Umstände der Menschen seyen … Die Russen nennen diese Ueberbleibsel Zarewei oder Königliche Wiesen.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin
p.pe: Golden Horde Tatars (the 'Great Tartary' of Khan Achmet)
p.t: there are the remains of a very ancient city, which was the seat of Achmet, King of Great Tartary, and which bear witness to how changeable human fortunes are … The Russians call these remains Tsarevy [pody], or Royal Meadows.
p.c: The right edge of these pages is cut off in the scan. The historical dating is Gmelin's reading of Russian history, not something he found on site.
p.tg: tsarev sarai golden horde bricks ruins khan achmet

p.h: Karakorum: an old Uighur town, walled by Ögedei
p.g: The Chinese commentary says that Khorin (Karakorum) had been the town of a Uighur khan in Tang times. The Mongols first used it as their assembly place and in 1235 surrounded it with a wall about five li (Bichurin: about 3.5 versts) round. In the same year, the annal adds, Ögedei built the Wan'an palace there.
p.q: Во вторый мѣсяцъ Монголы обвели стѣною Хоринь. Хоринь былъ прежній городъ Хойхорскаго Пиця-Хана, жившаго при династіи Тханъ. Монголы прежде назначили его сборнымъ мѣстомъ, а нынѣ обвели стѣною, имѣвшею около пяти ли окружности.
p.s: Tongjian gangmu (Chinese commentary), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
p.t: In the second month the Mongols surrounded Khorin with a wall. Khorin was formerly the town of the Uighur (Khoikhor) Pijia khan, who lived under the Tang dynasty. The Mongols earlier made it their place of assembly, and now surrounded it with a wall about five li in circuit.
p.c: The Chinese compilers are writing long after the event; the Uighur capital (Ordu-Baliq) actually lay some distance from Karakorum, a point this source does not raise.
p.tg: karakorum city wall uighurs ogedei capital

p.h: Derbent: the Iron Gate, its towers cut down by the Tartars
p.g: Returning south along the Caspian, Rubruck passed Derbent, the 'Iron Gate'. The town ran more than a mile between mountain and sea, with a strong castle on top, very strong walls without ditches and towers of large polished stones; but the Tartars had cut down the tops of the towers and the battlements to the height of the walls. The land within, he says, used to be like a paradise.
p.q: Fortissimos muros habet sine fossatis, et turres de lapidibus magnis et politis; sed Tartari destruxerunt summitates turrium et propugnacula murorum, equantes turres muro. Infra illam civitatem solebat terra esse sicut paradisus.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: It has very strong walls without ditches, and towers of large polished stones; but the Tartars destroyed the tops of the towers and the battlements of the walls, levelling the towers with the wall. Within that city the land used to be like a paradise.
p.tg: derbent iron gate stone towers destruction walls

p.h: Semur, a great city destroyed by the Tartars
p.g: Near Mount Ararat, at the lake where ten thousand martyrs were said to have been crucified, Jordanus says there was once a very great city called Semur, destroyed by the Tartars. He adds that he had been over almost the whole of that country. He does not say when the city was destroyed, and it has not been securely identified.
p.q: et vocatur pars illa montis Ararat; et fuit ibi civitas una quæ Semur vocabatur, magna valdè, quæ per Tartaros fuit destructa. Ego fui per totam terram istam, ferè.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.t: and that part of the mountain is called Ararat; and there was a city there called Semur, very great, which was destroyed by the Tartars. I have been over almost the whole of that land.
p.c: He travelled the region, but the city's destruction is reported, not witnessed; the city is unidentified.

p.h: A town where only Tatars may live
p.g: Kohl reports that the Russian government had made the old capital a Tatar reserve: apart from officials, only Tatars were allowed to live there. The government had also preserved the Khans' palace. He found the town crowded and noisy with music, and a complete contrast to the new Russian cities of Sevastopol and Simferopol.
p.q: Baktshiserai has been declared their exclusive possession, and, with the exception of official personages, no other than a Tartar is allowed to reside in it. The government has also had the good taste to bestow much pains on the preservation of the palace of the ancient Khans, once the dreaded enemies of Muscovy.
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.c: The residence rule is what Kohl was told; he does not cite the decree.
p.tg: bakhchysarai russian policy khan's palace town

p.h: Perekop: a stone town and a ditch across the isthmus
p.g: At the neck of the Crimea stood Perekop, 'a stone town' where Crimean Tatars and Turks lived, with artillery. A ditch ran from sea to sea across six versts, two sazhens wide and three deep, with stone towers along it. Beyond the ditch people ploughed fields. A precise official description of a Crimean Tatar fortress.
p.q: А въ Перекопи городъ каменной, а въ немъ живутъ Крымскіе Татара и Турчаня, и нарядъ въ городѣ есть. А Перекопи отъ моря до моря на 6 верстахъ, а поперегъ Перекопи съ двѣ сажени косыхъ, а въ глубину три сажени, а по рву стоятъ башни каменныяжъ
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.t: And in Perekop there is a stone town, and Crimean Tatars and Turks live in it, and there is artillery in the town. And Perekop runs from sea to sea for 6 versts, and across Perekop [the ditch] is some two slanting sazhens, and three sazhens deep, and along the ditch stand stone towers too
p.c: The editor glosses 'nariad' as artillery.

p.h: Bakhchysarai: five thousand Tatars line the streets
p.g: Craven rode into Bakhchysarai, 'formerly the chief residence of the Khans', escorted by some hundred well-dressed Tatar horsemen. She was told the town had 5,000 Tatar inhabitants and thought every man was out lining the streets; most looked at the ground rather than at an unveiled woman's face, while some laughed at the novelty. She adds that the town made sword blades said to rival Damascus work.
p.q: There are five thousand Tartar inhabitants here; I do not believe there was a man left in his house, the streets being lined with Tartarian men on each side; their countenances were very singular, most of them kept their eyes fixed on the ground, as we passed
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars of the khan's former capital

p.h: Every unknown ruin 'comes from the Tatars'
p.g: Riding through saxaul woods, the caravan passed ruins of 'an earlier town or fortress'. Eversmann saw walls of sun-dried bricks four to five inches thick mixed with some fired ones, two window openings with pointed arches in the largest building, three rings of walls now slumped into banks, and many unglazed potsherds. The Kazakhs called the place Kutschuk and said the Tatars built it, but he warns that they credit everything unknown in their steppe to the Tatars simply because the Tatars lived there just before them.
p.q: Diese Ruinen, die wahrscheinlich früher eine Festung gewesen sind, werden von den Kirgisen Kutschuk genannt, und sollen, wie sie behaupten, von den Tataren herstammen; aber auf ihre Aussage ist durchaus nicht zu bauen, sie lassen alles, was ihnen in ihrer Steppe unbekannt ist, von den Tataren herstammen, weil diese zunächst vor ihnen dort gehaust haben.
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.pl: Old bed of the Jana Darya, Kyzylorda region, Kazakhstan
p.pe: Kazakhs (Kirghiz) as informants; 'Tatars' as the supposed builders
p.t: These ruins, which were probably once a fortress, are called Kutschuk by the Kirghiz and are supposed, as they claim, to come from the Tatars; but their statement is not to be relied on at all: they make everything that is unknown to them in their steppe come from the Tatars, because these lived there immediately before them.
p.tg: ruins fortress mud brick attribution folk history

p.h: Samarkand's colleges, once haunted by lions and wolves
p.g: Timur's old capital had shrunk. Izzet Ullah found it defended only by a mud wall and an earth citadel, Ulugh Beg's observatory reduced to a mound of rubbish, and the great 'Madressa Khanum' (the Bibi Khanum complex) in ruins. He says that before Shah Murad repopulated it, the city had been so run down that lions and wolves haunted the colleges.
p.q: Samarkand is defended by a mud wall, as well as a citadel of earth… There are many large colleges in the city ; the largest is the Madressa Khanum, but it is now in ruins… Before the reign of Shah Murad Be, Samarkand was in an entirely dilapidated condition, and the colleges were haunted by lions and wolves.
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.pe: Uzbeks of the Emirate of Bukhara
p.c: The ruins he saw; the lions and wolves are local report.
p.tg: samarkand ruins mud walls madrasa bibi khanym

p.h: 124 cities once, now 'movable cities'
p.g: The Tartars say there were 124 cities in East Tartary under the Yuan (Mongol) dynasty. The author will not vouch for it, since the Tartars in China themselves could not tell him whether they still stand, only that there were many low huts and earthen walls. Their real towns, 'so to speak', move with them and their herds.
p.q: De Tarters verhalen, dat, onder de regeering van den Stam Ivena, in dit Oosterlijk Tartarye hondert en vier en twintigh steden lagen: dan of de zelve noch tegenwoordigh daar te vinden zijn, zou ik voor de waarheit niet derven na-zeggen … maar wel, dat 'er meenigte van lage hutten, en aerde wallen waren. Zy hebben, zoo te zeggen, beweeghlijke en verplaatzelijke steden
p.s: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
p.t: The Tartars relate that under the rule of the Yuan dynasty there lay in this East Tartary one hundred and twenty-four cities; but whether they are still to be found today I dare not affirm as true … but [they said] indeed that there were many low huts and earthen walls. They have, so to speak, movable and portable cities
p.c: In this compiled part the 'me' may be Martini's voice rather than Nieuhof's.
