p.h: Torzhok's two-week siege and the road to Novgorod
p.g: After Moscow, Pereyaslavl, Yuryev, Dmitrov, Volok and Tver, the Tatars besieged Torzhok. As at other towns, they fenced it with a palisade and battered it with siege engines for two weeks while Novgorod sent no help. They took it on 5 March and chased the fugitives along the Seliger road 'cutting down people like grass' as far as Ignach Krest, 100 versts from Novgorod. There they turned back, which the chronicler credits to God and St Sophia.
p.q: придоша безаконьнии и оступиша Торжекъ, на Сборъ чистои недѣли, и отыниша тыномъ всь около, якоже иніи гради имаху, и бишася ту оканнии порокы по двѣ недѣли … Тогда же гоняшася оканьнии безбожници отъ Торжку Серегерьскымъ путемъ оли и до Игнача креста, а все люди сѣкуще акы траву, за 100 верстъ до Новагорода
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.t: the lawless ones came and surrounded Torzhok, on the Sunday of Orthodoxy, and fenced it all round with a palisade, as they took other cities, and the accursed ones battered it there with siege engines for two weeks … Then the accursed godless ones pursued from Torzhok along the Seliger road as far as Ignach Krest, cutting down all the people like grass, to within 100 versts of Novgorod
p.tg: torzhok siege palisade ignach krest novgorod

p.h: Urga, a capital made of tents
p.g: Urga (modern Ulaanbaatar), the seat of the Khalkha living Buddha and of the Qing governors, was mostly a town of felt tents. Timkovsky says every dwelling, including the Russian house, stood inside a palisade, with tents in the courtyards and only a small Chinese-style house of two rooms. Elsewhere he describes its temples and a separate Chinese trading quarter, the maimatchin.
p.q: Ourga consists chiefly of kibitkas: the evening being foggy we did not see it till we were within three wersts of it. … Our abode, like all the habitations in Ourga, was surrounded with palisades; in the first court there was a tent for the guard; in the second four very spacious tents had been erected for us, behind which was a small Chinese house
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols; Manchu and Chinese officials

p.h: Entering Bukhara: earth houses and a brick palace
p.g: The Russian embassy entered Bukhara through a tall gate and narrow streets of gloomy, flat-roofed earth houses to the great square with its mosques and colleges. The palace was reached through a vaulted brick corridor lined with soldiers, and the audience hall had white plaster walls and a painted plank ceiling.
p.q: after passing the gate which was very lofty, we continued our route through a narrow winding street, of gloomy houses, built of earth, and flat roofed. At last we arrived at the great square, surrounded with mosques, colleges or madrissa, and the enclosure of the palace. After dismounting, we entered a vaulted corridore built of brick
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.tg: bukhara palace earth houses brick embassy

p.h: A street full of 'Tatars' of every kind
p.g: As Wolff rode into Bukhara in his clerical robes, crowds lined the streets and rooftops. His list of onlookers shows how many different peoples could be called 'Tatar' in one city: Nogai Tatars from Russia, Kazakhs and Kirghiz from the steppe, and a 'Tatar' from Yarkand in Chinese Turkestan.
p.q: It was a most astonishing sight ; people from the roofs of the houses, the Nogay Tatars of Russia, the Cassacks and Girghese from the deserts, the Tatar from Yarkand or Chinese Tartary, the merchant of Cashmeer, the Serkerdeha or grandees of the king on horseback, the Affghauns, the numerous water-carriers, stopped still and looked at me
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.pe: Nogai Tatars, Kazakhs, Kirghiz, Turkic people of Yarkand, Uzbeks, Jews, Afghans
p.tg: bukhara nogai kazakhs kirghiz crowds trade

p.h: Gartok: a famous market town of black tents
p.g: Gartok (Garoo), the chief wool mart of western Tibet, is not a town of houses at all but a camp of black tents occupied for six months of the year. In winter the people move downstream and the Chinese governors live in a fort. Each July a fair of 10,000 to 12,000 people gathers there. Gerard never got there; this comes from informants.
p.q: Is a collection of black tents inhabited by pastoral tribes for six months. In winter, the Tartars retire chiefly to Eegoong on the bank of the river, two stages down the stream, and the Chinese governors reside at the Fort of Tuzheegung, where they have houses. Garoo is the most famous mart for wool in Chinese Tartary
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.c: From informants; Gerard was refused entry to Chinese territory.

p.h: Whirlwinds of fire: three hours that ended a city
p.g: A second account, printed by the chronicler John Stow and apparently drawn from a letter of the English survivor Thomas Glover, describes the fire as a storm of 'whirl wynds' that died down after three hours, leaving streets full of dead men and horses. Twenty-five people died in the English Company's house. The 'Tartar dog', the Crimean khan, retreated across the Oka that same night.
p.q: This crewell and sodayne destructyon cam vpon ye moscow in great and wonderfull whirl wynds, and at ye ende of thre owrs very calme agayne, and fayre wether, that men myght walke and se ye dede bodyes of men & horses to no small nomber … ye same daye that the tartar dogge had done this myscheffe, the nyght following he, with all his power, fled ouer the ryuar oca
p.s: Account printed by John Stow, apparently from a letter of Thomas Glover (ed. E. Delmar Morgan and C. H. Coote, 1886)
p.c: The editors' note (p. 340) explains the chain of letters behind this text.

p.h: A town of pied horses and silver plate on the Yenisei
p.g: Another branch of the Tatars, Abu'l Ghazi says, settled on the river Ikar (glossed in the margin as the Yenisei). Near its mouth stood a great town called Alachzin ('pied'), ruling smaller ones, whose people rode only piebald horses and, thanks to local silver mines, used nothing but silver plate. He adds that the Uzbeks had a tradition of such a nation but could not say where it was.
p.q: Near its Mouth there is a great Town, which commands several small ones thereabouts, call'd Alachzin, that is to say, pied; because the Inhabitants of that Town have none but pied Horses … There are rich silver Mines in the Neighbourhood of that Town; and 'tis for that reason that nothing is seen there but silver Plate.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pe: A branch of the Tatar tribe
p.c: Hearsay bordering on legend; Abu'l Ghazi himself says the Uzbeks know of it only 'by Tradition'. The page footnote compares a Russian tale of a 'pied people' in Siberia.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.
p.tg: siberia yenisei silver pied horses town tradition

p.h: The Tartars build a new city beside old Beijing
p.g: Odoric says the Tartars captured the ancient city of Cambalech and then built a second city half a mile away, called Taydo (Dadu, 'Great Court'). Yule's footnote dates the new city to Kublai Khan in 1267 and explains that it became the 'Tartar city' of later Peking. A clear case of a Tartar-built capital, recorded by someone who lived there.
p.q: I came to that noble city Cambalech, an old city of that famous province of Cathay. The Tartars took the city, and then built another at a distance of half-a-mile, which they called Taydo.
p.s: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)
p.c: Odoric's figures for the size of the two cities (more than forty miles round together) are rough; Yule discusses them in the notes.
p.tg: khanbaliq dadu kublai capital tartar city

p.h: A moving city with mosques and kitchens
p.g: Ibn Battuta reached Uzbek Khan's camp (the urdu, or horde) at the Five Mountains at the start of Ramadan. He describes it as a city on the move, with streets, mosques and cook-houses whose smoke rose as they travelled, all of which became stationary when the camp halted. He ranks Uzbek among the seven great kings of the world.
p.q: at this place, which is termed the urdu, or camp, we arrived on the first of the month Ramadan. Here we witnessed a moving city, with its streets, mosques, and cooking-houses, the smoke of which ascended as they moved along. When, however, they halted, all these became stationary.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (as redacted by Ibn Juzayy; abridged text translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.pe: Golden Horde (Turks and Mongols under Uzbek Khan)
p.tg: ordu horde moving city mosques uzbek khan

p.h: Kiev besieged: you could not hear for the carts and camels
p.g: Batu came to Kiev 'in heavy strength' and ringed the city. The chronicler's famous line: inside the walls people could not hear each other for the creaking of Batu's carts, the bellowing of his camels and the neighing of his herds of horses. Batu then set up siege engines by the Liadskie (Polish) Gate, where the ravines came close, and battered the walls day and night.
p.q: Приде Батый Кыеву въ силѣ тяжьцѣ, многомъ множьствомъ силы своей, и окружи градъ и остолпи сила Татарьская, и бысть градъ во обдержаньи велицѣ. И бѣ Батый у города и отроци его обсѣдяху градъ, и не бѣ слышати отъ гласа скрипанія телѣгъ его, множества ревѣнія вельблудъ его, и рьжанія отъ гласа стадъ конь его
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.t: Batu came to Kiev in heavy strength, with a great multitude of his forces, and surrounded the city, and the Tatar force hemmed it in, and the city was under great siege. And Batu was at the city and his men besieged the city, and one could not hear for the noise of the creaking of his carts, the multitude of the bellowing of his camels, and the neighing of the herds of his horses

p.h: Karakorum and the older Uighur city: two sites on the Orkhon
p.g: Heikel quotes the Persian historian Juvaini: Ogedei founded Karakorum, and on the Orkhon were found the ruins of a city and palace that had belonged to the Uighurs, with inscribed stones before the palace gate. Heikel argues that Karakorum stood where the Erdene Zuu monastery was built about 1590, and was not the same as the older Uighur ruins of Khara Balgasun. Real cities rose and fell here, and their builders are named.
p.q: »Devant l'entrée de ce palais gisent des pierres couvertes de caractères gravés que nous avons vus. Sous le règne du Caan (Khan) Ogotaï on leva ces pierres, et l'on découvrit une fosse, dans laquelle il y avait une grande table de pierre, chargée d'une inscription».
p.s: Juvaini, History of the World Conqueror (13th century), quoted by Axel Heikel (1892) after d'Ohsson
p.t: 'Before the entrance of this palace lie stones covered with engraved characters, which we have seen. In the reign of the Qaan (Khan) Ogedei these stones were lifted and a pit was found, in which there was a great stone slab bearing an inscription.'
p.c: Juvaini is quoted through d'Ohsson's French; Heikel's placing of Karakorum at Erdene Zuu has since been confirmed by excavation.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: karakorum ogedei uighur capital khara balgasun erdene zuu

p.h: Ruined cities on the Syr Darya
p.g: Riding east, Carpini crossed the old Khwarazmian lands the Mongols had conquered in 1219 to 1221 and found them full of ruins. He names Ianckint, Barchin and Ornas. Rockhill's footnote on the same page quotes Carpini's longer account of how the Mongols took Ornas by diverting the river and flooding the city, and on the page before Carpini describes skulls and bones lying on the steppe 'like cattle-dung'.
p.q: We found in that country innumerable ruined cities, overthrown villages, and many deserted towns. There is a great river in that country whose name I do not know, and on which stands a city called Ianckint, and also another called Barchin, and still another called Ornas
p.s: John of Pian de Carpine (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.pe: Bisermins (Muslims of the Khwarazmian lands), conquered by the Tartars
p.c: Identifications of Ornas (Otrar or Urgench) are uncertain; see Rockhill's note.
p.tg: ruins khwarazm conquest otrar syr darya

p.h: The last Yuan emperor weeps for Daitu and Shangtu
p.g: Driven out of China, Toghon Temür flees through the Moltoschi gate lamenting his 'great capital Daitu', built in 1269 'of nine kinds of precious things' by Khubilai (Setsen Khan), and his cool summer seat Shangtu Keibung. He blames his own errors and bad counsellors for the loss. Earlier (p. 113) the chronicle credits Khubilai with building four great cities in eight years, 1264 to 1271, including the summer residence at Shangtu and the winter residence at Daitu; Schmidt's note identifies Daitu as present-day Peking.
p.q: Meine aufs mannigfaltigste geschmückte grosse Hauptstadt Daitu! Mein herrlicher kühler Sommersitz Schangtu Keibung … Meine Fehler sind Schuld, dass ich mein Reich verloren habe. … Mein, im gelblichen Schlangen-Jahre (1269) aus neunerlei Kostbarkeiten erbautes grosses Daitu! … Mein edles Daitu, vom machtvollkommenen Ssetsen Chaghan erbaut, woselbst weder im Sommer noch im Winter Langeweile bemerkbar war!
p.s: Sagang Sechen (1662), giving the lament of Toghon Temür; German translation by I. J. Schmidt (1829)
p.pe: Mongol Yuan dynasty; Toghon Temür (Ukhaghatu Khan)
p.t: My great capital Daitu, adorned in the most manifold ways! My splendid, cool summer seat Shangtu Keibung … My faults are to blame that I have lost my realm. … My great Daitu, built in the yellowish Snake year (1269) of nine kinds of precious things! … My noble Daitu, built by the all-powerful Setsen Khan, where neither in summer nor in winter was boredom to be felt!
p.c: A literary lament preserved in Mongol tradition three centuries later, not a record of the emperor's actual words.
p.tg: daitu dadu shangdu yuan khubilai capital

p.h: The Karakorum valley: Khitan ruins and irrigated fields
p.g: Near a large clear lake (Ugii Nuur) Zhang notes the branch road to Helin, the Chinese name for Karakorum, about a hundred li away, and a small old walled town built by the Khitans. The Orkhon plain itself was farmed: people irrigated their fields (and, the text adds, kept some vegetable gardens), though in early autumn the crops were already killed by three frosts.
p.q: 自泊之南而西分道入和林城相去約百余里泊之正西有小故城亦契丹所築也…中即和林川也居人多事耕稼悉引水灌之…時孟秋下旬麻麥皆槁問之田者云巳三霜矣
p.s: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Mongols; farmers of the Orkhon valley
p.t: From the south of the lake a branch road leads west into the city of Helin (Karakorum), about a hundred li away. Due west of the lake there is a small old walled town, also built by the Khitans... In the middle is the Helin plain. Most of the inhabitants farm, bringing water to all their fields... It was then late in the first month of autumn and the hemp and wheat had all withered; when I asked the farmers, they said there had already been three frosts.
p.c: Bretschneider (1888) thought Zhang passed near Karakorum without entering it.

p.h: A rich Tartar's camp looks like a big town
p.g: The Mongol camp could look like a settlement. Each wife of a great lord had her own large house with a train of smaller wagon-houses (Rubruck says Batu's wives each had more than 200), and the wives' courts were pitched in a row from west to east, a stone's throw apart. The result, he says, resembles a large town, though few men live in it.
p.q: la premiere des femmes fait poser sa petite court vers l'Occident, puis toutes les autres en font de mesme chacune en son rang: si bien que la derniere se trouue à l'Orient, & l'espace d'entr'elles est enuiron vn iet de pierre: de sorte que la court d'vn de ces riches Tartares semble vn gros bourg, où il y aura toutesfois bien peu d'hommes.
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: the first wife has her little court set up to the west, then all the others do the same, each in her rank, so that the last is at the east, and the space between them is about a stone's throw: so that the court of one of these rich Tartars looks like a big town, although there will be very few men in it.

p.h: Walled towns built by forced labour
p.g: The pilgrims told Wathen that Chinese rule was very unpopular, and that resentment had grown because the Chinese were building large fortifications and walled towns with the forced labour of the local people. After the revolts of the 1820s the Qing did build new walled garrison towns in the region. Here the builders of the walls are named plainly: Qing authorities using conscripted local workers.
p.q: The feeling of dislike, with which the Chinese are regarded, has been latterly much increased, in consequence of their carrying on vast works of fortification, and building walled towns, by the forced labour of the natives.
p.s: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
p.c: The informants were Muslim subjects hostile to Qing rule. The corpus lists no printed page here; 662 comes from the page sequence.
p.tg: walled towns forced labour qing fortification

p.h: A camp laid out in streets and lanes
p.g: Travelling in bands of up to twenty thousand, the Kalmyks pitched their tents 'in Streets and Lanes' like a town or village, each family knowing its place. Perry's homely proof: he saw their cows stop at their own tents when driven home to be milked. A clear eyewitness picture of the steppe camp as a moving town.
p.q: …sometimes 20000 of them or more in a Body, and pitch their Tents in Streets and Lanes, in the same regular Manner as in a Town or Village, and every one knows their due Place and Order; so that I have seen the Cows stop at their own Tents, when they drive them home to milk them.
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)

p.h: Bukhara, the greatest city of Tartary
p.g: Mohan Lal calls Bukhara the largest, most populous and richest city 'in the whole region of Tartary', and says it had 360 mosques and colleges, though he was not impressed by the students' Persian and Arabic. Shops opened only after the owners had finished their morning tea and closed at three, when trade moved to the Registan square.
p.q: Bokhara is the largest and most populous and wealthy city in the whole region of Tartary. The splendid mosques and magnificent colleges, which are 360 in number, contain students who are unqualified both in the Persian and Arabic languages, but they write a very good hand.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.c: The figure of 360 is a traditional round number rather than a count.

p.h: Moscow burned by the Crimean khan, 1571
p.g: Fletcher tells how the Crimean khan reached Moscow unopposed in 1571 and fired the suburbs. Because the city was built of wood, the blaze consumed most of it in about four hours, and crowds crushed each other at the gates. He gives the rumoured death toll of 800,000, which is far too high.
p.q: (which is all of wood, without any stone, brick, or lime, save certein out roomes) … consumed the greatest part of the citie almost within the space of foure houres, being of thirty miles or more of compasse. Then might you have seene a lamentable spectacle
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: The sentence begins on p.85 ('The citie he tooke not, but fired the suburbs'); only the p.86 part is quoted here, and the OCR of that page is broken by margin notes. The 800,000 dead is hearsay and far too high.

p.h: From Ozbeg's horde to a new church at Almaliq
p.g: The legates wintered with Ozbeg, khan of the Golden Horde, who fed, clothed and rewarded them and sent them on with his own horses to Almaliq, a city of the Chagatai khanate in the Ili valley (near modern Huocheng, Xinjiang). There, only a year after a bishop and six friars had been killed, they bought a plot, built a church and preached openly. The Tartar khans appear as hosts who moved envoys across their realms at their own cost.
p.q: Inde ad primum Tartarorum Imperatorem Usbec pervenimus, & obtulimus literas, pannos, dextrarium, cytiacam, & dona Pape, & post hiemem bene pasti, vestiti, & remunerati magnifice, & cum ejus equis & expensis pervenimus in Armalec Imperii medii, ubi fecimus Ecclesiam, emimus aream, fecimus fontes, cantavimus missas, baptisavimus plures, libere, & publice predicantes
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars of the Golden Horde (Ozbeg Khan) and of the Chagatai 'middle empire'
p.t: From there we came to the first emperor of the Tartars, Ozbeg, and presented letters, cloth, a warhorse, a 'cytiaca' (the editor guesses a strong liquor) and the Pope's gifts; and after the winter, well fed, clothed and magnificently rewarded, we travelled with his horses and at his expense to Almaliq of the middle empire, where we built a church, bought a plot of ground, made wells (or fonts), sang masses and baptised many, preaching freely and in public
p.tg: ozbeg golden horde almaliq church building

p.h: The Toghuzghuz khan's city of twelve iron gates
p.g: In his own route list, Ibn Khurradadhbih says the Toghuzghuz khan's capital lay three months' march beyond Upper Nushajan, through pasture land with large villages. The king lived in a great city with twelve iron gates and had a golden tent on top of his palace, visible five parasangs away, while the Kimek king camped among pastures in tents. Steppe Turks here have both cities and tents.
p.q: De Nouschadjan la supérieure à la capitale du khakân des Toghozghor, il y a trois mois de marche, à travers un pays de pâturage couvert de vastes bourgades … Leur roi réside dans une grande ville fermée par douze portes de fer … Le roi des Toghozghor possède une tente d'or placée au faîte de son palais; elle peut abriter cent personnes
p.s: Ibn Khurradadhbih (French translation by M. J. de Goeje, 1889)
p.t: From Upper Nushajan to the capital of the khaqan of the Toghuzghuz is three months' march, through pasture country covered with large villages … Their king lives in a great city closed by twelve iron gates … The king of the Toghuzghuz owns a golden tent set on the top of his palace; it can shelter a hundred people
p.c: From route reports, not a visit. The capital is usually identified with the Uyghur city Ordu-Baliq (Karabalgasun) in the Orkhon valley, near later Karakorum.
p.tg: uyghurs toghuzghuz capital iron gates golden tent kimek

p.h: The fall of Vladimir: palisade, siege engines, a burning church
p.g: The chronicle describes the Tatar method at Vladimir. They surrounded the city with a palisade (tyn), set up siege engines (poroki), took the city and set it on fire. The prince's family and the bishop, who had taken monastic vows as the end approached, shut themselves in the gallery of the cathedral. The Tatars broke down the doors, piled up timber and burned the church, suffocating everyone inside.
p.q: Безаконьнии же Измаильти приближишася къ граду, и оступиша градъ силою, и отыниша тыномъ всь … поставивше порокы взяша градъ и запалиша й огнемь … вбѣгоша въ святую Богородицю и затворишася въ полатѣ; погании же отбивше двьри зажгоша церковь, наволочивше лѣса, и издушиша вся.
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.t: And the lawless Ishmaelites drew near the city, and surrounded the city in force, and fenced it all round with a palisade … having set up siege engines they took the city and set it on fire … they ran into the church of the Holy Mother of God and shut themselves in the gallery; and the pagans, breaking down the doors, set fire to the church, having piled up timber, and suffocated them all.
p.c: 'Ishmaelites' is a biblical label, not an ethnic name.
p.tg: siege vladimir siege engines palisade church

p.h: Once a land with no towns at all
p.g: Polo begins his history of the Tartars by saying they originally lived on wide plains near 'Chorcha' (Manchuria) with no towns or villages, only rich pastures, and paid tribute to 'Unc Can', whom Europeans called Prester John. Yule's note identifies Chorcha as the Jurchen country and Unc Can as Toghrul, Wang Khan of the Keraits.
p.q: Originally the Tartars dwelt in the north on the borders of Chorcha. Their country was one of great plains ; and there were no towns or villages in it, but excellent pasture-lands, with great rivers and many sheets of water ; in fact it was a very fine and extensive region.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.c: Polo's early Mongol history is second- or thirdhand and mixed with the Prester John legend.
p.tg: origins no towns pasture prester john

p.h: The caliph of Baghdad made to eat his gold
p.g: Riccoldo's version of the fall of Baghdad, told a generation later by a man living in the city. The Tartars found the caliph in a marvellous palace heaped with treasure, starved him for three days, set gold, silver and jewels before him, and when he said he had only kept what his ancestors gathered, poured molten gold into his mouth. They then killed the people for forty days.
p.q: Quo tacente mandauerunt, quod liquaretur aurum et colaretur in os eius, et dixerunt ei: Aurum sitiisti, aurum bibe! Populum autem eius per quadraginta dies continuos occiderunt.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.pe: Tartars under Hulegu; the Abbasid caliph
p.t: When he fell silent they ordered gold to be melted and poured into his mouth, and said to him: 'You thirsted for gold, drink gold!' And they killed his people for forty days on end.
p.c: The molten-gold death is a legend; Persian sources say the caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled, and Hayton (W229) has him starved among his treasure.

p.h: Karasubazar, 'the first Tatar town'
p.g: Arriving in Crimea, Holderness describes Karasubazar (today Bilohirsk) as a crowded market town of narrow, irregular streets and an extraordinary number of shops: about two hundred for fruit alone and as many again for Tatar shoes. Elsewhere she calls its people almost entirely Tatar and its market the cheapest in the Crimea.
p.q: This is the first Tatar town, and is much more singular than pleasing: narrow and irregular streets, presenting a most extraordinary number of shops, occupied by Tatars, Jews, Armenians, Russians, and Greeks. For the sale of fruit alone, there are said to be two hundred shops
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.pe: Crimean Tatars with Jews, Armenians, Russians and Greeks

p.h: Balkh, 'mother of cities', in ruins
p.g: Approaching Balkh, once capital of Bactria, Moorcroft passed ruins said to be the elephant stables of the old kings of Turkestan, then entered through a broken gate into streets of rubbish, broken bricks and crumbling clay walls. On the next pages he says only one covered bazaar was still inhabited, the population was under a thousand families, and there were no relics of antiquity apart from one tiled shrine.
p.q: A short distance in advance brought us to the ruins of some buildings, said to have been the elephant stables of the kings of Turkistan: similar remains accompanied the road to the wall of the modern town, which we entered by a mean gateway, the folding-doors of which were off their hinges and lying in the mud, no insignificant type of neglect and decay.
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

p.h: Peking: a Tartar city and a Chinese city
p.g: Jean de Fontaney, one of the French Jesuits sent by Louis XIV, describes Peking as two joined cities, each four leagues round: the 'Tartar city', with the emperor's palace in the middle, and the 'Chinese city'. The streets were so crowded one could hardly walk. On the same page he describes the great bell of Peking set on a base of brick and stone.
p.q: Peking est composée de deux Villes: la premiere, au milieu de laquelle est le Palais de l'Empereur, s'appelle la ville des Tartares; & la seconde, la ville des Chinois. Elles sont jointes l'une à l'autre, & ont chacune quatre lieues de tour.
p.s: Jean de Fontaney, letter to Père de La Chaise (Zhoushan, 15 February 1703)
p.t: Peking is made up of two cities: the first, in the middle of which is the Emperor's palace, is called the city of the Tartars; and the second, the city of the Chinese. They are joined to each other, and each is four leagues round.

p.h: Karakorum: 'capital for five reigns'
p.g: The geography treatise explains that the Lingbei capital took its name, Helin (Karakorum), from the Qara Qorum river to its west. Chinggis made it his capital in 1220 and it remained the capital of five reigns. A small-character note adds that Ogedei walled the city and built the Wan'an palace in 1235, and goes on to list more halls outside the city built in 1237 and 1238. Khubilai moved the capital to Dadu (Beijing) in 1260.
p.q: 始名和琳以西有哈喇和琳河因以名城太祖十五年平定河北諸郡建都於此初立元昌路改轉運和琳使司前後五朝都焉(太宗乙未年城和琳作萬安宫…)
p.s: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: [Hening circuit] was first called Helin; because west of it is the Halahelin (Qara Qorum) river, the city was named after it. In the fifteenth year of Taizu (Chinggis), having pacified the prefectures north of the Yellow River, he established his capital here. At first Yuanchang circuit was set up, later changed to the Helin Transport Commission. It was the capital for five successive reigns. (In the yiwei year of Taizong [Ogedei, 1235] Helin was walled and the Wan'an palace built.)
p.c: The Siku copy writes 和琳 for the usual 和林. The words 'Taizu established his capital here' in 1220 are the history's claim; the annals date the building of the walls and palace to 1235.
p.tg: karakorum capital wan'an palace walls ogedei

p.h: Kazan: stone ruins of a Tatar capital, now Muscovite
p.g: Evliya calls Kazan a former throne city of Chinggis Khan's line, now 'an ill-fated capital in Muscovite hands'. He says thousands of khans (caravanserais), mosques, madrasas, baths and shops lie as domed and arched ruins, while people now live in some three thousand houses roofed with rushes and reeds, with twenty churches and seven mosques for the many Nogay and Hashdek Muslims.
p.q: ماتقدم بودخی جنقیز خانك تخت‌گاهی ایمش نیجه ملوکدن ملوکه قالمش حالا دست مسقوده بر دارالملك منحوس اولمش نیجه بیك عدد خان وجامع وعمارت ومسجد ومدرسه وتکیه وحمام ودکاکینلر وبزازستانلرك قبابلری وطاق کسرالری وقلعه‌لری رایکان دورور ... حالا اوچ بیك قدر صاز وقامش اورتولی اولری
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars ('Hashdek') and Nogays under Muscovite rule
p.t: Formerly this too was the throne city of Chinggis Khan, passing from king to king; now in Muscovite hands it has become an ill-fated capital. The domes and Chosroes-like arches and fortresses of many thousands of khans, great mosques, charitable foundations, mosques, madrasas, dervish lodges, baths, shops and cloth-halls stand abandoned … Today there are some three thousand houses roofed with rushes and reeds.
p.c: Scholars doubt that Evliya reached Kazan; the description may rest on hearsay. The picture of stone Islamic buildings left as ruins after the Russian conquest (1552) is striking either way.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.
p.tg: kazan ruins mosques madrasas domes muscovy

p.h: The stone houses of ruined Madjar on the Kuma
p.g: Describing the Kuma steppe, the book says the land once had settled people, as shown by ruined towns. On the left bank of the Kuma lie the ruins that Kalmyks call Madsharinka Balgusun, 'the beautiful city Madjar': a ditched enclosure with house foundations, gravestones with inscriptions and seven stone houses still standing. One Arabic inscription was said to record that the people of Madjar left the city for lack of wood and moved into the mountains.
p.q: … Häuser und verschiedenen Grabsteinen mit Inschriften, auch noch sieben stehende steinerne Häuser von mäßiger Größe. Die Grabsteine sollen theils arabische, theils unbekannte Aufschriften haben. Auf einem mit arabischer Inschrift soll stehen: daß das Volk der Madschari die Stadt wegen Holzmangel verlassen und ins Gebürge gezogen sey.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1785)
p.pe: Former inhabitants of Madjar; named by Russians, Kalmyks and Tatars
p.t: … houses and various gravestones with inscriptions, and also seven standing stone houses of moderate size. The gravestones are said to have partly Arabic, partly unknown inscriptions. On one with an Arabic inscription it is said to read that the people of Madjar left the city because of a shortage of wood and moved into the mountains.
p.c: The inscription's content is reported ('soll stehen', 'is said to read'), not read by the author.

p.tg: madjar ruins stone houses inscriptions golden horde

p.h: Bakhchysarai, Eski-Krim and Kefa: where the Crimean khans lived
p.g: Zuev, back from an Academy journey to the Crimea, sketches the khanate's capitals. The khans had lived for over 200 years at Bakhchysarai, having moved there from Eski-Krim (Staryi Krym), the old Genoese city, after Mengli Giray took the sea ports and expelled the Genoese; at first the Tatars had been at Kozlov (Yevpatoria). Under the current khan Şahin Giray the residence had moved to Kefa, the old Theodosia. He adds that rich Tatars and murzas mostly live in the country, not in towns.
p.q: Die Residenz der krimmischen Chans war sonst in Baktschisarai, in welcher Stadt sie über 200 Jahr ihren Sitz gehabt haben. Sie ward dahin von Eski-Krim (Alt-Krim), der Hauptstadt der Genueser, bald nachdem Mengli-Girei Chan alle Seeplätze erobert, und die Genueser aus ihren Besitzungen vertrieben hatte, verlegt.
p.s: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas
p.t: The residence of the Crimean khans was formerly at Bakhchysarai, in which town they had their seat for over 200 years. It was moved there from Eski-Krim (Old Crimea), the capital of the Genoese, soon after Mengli Giray Khan had conquered all the sea ports and driven the Genoese out of their possessions.
p.c: Pallas notes that Zuev's historical information is not entirely reliable; Mengli Giray took Kaffa with Ottoman help in 1475.

p.h: Winter in the towns, summer on the steppe
p.g: Having named the Khazar towns (Sarighshin and a second, garbled name) as the people's winter quarters, Ibn Rusta continues that in spring they go out to the steppe and stay there until winter comes. The two towns held many Muslims, with mosques, imams, muezzins and Quran schools. It is a pattern of town and pasture later seen among the Golden Horde.
p.q: المدينتين فاذا كان ايام الربيع خرجوا الى الصحارى فلم يزالوا بها الى اقبال الشتاء وفى هاتين المدينتين خلق من المسلمين لهم مساجد وائمة ومؤذنون وكتاتيب
p.s: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
p.t: [these two] towns. When spring comes they go out to the steppes and stay there until winter approaches. In these two towns there is a multitude of Muslims, who have mosques, imams, muezzins and Quran schools.
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page, which names the towns.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted.

p.h: Running the gauntlet past Tatar Astrakhan by moonlight
p.g: Nikitin sails down the Volga past Kazan, the Horde and Sarai, then meets three Tatars who warn of a sultan watching for merchants. Paid to guide the party around Astrakhan, they betray it to the khan ('zar'), and the Russian boats are chased. It is a first-person glimpse of the Volga still ruled by Tatar khanates.
p.q: We passed unmolested through Kazan, the Orda, Ooslan, Sarai, and Berekezany, and we entered the river Buzan. Here we fell in with three godless Tartars, who told us false tidings … We sailed by Astrakhan at moonlight. The zar perceived us, and at once the Tartars cried : " Do not fly ;" and the zar ordered the whole orda to chase us.
p.s: Afanasy Nikitin (translated by Count Wielhorski, 1857)
p.c: Translated from a difficult late fifteenth-century Russian text; 'zar' is the translator's rendering of the title Nikitin gives the khan of Astrakhan.
p.tg: volga kazan sarai astrakhan merchants raid

p.h: The last stand at Kazan, 12 October 1552
p.g: Following the chronicles, Erman describes Ivan IV's mines blowing up two towers of the kremlin, a last charge by the Muslim clergy in front of a mosque, and the khan Yediger making his final stand. The defenders handed Yediger over and died fighting. The chronicle also says Yediger set a thousand beautifully dressed young women in the Russians' path to tempt them, without success.
p.q: They surrendered Yediger into the hands of the Russians, exclaiming, "Take our ruler, and treat him as befits his rank; but we die with arms in our hands." It happened as they said; not one of the warriors survived the fall of Kasan, and the independence of the nation terminated on the 12th of October, 1552.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848), following the Russian chronicles
p.pe: Kazan Tatars and the army of Ivan IV
p.c: Russian chronicle tradition, told from the victors' side; the thousand women and the defenders' words are literary touches that cannot be checked.
p.tg: siege of kazan 1552 ivan iv yediger

p.h: Vladimir besieged: scaffolds, catapults and a palisade
p.g: After parading the captured prince Vladimir Iurevich before the Golden Gate so his brothers on the walls could see him, the Tatars camped around the city. On the Saturday before Lent they built scaffolds and set up 'poroki' (stone-throwing engines), and in one night surrounded the whole city with a timber palisade. The next morning they attacked. It is a precise picture of Mongol siege method.
p.q: Въ суботу мясопустную почаша наряжати лѣсы и порокы ставиша до вечера, а на ночь огородиша тыномъ около всего города Володимеря; въ недѣлю мясопустную по заутрени приступиша къ городу, мѣсяца февраля въ 7, на память святаго мученика Ѳеодора Стратилата.
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.t: On Meatfare Saturday they began to prepare scaffolds and set up siege engines until evening, and in the night they fenced the whole city of Vladimir round with a palisade; on Meatfare Sunday after matins they advanced on the city, on the 7th of February, the feast of the holy martyr Theodore Stratelates.
p.c: The editors note that the date and saint's day do not quite match (the feast is 8 February).
p.tg: vladimir siege catapults palisade golden gate

p.h: A khan who loved towns, and chiefs who would not stay
p.g: Mirza Haidar explains why his grandfather Yunus Khan kept leaving Kashgar and Aksu: the Khan liked cities and houses, but his amirs and soldiers refused to live in towns, so he had to follow them back to the steppe. It is a clear statement from inside a Mongol dynasty of the nomads' dislike of town life.
p.q: The substance of the whole matter is that the Khan was very fond of cities and houses, but the Amirs and soldiers of Moghulistan always avoided the towns, and for this reason the Khan spent most of his time in Moghulistan.
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.pe: Moghuls (Muslim Mongols of Moghulistan) under Yunus Khan
p.c: Mirza Haidar says the accounts he heard of these events differed.
p.tg: nomads towns yunus khan aksu kashgar

p.h: Bukhara's brick bazaars and the Registan
p.g: Burnes describes Bukhara as a city of lofty, arched brick bazaars, each trade in its own quarter, massive colleges, mosques and minarets, twenty caravanserais and about a hundred ponds and fountains of squared stone. People believed the tallest minaret, about 150 feet, reached the level of Timur's Samarkand. In the Registan square a visitor could meet Turkmen, Kalmyks and Kazakhs from the deserts.
p.q: when the traveller passes its gates he winds his way among lofty and arched bazars of brick, and sees each trade in its separate quarter of the city; here the chintz sellers, there the shoemakers; one arcade filled with silks, another with cloth. Every where he meets with ponderous and massy buildings, colleges, mosques, and lofty minarets.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.pe: Uzbeks and the peoples of Central Asia

p.h: Tombstones of Bolgars or Tatars at Bolgari
p.g: In December 1768 Pallas visited the ruins of Bolgari on the Volga, which he calls the former capital of the Bolgars, with a rampart about six versts round, a stone minaret and vaulted buildings. The old gravestones there carry mostly Arabic and a few Armenian inscriptions, dated by the Muslim calendar from 619 to 742 (about 1222 to 1341). He reads them as the graves of Bolgars or Tatars of every rank, and notes that some of the dead came from Shemakha and Shirvan, a sign of long-distance trade.
p.q: Man hat bey Bolgari eine Menge alter Grabsteine mehrentheils mit arabischen, jedoch auch einige mit armenischen Aufschriften gefunden… Die Innschriften enthalten nichts, als einen mahometanischen Denkspruch, … den Namen des Verstorbenen und dessen Abstammung oder Würde. Es sind theils vornehme Bolgaren oder Tataren beyderley Geschlechts, theils Geistliche, theils Gemeine und vielleicht Kaufleute.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Volga Bulgars and Tatars of the Golden Horde period
p.t: At Bolgari a great number of old gravestones have been found, mostly with Arabic but also some with Armenian inscriptions… The inscriptions contain nothing but a Muslim motto, … the name of the deceased and his descent or rank. They are partly noble Bolgars or Tatars of both sexes, partly clergy, partly common people and perhaps merchants.
p.c: Pallas relies on translations of the inscriptions made earlier on Peter the Great's orders; the dates are his conversion of Hijri years.

p.h: Samarkand, 'once the metropolis of all Tartary', now in ruins
p.g: Guagnini calls Samarkand a very large city that was once the capital of all Tartary but now lies disfigured by ruins, with many traces of antiquity, and the burial place of Tamerlane, 'that king of the Tartars' who, he repeats, carried the captured Ottoman sultan Bayezid round Asia in a cage bound with golden chains. For modern readers interested in 'lost Tartarian cities', this is a sixteenth-century writer naming a real capital and explaining its ruins by Timur's fallen empire.
p.q: Sarmacandia Orientem versus procedendo, ultra Turcomaniam, urbs est amplissima, quae olim totius Tartariae Metropolis extitit, nunc vero ruinis deformis iacet, una cum multis antiquitatis vestigijs. In ea sepultus est Tamerlanes ille Tartarorum Rex, qui olim Turcarum Imperatorem Baiazetem … captivum aureis catenis vinctum, in cavea velut avem per totam Aziam circumvehebat.
p.s: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
p.t: Going eastward beyond Turkmenia, Samarkand is a very large city, which was once the metropolis of all Tartary but now lies disfigured by ruins, together with many traces of antiquity. In it is buried Tamerlane, that king of the Tartars, who once carried the Turkish emperor Bayezid … captive, bound in golden chains, in a cage like a bird through all Asia.
p.c: Guagnini never went there. Samarkand in the 1570s was a living Shaybanid (Uzbek) city, and the iron-cage story of Bayezid is a famous legend.

p.h: Heliopolis: a round city in Tartary with streets like Amsterdam
p.g: From the top of a column like London's Monument, the narrator surveys Heliopolis. It is round, about three miles across, ringed by a moat fed by rivers, with no building over two storeys. It has three wards named after the Sun, the Council and the Schools, and wide, clean, straight streets like Amsterdam's, lined with trees and flushed by running water.
p.q: It is divided into three Quarters or Wards, of which the first in the heart of the City, derives its name from the Sun; the second from the Council; and the third from the Schools. The Streets are wide, clean and streight, like those of Amsterdam
p.s: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy' (English translation, 1689)
p.w: Claimed travels of the mid-1600s; printed 1689
p.c: Almost certainly fiction: the city is an ideal community in the manner of Campanella's City of the Sun, not a place any traveller recorded.

p.h: Caffa: Tatar and Genoese buildings blown up by Russian officials
p.g: Xavier describes what happened to Caffa after the Russian annexation of 1783. The Genoese walls and towers were pulled down for barracks, the great Turkish baths and the old cathedral-turned-mosque were demolished with pickaxe and gunpowder in 1833, and the Tatar population was expelled. It is a first-hand record of who actually destroyed the old buildings of a Tatar-era city.
p.q: In 1833, the ignorance of a civil governor, Kasnatcheief, completed this afflicting work of destruction, which extended at the same time to the great baths that still remained untouched. A fortnight's work with the pickaxe and gunpowder razed to the ground the two admirable monuments with which the Genoese and the Turks had adorned the town.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.c: The authors are hostile to Russian officials; the demolition itself is widely recorded, but the blame is their own judgement.
p.tg: caffa demolition ruins mosque russian conquest

p.h: Tver rises against the khan's cousin
p.g: Uzbek Khan's nephew Shchelkan came to Tver as envoy. The Moscow chronicle says he meant to kill the Tver princes, rule Tver himself, put Tatar princes into the Rus towns and bring the Christians to the 'Tatar faith' (Islam). Tver rose, and Shchelkan was burned in the prince's palace; the Horde merchants in the town were killed too. Uzbek's revenge helped Moscow's rise.
p.q: Пріиде во Тверь посолъ силенъ зѣло царевичь Щелканъ изъ Орды, отъ царя Азбяка; бѣ же сей братаничь царю Азбяку, хотя князей Тверскихъ избити, а самъ сѣсти на княженіи во Твери, а своихъ князей Татарскихъ хотя посажати по Рускимъ градомъ, а христіанъ хотяше привести въ Татарскую вѣру.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
p.pe: Shchelkan (Chol-khan), son of Diuden and nephew of Uzbek Khan; the people of Tver
p.t: There came to Tver a very powerful envoy, the tsarevich Shchelkan, from the Horde, from Tsar Uzbek; he was Uzbek's nephew, and he wanted to kill the Tver princes and himself sit as prince in Tver, and to set his own Tatar princes over the Russian towns, and he wanted to bring the Christians into the Tatar faith.
p.c: Shchelkan's plans are the chronicler's allegation, written two centuries later from Moscow's side.
p.tg: tver uprising uzbek khan islam horde envoy

p.h: Kunduz: a capital of mud huts and tents
p.g: The capital of the powerful Uzbek ruler Murad Beg was, Wood says, one of the most wretched towns in his lands: a few hundred mud hovels mixed with straw sheds and Uzbek tents, with fields running into the town and a fortress that was just a walled mound. On the next page he describes the ruler's citadel as an irregular building of kiln-dried brick with a moat.
p.q: Kunduz, though the capital of Murad Beg, is one of the most wretched in his dominions. Five or six hundred mud hovels contain its fixed population, while dotted amongst these, and scattered at random over the suburbs, are straw-built sheds intermixed with the Uzbek tent or Kirgah. … Nothing, in short, can be imagined less resembling a metropolis.
p.s: John Wood
p.c: Wood openly links the town's poverty to his low opinion of Uzbek character; the physical description is what he saw.
p.tg: kunduz mud huts tents capital uzbeks

p.h: Kazan, a city of log houses, burned to the ground
p.g: Arriving in June 1843, Haxthausen calls Kazan 'the gloriously situated old Tatar city', but finds it still in ruins from the great fire of 1842. His count is striking: only about one house in nine was stone, the rest were timber, and wooden plank walkways carried the flames from street to street.
p.q: Kazan still lay for the most part in ruins ; a great fire the year before had reduced the vast city to ashes. … Of 4500 houses in Kazan only about 500 were built of stone; the rest were log-houses. The streets, with few exceptions, were unpaved
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

p.h: Mamai's Sarai and Uslam's little towns on the Dnieper
p.g: On the lower Dnieper the book lists a little town called 'Mamai's Sarai' (palace), and below it 'Uslam's little towns', while along the Konskie Vody stand '7 keshens of Tatar mosques'. The first name ties the place to Mamai, the 14th-century Horde commander defeated at Kulikovo. The clerks record the ruins as Tatar but say nothing more about who built them or when.
p.q: А по правой сторонѣ Конскихъ-водъ, отъ Днѣпра 60 верстъ, 7 Кешеней Татарскихъ мечетей. … Да ниже Московки, съ Крымской стороны 50 верстъ, на Днѣпрѣ городокъ Мамаевъ-сарай. А ниже Мамаева-сарая 50 верстъ, на Днѣпрѣ Усламовы городки.
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.pe: Tatars (named after the Horde leader Mamai)
p.t: And on the right side of the Konskie Vody, 60 versts from the Dnieper, are 7 keshens of Tatar mosques. … And below the Moskovka, on the Crimean side, 50 versts, on the Dnieper is the little town of Mamai's Sarai. And 50 versts below Mamai's Sarai, on the Dnieper, are Uslam's little towns.
p.c: The book gives names only; 'keshen' is the Turkic word for a domed tomb.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.
p.tg: mamai sarai dnieper keshene mosques ruins

p.h: Astrakhan: Tatars kept outside the stone walls
p.g: Bruce describes Astrakhan as a Russian city with high stone fortifications, stone towers and wooden houses. The Tartars, the former inhabitants, were no longer allowed to live inside the walls, only in suburbs fenced with palisades. He dates the Russian capture to 1554, after the fall of Kazan.
p.q: The city is of a considerable bigness, and at present inhabited almost entirely by Russians ; the former inhabitants of the country, being Tartars, are not permitted to live within the walls, but in the adjacent suburbs, which are only fenced round with pallisades : the fortifications of the city are all of stone, very high
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.c: Astrakhan fell to Ivan IV in 1556; Bruce's 1554 marks the first Russian campaign.

p.h: Bakhchysarai's mosques and fountains
p.g: The old Khans' capital, Holderness reports, was said to have had thirty-one mosques and seventy-five fountains in 1803. She adds that its fine fountains survived, while those of almost every other Crimean town had been destroyed.
p.q: Bachtcheserai is said to have contained, in 1803, thirty-one mosques, and seventy-five fountains: except Dr. Clarke, no late travellers have noticed the fine fountains which are still preserved here, though those of almost every other town have been destroyed.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: The mosque and fountain count is a reported figure, not her own count.

p.h: The horde: a town of 500 felt huts with a bazaar
p.g: A Kalmyk horde, Bergmann explains, was laid out like a moving town: the huts stood well apart to leave grazing, with three main quarters, the prince's, the priests' and the market, called bazar in Kalmyk as in Tatar and Russian, and the ordinary huts around them. His horde, of about 500 felt huts, was the chief one on the Volga because the head of all the Dalai Lama's followers in Russia lived there. He adds that since the vice-khan Ubashi led more than 70,000 Kalmyk households out of Russia in 1771, no new khan had been named until recently.
p.q: im Kalmükischen, so wie im Tatarischen und Russischen, den Namen Basar führt. … Die Horde, zu welcher ich mich … ist die vorzüglichste von allen kalmükischen Horden an der Wolga; nicht sowohl wegen der Anzahl der Filzhütten, die aus ungefähr 500 besteht, als weil das Oberhaupt aller in Rußland lebenden kalmükischen Anhänger des Dalai Lama, seinen Sitz darin aufgeschlagen hat.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.pl: Kalmyk steppe west of the lower Volga (Kalmykia)
p.t: [the market,] which in Kalmyk, as in Tatar and Russian, is called bazar. … The horde in which I am is the foremost of all the Kalmyk hordes on the Volga, not so much because of the number of felt huts, which is about 500, as because the head of all the Kalmyk followers of the Dalai Lama living in Russia has set up his seat in it.
p.tg: horde camp bazaar lama felt huts

p.h: The court moved to Beijing to face the Tartars
p.g: Describing the province of Nanjing, Cruz says the king once lived there because the land is fertile and pleasant, but moved his court to Beijing ('Paquim') to be nearer the wars against the Tartars. It is an early European statement of why Beijing became the capital.
p.q: Tem esta prouincia dezaseys cidades, residio ãtiguamẽte nesta cidade el Rey por ser terra muy fertil, fresca e apraziuel, e mudou a corte pera ho paquim pera de mais perto acudir aas guerras dos Tartaros.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Ming emperors; Tartars on the northern frontier
p.t: This province has sixteen cities. The king anciently resided in this city, because it is a very fertile, fresh and pleasant land, and moved the court to Paquim [Beijing] in order to attend more closely to the wars of the Tartars.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed.

p.h: Jehol: kept outside the palace gates
p.g: The guard marched through Jehol ('Gehor'), a town about three miles long, to the palace with the presents, but only the ambassador and gentlemen were allowed in. The soldiers went back disappointed, though Holmes says the palace's extent and elegance against the mountains, lit by the rising sun, were beyond description.
p.q: none, except his Excellency and the gentlemen, were suffered to enter the gates ; all the others returned mortified and terribly disappointed … the extent and elegance of it was beyond description, and contrasted with the adjacent mountains and precipices, the scene was great and beautiful indeed
p.s: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)

p.h: Villages of felt tents strung along the valleys
p.g: After defining 'Little Tartary' (Crimea, the Kuban, part of Circassia and the steppe between Russia and the Black Sea) on the previous page, de Tott contrasts the settled Tatars of the Budjak and Crimea, who live in villages, with the Nogais, who have only felt tents. Yet the Nogais are not aimless wanderers: their tents stand in single lines along valleys, forming 'villages' tens of leagues long that mark out each horde.
p.q: The latter province, called at present the Boudjak, is inhabited by Tartars settled in villages, as well as those of the peninsula, but the inhabitants of the three other provinces have only tents made of felt, which they remove at pleasure… their tents ranged along them in one line, form a kind of villages
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.pl: Budjak and Nogai steppe (Bessarabia to the Sea of Azov)
p.pe: Nogai Tatars; Budjak and Crimean Tatars
p.c: The exact length he gives for these tent-villages is damaged in the OCR.
p.tg: nogai felt tents villages little tartary budjak

p.h: 1771: why the Volga towns escaped the Kalmyk flight
p.g: Bergmann retells the great flight of the Torghut Kalmyks from the Volga back towards Zungharia in 1771. The common people were told the march would only go as far as the Emba, as a threat to win concessions from Russia, and were promised plunder of Russian property. Because the hordes on the western bank could not cross to join the rest, the Russian towns on that side were saved, and the fleeing Kalmyks contented themselves with plundering the stores of the Russian, Armenian and Tatar merchants in the horde's bazaar.
p.q: Was den Uebergang der westlichen Horden verhinderte, rettete die russischen Städte, die auf derselben Seite der Wolga lagen. Die Zerstörung derselben wäre unvermeidlich gewesen, wenn die Kalmüken auf dieser und jener Seite im Stande gewesen wären, sich einander die Hände zu bieten.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.t: Whatever prevented the western hordes from crossing saved the Russian towns lying on that side of the Volga. Their destruction would have been unavoidable if the Kalmyks on this side and that had been able to join hands.
p.c: Retrospective history written thirty years later from informants and documents.

p.h: Bakhchysarai: 31 mosques and 517 shops
p.g: Pallas counts the old khans' capital: thirty-one mosques, most of well-built freestone with elegant minarets, Greek and Armenian churches, two synagogues, Turkish baths, sixteen inns (six of stone) and 517 shops. Among them are makers of famous Tartar knives, saddlers, felt-makers and sellers of buza (millet beer). On the next page he adds that Catherine II let the Tatars keep sole possession of the town.
p.q: There are thirty-one metshets in this town, most of which are well built of free-stone, and surrounded with lofty towers of elegant workmanship; … twenty-three, in which large and small Tartar knives, of great celebrity on account of their superior temper, together with other cutlery, are manufactured in great perfection;
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

p.h: Kasimov: a Tatar prince's town on the Oka
p.g: When 'wind-swift' Tatars of Sayyid Ahmad's horde raided Muscovy, Sultan Kasim drove them off, and in gratitude the grand prince granted him a yurt (here, a domain) on the Oka in the Murom district, and 'there he built a town'. Hammer adds that the district town that still bears his name, on a height at the mouth of the Babinka, ringed by an earthen rampart, was in his day home to about five hundred Tatars with their own quarter and mosque. A rare case of a Tatar town founded inside Russia with Russian consent.
p.q: Aus Dankbarkeit dafür räumte der Grossfürst dem Kasim einen Jurt an der Okka, im Gebiethe von Murom, ein. Dort baute er eine Stadt … Seinen Nahmen erhält noch heute die am Einflusse der Babinka in die Okka gelegene Kreisstadt, welche, auf einer Anhöhe gelegen, mit einem Erdwall umgeben, noch heute von einem halben Tausend Tataren bewohnt, durch tatarische Slobode und Moschee das Andenken ihres Ursprunges bewahrt.
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), from the Russian chronicles and a 19th-century geography handbook
p.pe: Sultan Kasim, a Tatar prince in Muscovite service, and his Tatars
p.t: Out of gratitude the grand prince granted Kasim a yurt on the Oka, in the district of Murom. There he built a town … His name is still borne today by the district town at the mouth of the Babinka into the Oka, which, lying on a height and surrounded by an earthen rampart, and still inhabited today by half a thousand Tatars, preserves the memory of its origin through its Tatar quarter and mosque.
p.c: The same sentence oddly says Kasim named the town after 'the Khan of the Crimea'; the modern details come from a handbook, not Hammer's own visit.
p.tg: kasimov tatar town mosque earthen rampart muscovy

p.h: Bulgar on the Volga: mosques and wooden houses
p.g: The author notes that the Burtas live in wooden houses, and that Bulgar is a city with Muslims and mosques, with a second Muslim town nearby, about ten thousand people in all. This is the Bolgar whose later ruins Russian and German travellers credited to the Tatars or the Bulgars. He also remarks on the very short summer nights.
p.q: In the district of Bertas the houses are built of wood. … Bulgar is the name of a city, where there are Mussulmans and mosques ; and near Bulgar is another town called *, where there are also Mussulmans and mosques. In these two cities there are about ten thousand inhabitants.
p.s: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
p.c: The asterisk marks a town name the translator could not read in his manuscripts (probably Suvar).
p.tg: bolgar mosques wooden houses volga bulgaria

p.h: A hundred thousand guards for the emperor's ploughing
p.g: When the Chongzhen emperor went out to plough a furrow at the temple of agriculture as an example to his people, the fear of a Tartar 'flood' was so great that a hundred thousand men guarded him, even though the temple lay inside the city's second wall. A vivid picture of a capital living under threat.
p.q: Tanto se temian entonces de la inundacion de los Tartaros, que con ser el sitio deste Templo en lo interior de la segunda muralla de la ciudad, assistieron a la guarda de la persona Real cien mil hombres
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Chinese court fearing a Tartar (Manchu) attack
p.t: So much did they then fear the flood of the Tartars that, although the site of this temple is inside the second wall of the city, a hundred thousand men attended to guard the royal person
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.

p.h: Samarkand, Timur's capital, shrunk to a provincial town
p.g: Burnes could not safely visit Samarkand, so he describes it from report: once Timur's capital, now a town of 8000 to 10,000 people, with gardens and fields where streets and mosques had been. Three colleges survived, including Ulugh Beg's with enamelled bricks, and Timur's tomb under a lofty dome decorated with agate. Its possession still made a Bukhara king legitimate.
p.q: The city has now declined from its grandeur to a provincial town of 8000, or at most 10,000, inhabitants, and gardens and fields occupy the place of its streets and mosques; but it is still regarded with high veneration by the people.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: Burnes did not see Samarkand; this is hearsay from Bukhara.

p.h: The Tatars' own old capital
p.g: Jesse calls Bakhchysarai one of the few Crimean towns inhabited only by Tatars, who still loved 'the ancient capital of their race'. He lists its trades: leather cushions, slippers, whips and saddles, black lambskin caps, and the shaggy woven cloaks called bourkas.
p.q: This is one of the few towns in the Crimea inhabited solely by Tartars, who still cling with affection and reverence to the ancient capital of their race … a few employ themselves in the manufacture of leather cushions, slippers, whips, saddles, &c., fur caps of the black lamb-skin, and cloaks called bourkas.
p.s: Captain William Jesse

p.h: The Great Khan's square capital, by hearsay
p.g: Conti, as retold by Poggio, describes Cathay, whose lord is the Great Khan, and its capital Cambaleschia (Khanbaliq, the Mongol name for Beijing): a square city with a central palace-fortress and four round corner fortresses linked by a vaulted wall. By Conti's time the Mongols had been expelled and a Ming emperor ruled there, so this is a mix of older fame and report.
p.q: The lord of this country is called the Great Khan, which in the language of the inhabitants means emperor. The principal city is called Cambaleschia. It is built in the form of a quadrangle, and is twenty-eight miles in circumference. In the centre is a very handsome and strong fortress, in which is situated the king's palace.
p.s: Niccolò de' Conti as recorded by Poggio Bracciolini (translated by J. Winter Jones, 1857)
p.c: Conti did not visit Cathay as far as the text shows; the title 'Great Khan' for the ruler of China was out of date by then.
p.tg: khanbaliq cathay great khan fortress palace

p.h: Kazan, called 'Shahr-i Bolgar' by Turks and Tatars
p.g: In a note on old place names, Strahlenberg observes that Turks and Tatars still call Kazan 'Schaire Bolgar', the Bolgar capital, although it was only taken by Tsar Ivan Vasilievich, and his father Vasily already bore the title 'lord of the Bolgars'. He uses this to argue that 'Bolgar' in Russian titles covered all the peoples living along the Volga.
p.q: da nemlich die Stadt Casan anjetzo von den Türcken und Tatern, Schaire Bolgar, d. i. die Bolgarische Haupt-Stadt genannt wird, selbe aber allererst von Iwan Wasiliowitz dem 2ten eingenommen, dessen Vater Wasili Iwanowitz aber bereits den Titul, Herr über Wolgarski, gebraucht
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.t: since the city of Kazan is at present called by the Turks and Tatars 'Schaire Bolgar', that is, the Bolgar capital, though it was only taken by Ivan Vasilievich the Second, whose father Vasily Ivanovich already used the title 'Lord over Wolgarski'

p.h: Twelve catapults at Kolodiazhin, and a town Batu could not take
p.g: After Kiev, Batu marched into Volhynia. At Kolodiazhin he set up twelve siege engines but could not break the wall, so he talked the defenders into surrendering and then killed them. Kremenets, Daniil's town, he judged impossible to take and left alone. Vladimir-in-Volhynia was stormed and its people slaughtered. The passage shows that walls and position still mattered against the Mongols.
p.q: приде къ городу Колодяжьну, и постави порока 12 и не може разбити стѣны, и начатъ перемолвливати люди; они же, послушавше злого съвѣта его, передашася и сами избити быша. … видивъ же Кремянець градъ Даниловъ, яко невозможно пріяти ему, и отъиде отъ нихъ
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Tatars (Mongols under Batu); towns of Prince Daniil of Galicia
p.t: he came to the town of Kolodiazhin, and set up 12 siege engines and could not break the wall, and began to talk the people over; they, heeding his evil counsel, surrendered and were themselves slaughtered. … and seeing Daniil's town of Kremenets, that it was impossible for him to take it, he went away from them

p.h: A Mongol monastery town where Russians trade furs
p.g: The Regent told Turner that Russia had courted the Taranaut Lama (the head lama of the Khalkha Mongols) with embassies and presents, including an illustrated Russian Bible Turner saw. As a result Russian traders visited the lama's seat at 'Kharka', where hides from 'Calmuc Tartary' and the furs of the Russia-China trade changed hands. The same page describes a Kalmyk pilgrimage bringing 200 to 300 horses to the Panchen Lama.
p.q: the Russian traders have since resorted occasionally to Kharka, the place of Taranaut Lama's residence, where they still carry on by their agents a considerable traffic. This principally consists in the sale of bulgar hides, which are prepared in the adjacent districts, and brought also from Calmuc Tartary to the same mart
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.pl: Khalkha, Mongolia (seat of the Taranaut Lama)
p.pe: Khalkha and Kalmyk Mongols; Russian traders
p.c: Reported by the Regent; 'Kharka' is probably the Khalkha lama's monastery town (later Urga, now Ulaanbaatar), but Turner does not locate it.

p.h: Caffa: Tartar songs among the ruins
p.g: Arriving at night at Theodosia, the old Caffa, Alexander found ruin on every side. He heard Tatars singing under an arch in a melancholy strain, as if mourning the decay of the once-flourishing city, and noted the crumbling citadel walls by the shore. The town's houses, he says, were built partly in the Tatar and partly in the Genoese style. From there he crossed the steppe by 'the commercial Tartar city of Karasubazar'.
p.q: we heard some Tartars under an arch singing in a most melancholy strain, and seemingly mourning over the decay of this once flourishing city: the dilapidated walls of a citadel were on the sea-shore, and near them was the stranded wreck of a Greek mystico. The houses of Caffa were built partly in the Tartar and partly in the Genoese style of architecture.
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars; the former Genoese colony
p.c: 'Seemingly mourning' is his romantic reading of a song he could not follow.

p.h: What ‘the Horde’ meant
p.g: Schlözer explains that orda, from which the German word Horde was corrupted, is Turkish and Tatar ordu: first a field camp, then the sutlers' quarter of the camp and everyone who trailed after the army. Because the Mongols and Tatars of Kipchak long stayed nomads and warriors, Russian annals added a third meaning: the headquarters of the khan to whom the Russians paid tribute. ‘Going to the Horde’ meant appearing before the overlord as supplicant, vassal or litigant, just as Greek princes after 1453 went ‘to the Porte’ of the sultan.
p.q: Weil nun die Mogolen und Tataren in Kaptschak lange Zeit Nomaden und blosse Krieger blieben: so kam in den rußischen Annalen eine IIIte Bedeutung auf, nach der Orda das Hauptquartier des tatarischen Heerführers, und zwar desjenigen, unter dessen Joche die Russen stunden, bezeichnete. In die Orde gehen, hieß nun so viel, als wie Supplicant, wie Vasall, wie Beklagter, oder wie Ankläger, vor dem Ober Regenten erscheinen.
p.s: August Ludwig Schlözer (1785), footnote
p.pe: Mongols and Tatars of the Kipchak khanate
p.t: Because the Mongols and Tatars in Kipchak long remained nomads and mere warriors, a third meaning arose in the Russian annals, by which Orda denoted the headquarters of the Tatar commander, namely the one under whose yoke the Russians stood. To go to the Horde now meant to appear before the supreme ruler as a supplicant, as a vassal, as a defendant or as an accuser.
p.tg: horde ordu camp golden horde russian annals

p.h: Tobolsk: a timber capital with two brick buildings
p.g: The capital of Russian Siberia, as Tulishen saw it, had no walls; about a thousand families lived in houses of large timber, with two big brick public buildings and wooden government offices, and a lower town of about 2000 families by the river. It is a plain eyewitness picture of Tobolsk as a Russian timber town seven years after its first stone kremlin was begun.
p.q: It contains above a thousand families, who live in houses constructed of large timber. There are also two large public buildings of brick, and several Government offices built of wood in the usual manner. On the low ground, along the banks of the river, there is another portion of the town, built also of wood, and containing above 2000 families.
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

p.h: The last Yuan heir falls back to Karakorum
p.g: In the summary of the fall of the Mongol dynasty, the Ming founder takes Tatou (Dadu, the Mongol capital at Beijing), which the last Yuan emperor had abandoned, and the heir retreats to Holin, 'or Caracorom', founding a new dynasty in Tartary, the Northern Yuan. Karakorum here is still a working Mongol capital more than a century after its founding.
p.q: Le Prince héritier, fils de cet Empereur fugitif, se retira à Holin ou Caracorom, & fonda en Tartarie une nouvelle Dynastie appellée les Yuen du nord
p.s: Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine (dynastic summary heading vol. 10)
p.pe: Mongols (Yuan dynasty, then the Northern Yuan)
p.t: The heir prince, son of this fugitive Emperor, withdrew to Holin or Karakorum, and founded in Tartary a new dynasty called the Northern Yuan

p.h: Martini watches the Tartars ride back into Peking
p.g: After putting down Jiang Xiang's revolt in Shanxi, the Tartars plundered Datong and burned Puzhou, where the Christians' church was lost. Martini says he saw them return to Peking loaded with riches. Dorgon ('Amavangus') went on to the Western Tartars (Mongols) to ratify the young Shunzhi emperor's marriage and brought back a huge herd of horses.
p.q: But yet they Plundered the City Taitung, and burned the City of Pucheu, where the Church of the Christians also perished. From hence the Tartars returned to Peking, where I saw them enter overloaden with Riches and triumphant Laurels ;
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: Martini says he saw the return himself; the campaign in Shanxi he knew by report.

p.h: Khanbalik and Ordu-Balik: the 'king's city' and the 'royal camp'
p.g: Stritter's description of Beijing explains that the Inner City was part of the city built by Kublai, the 'Kambalu' of Marco Polo, from the Mongol 'Khan' and 'balga' or 'balgasun' (town), meaning the king's city, which Persians and Arabs turned into Khanbalik. It adds that eastern writers used the name for any royal residence, including towns in Tartary, and that Orda-Balik or Ordu-Balik likewise meant 'the royal camp'.
p.q: Was jetzt von Chan Balik u. s. w. ist gesagt worden, gilt auch von Orda Balik, Ordu Balik, oder Orda und Ortu, welche Wörter im Mongolischen königlich bedeuten. So nannte man Orda-Balgasun, Ordo Balga, Ordo Balk, das königliche Hoflager.
p.s: J. G. Stritter, description of Peking, in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 2 (1781)
p.pe: Mongols of the Yuan dynasty; Persian and Arab writers
p.t: What has now been said of Khan Balik and so on applies also to Orda Balik, Ordu Balik, or Orda and Ortu, which words mean royal in Mongolian. Thus the royal camp was called Orda-Balgasun, Ordo Balga, Ordo Balk.
p.tg: khanbalik ordu horde place names kublai

p.h: Chagan-balgas: a Mongol emperor's capital abandoned after a year
p.g: Crossing Chahar country, Bichurin passed the ruins of Chagan-balgas, 'White Wall', known in Chinese history as Shahen. He says it was begun as the Middle Capital for Chinggis Khan's descendants ruling China, but the work was stopped the next year as too heavy a burden on the people, and it had lain in ruins ever since: an earthen rampart seven li round with four gates. A real Mongol-built city, identified from Chinese records.
p.q: Сей городокъ извѣстенъ въ Китайской Исторіи подъ названіемъ Ша-хенъ. Его начали строить … и назначили быть Среднею столицею (по-Китайски Чжунъ-ду) для потомковъ Чингисовыхъ, царствовавшихъ въ Китаѣ; но въ слѣдующемъ году сія работа, какъ чрезмѣру отягчительная для народа, прекращена, и онъ съ того времени донынѣ лежитъ въ развалинахъ. Сей городъ состоитъ изъ землянаго вала и въ окружности содержитъ семь ли
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.pe: Mongols of the Yuan dynasty; Chahar Mongols
p.t: This small town is known in Chinese history under the name Shahen. They began to build it … and designated it to be the Middle Capital (in Chinese Zhongdu) for the descendants of Chinggis reigning in China; but in the following year this work, as excessively burdensome for the people, was stopped, and since then it has lain in ruins to this day. This town consists of an earthen rampart and is seven li in circuit
p.c: The founding year is illegible in the OCR and is omitted. Bichurin passed the ruins at a distance; the history comes from Chinese sources.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: How the Russians built their fort among the Yakuts
p.g: Sauer gives a short history of the conquest: Cossacks first heard of the Yakuts in 1620; a chief named Millach went over to the Russians and gave them forty archers to defeat his rival Tygin. Tribute was collected from 1630, and in 1632 the first ostrog (fort) was built on a hill, later moved to where Yakutsk stands. The Russian town grew out of a local feud.
p.q: Millach is the first chief reported to have gone over to the Russians. … He supplied the Russians with food, and gave them 40 archers to subdue Tygin and his tribe, which was accomplished on Tygin's falling in the field. Tribute was collected in 1630, and in 1632 the first ostrog was built among them on the mountain Tshebedal, but afterwards removed to the place where the town now stands.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)
p.c: Sauer's history comes from local informants and records he does not name.

p.h: Sibir, 'the capital of the Tartars'
p.g: Cochrane retells the Cossack Yermak's conquest: after taking Tyumen he marched on Sibir, 'the capital of the Tartars', twelve miles from where Tobolsk now stands, entered it in triumph on 26 October and 'from the head of a banditti, became a sovereign prince'. He notes that the town's name 'seems to have given name' to all Asiatic Russia. He admits the history is translated from a note printed on a map given him by the governor of Tobolsk.
p.q: Yermak instantly directed his march against Sibir, the capital of the Tartars, distant twelve miles, and on the 26th October entered it in triumph, received the oath of allegiance of his new subjects, and, from the head of a banditti, became a sovereign prince.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), translating a biographical note on a map
p.c: Second-hand history, as Cochrane says on n112.

p.h: The Tartar raid of 1550 and a city retaken
p.g: Portuguese prisoners in China were told that after some years of truce, the Tartars made a great invasion in 1550 and took a very important city. The Chinese besieged it but could not storm it; on the advice of a low-born man they found a way to kill the Tartars and their horses and recovered the city. Cruz does not name the city or the method. The date matches the great Mongol raid on the Beijing region in 1550.
p.q: Afirmouse aos Portugueses q̃ estauam catiuos … q̃ ha algũs annos q̃ auia entre os Chinas e Tartaros treguas: e no anno de cincoenta fizeram os Tartaros hũa grãde ẽtrada na China, da qual lhe tomaram hũa cidade muy principal … por cõselho de hũ homẽ de baixa sorte, tiuerã meo cõ que a elles e aos cauallos matarã, e ficarã outra vez señores da cidade.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.t: It was affirmed to the Portuguese who were captives … that for some years there had been truces between the Chinese and the Tartars; and in the year fifty the Tartars made a great incursion into China, in which they took from them a very important city … on the advice of a man of low rank they found a means by which they killed them and their horses, and became masters of the city once more.
p.c: Prisoners' hearsay; the city is not named.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this blackletter print is garbled); long s normalized, the Tironian sign for 'and' given as 'e', a few contractions (de, per, pro, terra) expanded, other abbreviation marks kept as printed.

p.h: Khanbaliq, a hundred miles round
p.g: Cathay, Pegolotti explains, is a province of many towns, and its chief city, where merchants gather and do most of their business, is Cambalecco (Khanbaliq, the Yuan capital on the site of Beijing). He passes on the merchants' claim that the city is a hundred miles round and packed with people and houses.
p.q: Il Gattajo si è una Provincia, dove à molte Terre, e molti Casali; infra l'altre si ha una, cioè la mastra Cittade, ove riparano mercatanti … la quale Cittade si chiama Cambalecco. E la detta Cittade gira cento miglia, ed è tutta piena di gente, e di magione
p.s: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
p.pe: The Cathay of the Great Khan (Yuan China)
p.t: Cathay is a province in which there are many towns and many villages; among them there is one, the chief city, where merchants resort … and this city is called Cambalecco. And the said city is a hundred miles round, and all full of people and houses
p.c: The hundred-mile circuit is merchants' exaggeration; the city name is badly misread in the OCR ('Cam baleito').

p.h: Few old ruins, many new towns
p.g: Introducing his list of old remains, the author says that in Zungharia more recently destroyed and newly built towns are known than ancient ruins, though on the Ili stand the ruins of a town with four stone towers. The Kazakh steppes, he adds, seem hardly fit for settled farming, yet he lists the 'remains of former inhabitants' known to him: ruins, stone mosques, tombs and burial mounds.
p.q: In der Soongorey sind mehr neuzerstörte und neuerbauete Städte als Ruinen von alten bekannt.
