Am Ilibache … sind Ruinen einer Stadt mit 4 steinernen Thürmen. … Die Kirgisischen Steppen, scheinen wie die Kumanische (S. 97.) und Kalmückische kaum eines europäischen Anbaues mit beständigen Wohnungen, Ackerbau … fähig, doch sind mir folgende Nachbleibsel voriger Bewohner bekannt geworden.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1785)
p.t: In Zungharia more recently destroyed and newly built towns are known than ruins of old ones. On the Ili river … are the ruins of a town with 4 stone towers. … The Kirghiz steppes, like the Kuma and Kalmyk steppes, seem hardly capable of European cultivation with permanent dwellings, farming … yet the following remains of former inhabitants have become known to me.
p.n: OCR normalized (checked against the page image; the OCR text is badly garbled).

p.h: Otrar: where the war began
p.g: Yelü Chucai names Otrar ('O-ta-la'), ruling more than ten other towns, as the cause of the Mongol invasion of Central Asia. Its governor had Chinggis Khan's envoys and several hundred merchants with them killed and seized their goods. Bretschneider notes that Persian historians tell the same story.
p.q: One time the chief of this place ordered several envoys (of Chinghiz), and several hundreds of merchants (who were with them), to be put to death, and seized upon their goods. That was the cause of the army being directed against the Western people.
p.s: Yelü Chucai's Si yu lu, in a Yuan-era abridgement (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Chinggis Khan's envoys and merchants; the governor of Otrar

p.h: Kazan: a noble city rising from its ashes
p.g: Cochrane found Kazan still rebuilding after a great fire five years earlier. A cathedral had stood on the site of the ancient mosque, and the old palace had been destroyed by an explosion in the citadel. Wooden houses and even wooden street paving had fed the fire, and the emperor was now encouraging brick. Of about 40,000 people, he says 12,000 were Tatars, living mainly in the marshy suburbs, with many mosques.
p.q: It had formerly a cathedral on the site of the ancient mosque, as also a palace; both were destroyed by an explosion in the citadel. The destruction of the city was indeed nearly complete, and it is difficult to conceive how any vestige could remain, a high wind driving a mass of flame over houses built, and streets absolutely paved with wood.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: The fire is real (Kazan burned in 1815), but the history of the cathedral and palace is what Cochrane was told.

p.h: Jehol: the emperor's hunting palaces in 'Chinese Tartary'
p.g: Amiot explains why the painter-brother Attiret was summoned north: some ten thousand Dzungars had fled their ruler's usurper with families and baggage to submit to the emperor, who settled them in 'Chinese Tartary' and ordered their leaders to Gé-hol (Jehol, modern Chengde), where he hunted each year and had palaces nearly as fine as those around Peking. Attiret, it was guessed, was wanted to paint the portraits of the leading newcomers at the ceremony.
p.q: L'Empereur leur ordonna de se rendre à Gé-hol, lieu de la Tartarie Chinoise où il va chaque année pour prendre le divertissement de la chasse, & où il a des palais presque aussi beaux que ceux qui sont aux environs de Peking.
p.s: Joseph-Marie Amiot, letter to Père de La Tour (Peking, 17 October 1754)
p.t: The Emperor ordered them to go to Gé-hol, a place in Chinese Tartary where he goes every year for the pleasure of hunting, and where he has palaces almost as beautiful as those around Peking.

p.h: A ruined city on the upper Yenisei
p.g: Under 'Kemtschyk' Strahlenberg notes the ruins of an ancient city where the Kemchik joins the upper Yenisei, and guesses that it was the place in Marco Polo where Kublai Khan's people went to meet the Venetian envoys. Elsewhere he says a Russian from Krasnoyarsk found old writings there, where a chapel once stood.
p.q: Kemtschyk, A River, which falls into the River Yenisei, near its Source, where formerly stood an ancient City, the Ruins of which are yet to be seen.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.pe: unknown builders; Strahlenberg links it to Kublai Khan's time
p.c: The link to Marco Polo is Strahlenberg's own conjecture.

p.h: Astrakhan falls to the Russians without bloodshed
p.g: In his history of Astrakhan, drawn from Russian records, Gmelin tells how the Russian flotilla sailing down the Volga halted at the ruins of Tsarevy Pody, 'which the Russians also call Bolshoi Sarai' (Great Sarai), before sailing on to Astrakhan. The few inhabitants opened the gates and fled, and the city passed to the Russians without bloodshed, while Prince Vyazemsky stormed the camp of the khan 'Emchurtschey' (Yamgurchi) and found many cannon once carried off from Russia. The khan had already sent his treasure and his harem out to sea on ships and fled.
p.q: bey … den von mir schon beschriebenen berühmten Ueberbleibseln der Tatarischen Stadt Zarewpody, welche die Rußen auch sonsten Bolschoi Saray zu nennen pflegen, … Die wenigen Innwohner, so bald sie die Ankunft der Rußen erblickten, öfneten die Thore, und flohen in bekannte Schlupfwinkel. Mitten in ihrer Flucht aber fielen die meiste in die Hände der Christen, und die Stadt übergieng daher an die letztere ohne alles Blutvergießen.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (history compiled from Russian sources)
p.t: at the famous remains, already described by me, of the Tatar city of Tsarevy Pody, which the Russians also usually call Bolshoi Sarai, … The few inhabitants, as soon as they saw the Russians arrive, opened the gates and fled into known hiding places. In the midst of their flight, however, most fell into the hands of the Christians, and so the city passed to the latter without any bloodshed.
p.c: Second-hand history written two centuries after the event, from the Russian side.

p.h: Moscow 'singed' by the Tartars twelve times
p.g: Kohl says no European city except Constantinople had burned so often as Moscow, and that the Tartars alone had set it alight more than twelve times. He adds that about two-thirds of its 12,000 houses were still wooden, the rest built of soft local limestone and brick.
p.q: Constantinople excepted, there is, perhaps, no city in Europe that has been so often burnt to the ground. By the Tartars alone it was well singed more than twelve times.
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.c: A round, popular-history figure.

p.h: Kaffa, 'Little Constantinople', in ruins
p.g: Kaffa (Feodosia), called by the Tartars 'Little Constantinople', had been the Genoese capital in the Crimea and stayed populous under Tartar rule. After the Russian conquest and mass emigration it was 'a prodigious heap of ruins'. Pallas credits the strong freestone walls and towers, still almost whole, to the Genoese, and admires the great mosque in the centre of the town.
p.q: …though it was also called by the Tartars Kutshuk-Stambul, or Little Constantinople. Being erected in an excellent situation very favourable to commerce, it was the principal place in the Crimea, possessed by the Genoese. Even under the Tartar government, it was a populous town, flourishing by its trade,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

p.h: Kazan Tatars in multinational Kizlyar
p.g: Güldenstädt describes the Russian frontier town of Kizlyar on the Terek as eight national quarters inside an earth rampart: Armenians, Georgians, baptised Nogais and Kumyks, Terek Cossacks, Muslim Kumyks and Nogais, Circassians, Persian merchants, and Tatars who had moved from Kazan, farmed, and alone paid the Russian poll tax. Most houses were thin timber frames with wattle walls plastered with clay and chopped straw; few were of logs or brick, because timber was hard to get.
p.q: Das Quartier der Kasanischen Tataren … Sie sind von Kasan hieher gezogen, treiben Ackerbau und zahlen Kopfgeld, welches von keinen andern Einwohnern am Terek geschieht. … Die mehresten sind von dünnen Fachwerk mit geflochtenen und denn mit Thon und gehackten Stroh beworfenen Wänden.
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1787)
p.t: The quarter of the Kazan Tatars … They moved here from Kazan, farm, and pay poll tax, which no other inhabitants on the Terek do. … Most [houses] are of thin timber framing with wattled walls, then plastered with clay and chopped straw.
p.tg: kizlyar kazan tatars town quarters wattle poll tax

p.h: Astrakhan, 'ancient capital of the Tatar kingdom'
p.g: The authors sketch Astrakhan's history: part of Batu Khan's Kipchak empire (the Golden Horde), then an independent Tatar khanate, taken by Ivan the Terrible in 1554, after which its prosperity faded. In their day it was a provincial town, but its old walls and battlemented towers still recalled its past. Over 5,000 Tatars lived there as traders, and their mosques and bath domes gave the town an oriental look.
p.q: At present the ancient capital of the Tatar kingdom is merely the chief town of a government … It contains a great number of squares, churches, and mosques. Its old embattled towers and its walls, which still include a considerable space of ground, remind the traveller of its ancient warlike renown.
p.s: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde and the Astrakhan khanate
p.c: The history is the authors' summary; they do not say who built the walls and towers they saw.
p.tg: astrakhan golden horde walls ivan the terrible

p.h: Wooden forts against the Russians on the Amur
p.g: In an edict of 1682 the Kangxi emperor weighs the report that the Russians (Luocha) raiding the Amur could be driven out with three thousand men. War, he says, is not a good thing; instead he orders fifteen hundred troops from Ula and Ningguta, with boats, cannon and muskets, to build wooden forts at Heilongjiang (Aigun) and Humar facing the enemy, and to farm so they can hold out. This is the start of the Albazin war that ended with the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689).
p.q: 第兵非善事宜暫停攻取調烏拉寧古塔兵一千五百名並置造船艦發紅衣礮鳥鎗及演習之人於黑龍江瑚瑪爾二處建立木城與之對壘相機舉行
p.s: The Kangxi emperor, edict of 1682, in Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: But war is not a good thing; it is fitting to pause the attack for now. Transfer fifteen hundred soldiers from Ula and Ningguta, have boats built, and send red-barrel cannon and muskets with men trained to use them to Heilongjiang and Humar, to build wooden forts in both places, face the enemy's lines and act as opportunity allows.
p.c: The edict is dated 1682 (Kangxi 21) in the heading on the preceding page.
p.tg: russians albazin wooden forts amur kangxi

p.h: Caffa, a fallen Genoese trading city
p.g: Caffa (ancient Theodosia, modern Feodosia) belonged to the Turks, not the Khan. Chevalier describes it as a once-great Genoese trading port that had declined under Ottoman rule but still had five or six thousand houses and a mixed population, mostly Christian, with dozens of churches.
p.q: it was one of the most trading Towns of the Levant … yet there are still remaining about five or six thousand Houses; the Inhabitants are Greeks, Italians, the remainder of the Genoeses, Armenians, Jews, Turks and Tartars, but the most part of them are Christians
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars, Turks, Greeks, Armenians, Jews and Italians

p.h: Omyl, a city the Mongols rebuilt
p.g: In the country of the Black Kitayans (Kara-Khitai), Carpini found a city the Mongols had built anew, with a house put up by the Emperor, where the friars were invited to drink. Rockhill's note explains that Imil was first built by the Kara-Khitai around 1125 and was Guyuk's own appanage.
p.q: After that we entered the country of the Black Kitayans, in which they (i.e., the Mongols) have built anew, as it were, a city called Omyl, in which the Emperor has erected a house where we were invited to drink
p.s: John of Pian de Carpine (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.pe: Mongols in the land of the Kara-Khitai

p.h: The Crimean Tatars' two walled places
p.g: Barbaro says the Crimean plain was ruled by Tatars who could raise three or four thousand horse and had two walled but weak places: Solkhat, also called Crimea ('Incremin', meaning fortress), and 'Cherchiarde', meaning forty places. These are Eski Kırım and Kırk Yer (Chufut-Kale), early seats of the Crimean khans.
p.q: The champaigne of this He of Capha is vnder the Tartariens domynion … they haue twoo places walled, but not stronge, thone whereof is called Sorgathi, which they also called Incremin, that signifieth a forteresse ; and thother Cherchiarde, which signifieth xl placs.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.c: 'He' is the OCR's reading of 'Ile' (isle), Barbaro's word for the Crimean peninsula; the identifications with Eski Kırım and Kırk Yer are modern.

p.h: Tobolsk: Russian hilltop, Tatar lower town
p.g: Ides reached Tobolsk, the capital of Siberia, on 1 July 1692. The upper town on the hill was Russian, strengthened by a stone monastery with watchtowers; the lower town along the Irtysh belonged to Muslim Tatars and Bukharan merchants who traded up the river to the Kalmyks and on to China. He adds that several thousand Tatars served the tsar as horsemen.
p.q: Tobolesk: Which City, besides its own strength, is re-inforced with a large Stone Cloyster, with high Watch-Towers, which may pass for a Fortification. This place is situate on a high Hill … the bottom of which along by the River Rhitisch, is inhabited by the Mahometan Tartars and Buchars, which drive a great Trade up the Rhitisch or Irtis, into the Kalmakian Territories, and carry their Goods to China.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

p.h: Tsar Ivan counts his years from the conquest of Kazan and Astrakhan
p.g: Ivan IV's letter to Queen Elizabeth is dated not only by the year of the world and his reign but by his two great conquests of Tatar khanates: Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1554 to 1556). The seizure of these Tatar cities was so important to Muscovy that it became part of the Tsar's official dating and of his title.
p.q: the 23 yere of our Empire, since the wynning of Casane xvii yere, and of Astrecane XV yere.
p.s: Tsar Ivan IV, letter to Queen Elizabeth written at Vologda, 1569 (contemporary English version; ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Former Tatar khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan, now Russian
p.tg: kazan astrakhan conquest ivan iv khanate

p.h: A market at the Mongol camp
p.g: Besides the official caravans to Beijing, Russian merchants traded privately at the headquarters of the Mongols, a moving camp usually pitched where the Orkhon and Tuul rivers meet. An annual fair grew up there, which on the next page becomes a scene of drunken Russian 'riot and confusion' that angered the Kangxi emperor.
p.q: private merchants continued as before to carry on a separate trade with the Chinese, not only at Pekin, but also at the head quarters of the Mongols. The camp of these roving Tartars was generally to be found near the conflux of the Orchon and Tola, between the Southern frontiers of Siberia and the Mongol desert. A kind of annual fair
p.s: William Coxe (compiling Müller and Pallas)

p.h: The Khan's army at the siege of Zbarazh
p.g: In the history section, Chevalier describes the Polish commander Firley fortifying the town and castle of Zbarazh (in today's western Ukraine) before a huge Tartar and Cossack army surrounded it. He compares the host to those of Attila and Tamerlane, and on the next page stresses that the Khan himself was present in person.
p.q: the Army of the Tartars and Cossacks came and encompassed them in on all sides in such numbers, that there have been seldom seen the like forces together, since those of Attila and Tamerlan
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars allied with Khmelnytsky's Cossacks
p.c: A partisan Polish-side narrative of the siege; the numbers are rhetorical.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Uvek: a Tatar town known only from coins and trinkets
p.g: Nine versts from Saratov, Lepekhin visited Uvek, the site of an old Tatar settlement (he heads the page 'a Tatar gorodishche', or town site). He says it belonged to the Tatars because silver and copper Tatar coins, rings, earrings and copper vessels are found there, but that no records say who destroyed it or when. He also thought the wild hemp growing round about had been sown long ago by the Tatars who once lived there.
p.q: Daß dieser Ort den Tatarn gehört habe, beweisen … die sowohl silbernen, als kupfernen, tatarischen Münzen und andere Kleinigkeiten, welche man daselbst antrift, z. E. Ringe, Ohrengehänge, kupferne Geschirre und dergleichen. Von wem und wenn der Platz zerstöret worden, läßt sich wegen gänzlichen Mangels an Nachrichten nicht sagen.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.pe: Tatars (the former inhabitants of a Golden Horde town site)
p.t: That this place belonged to the Tatars is proved by the silver as well as copper Tatar coins and other small things found there, for example rings, earrings, copper vessels and the like. By whom and when the place was destroyed cannot be said, for complete lack of records.
p.c: The next page, where he lists the dates on the coins he kept, is too damaged in the scan to quote.
p.tg: uvek coins golden horde ruins saratov

p.h: Astrakhan, where the khan wintered on a road of hay
p.g: Ibn Battuta travelled with the khan's court to Astrakhan, 'one of his cities', on the Volga (Athal). The khan wintered there, and when the river froze the local people were ordered to lay thousands of bundles of hay on the ice as a roadway.
p.q: At this place the Sultan resides during the very cold weather ; and when this river, as well as the adjoining waters, are frozen, the King orders the people of the country to bring thousands of bundles of hay, which they do, and then place it upon the ice, and upon this they travel.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

p.h: Kalmyks in Leh, and the mosque that came of it
p.g: The only mosque in Leh, Izzet Ullah was told, was founded by Ibrahim Khan, a Mughal noble sent to help the king of Ladakh when the Kalmaks had seized the city. The king converted to Islam and swore vassalage, then soon went back to his own faith. This is a memory of the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal war of 1679 to 1684. On the same page he describes Leh's thousand houses of stone or unburnt brick, three or four storeys high.
p.q: It was founded by Ibrahim Khan, one of the nobles of the Mogul Court, at a time when the Kalmaks … had got possession of the city, and the Raja of Tibet had recourse to the Sultan of Hindustan for succour. Ibrahim Khan, who was sent to his assistance, defeated the Kalmaks, and restored the Raja;
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.c: Local tradition about events some 130 years earlier.

p.h: Siberia, the Nogays and a coin-minting town on the Irtysh
p.g: Following 'Lorenzo' again, the Cihannuma says the Nogay Tatars are subject to the Crimean khans, that north of them lived the Bulghars, and north of the Bulghars lies the land of Siberia, mostly forest, where some Nogay Tatars live. There is a town there called Hanam, very prosperous and famous for trade, where jewels are sold, and Tatars of Cathay and Muscovites gather to trade. It gives an Ottoman reader a Siberia of towns and markets, not an empty waste.
p.q: بولغار قومندن شماله سیبریا اولکه‌سی دوشر اکثری اورمانلقدر ونوغای تاتارلرینك بعضی انده ساکن اولورلر وهمه خانام برشهرلری وار غایت معمور وتجارتله مشهوردر
p.s: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
p.pe: Nogay Tatars, Siberian Tatars ('Kesellu' Tatars), Bulghars
p.t: North of the Bulghar people lies the land of Siberia; most of it is forest, and some of the Nogay Tatars live there. They have a city called Hanam, very prosperous and famous for trade.
p.c: Compiled from European atlases; the town names are garbled forms of names on Western maps.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled).

p.h: Staryi Krym, the old capital, in ruins
p.g: Holderness calls Starai Krim, 'once the capital of the peninsula', little better than a heap of ruins, its few inhabitants Armenian shopkeepers. In a footnote she says the ruins were very extensive and that the town had still been flourishing at the Russian conquest.
p.q: These ruins are very extensive, and we know that at the first conquest of the country by the Russians, it was a flourishing town, though not to be compared to what it was when held by the Genoese.
p.s: Mary Holderness (footnote)
p.c: Staryi Krym (the medieval Solkhat) was a Golden Horde and early Crimean Khanate centre; her remark that it was once 'held by the Genoese' may confuse it with nearby Genoese Caffa.

p.h: Kuznetsk, a Russian town among 'blacksmith Tatars'
p.g: Describing the Kuznetsk mountains, Humboldt notes that the Russian town of Kuznetsk on the Tom was founded in 1618 in the midst of Tartars, or Turks, who worked iron. A footnote explains the name: the Russians called them 'Kuznetsk Tatars', from kuznets, blacksmith. He adds that the first Russian foundations of Tobolsk, near the old Tatar capital of Isker or Sibir, and of Tiumen were only some thirty years older.
p.q: la ville de Kousnetsk (au milieu de Tartares ou Turcs forgerons en fer) fut fondée en 1618, c'est-à-dire déjà 31 ou 32 ans après les premières fondations russes de Tobolsk (près de l'ancien Isker et Sibir) et de Tiumen.
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt
p.pe: Kuznetsk Tatars (Turkic iron-smiths of the Tom valley)
p.t: the town of Kuznetsk (in the midst of Tartars, or Turks who were iron-smiths) was founded in 1618, that is, already 31 or 32 years after the first Russian foundations of Tobolsk (near the old Isker and Sibir) and of Tiumen.
p.tg: kuznetsk blacksmiths tobolsk isker siberian tatars

p.h: Tatar forts on the Irtysh stormed by Yermak's men
p.g: The 1882 editor matches Spafarii's list of Tatar villages on the Irtysh with the Tobolsk chronicle of Semyon Remezov. In 1582, that chronicle says, Yermak's officer Bogdan Bryazga stormed a fortified Tatar town at the mouth of the Aremzyanka, and further down met resistance at the old Tatar fortress of Turtas, whose traces the historian Müller later searched for in vain. Beyond Turtas, Spafarii's list shows Tatar villages giving way to Ostyak ones.
p.q: Слѣдуя внизъ по Иртышу, при устьѣ р. Аримдзянки (гдѣ Спаѳарій называетъ Аримдзянскую волость), Брязга взялъ приступомъ татарскій укрѣпленный городокъ … Здѣсь въ лѣтописи упоминается старинная татарская крѣпость, Туртасское городище, слѣды котораго тщетно разыскивалъ исторіографъ Миллеръ во время своего путешествія по Сибири.
p.s: Yu. V. Arsenyev (editor's note, 1882), summarising the Tobolsk (Remezov) chronicle
p.t: Going down the Irtysh, at the mouth of the Arimdzyanka (where Spafarii names the Arimdzyansk district), Bryazga took by storm a fortified Tatar town … Here the chronicle mentions an ancient Tatar fortress, the Turtas gorodishche, whose traces the historiographer Müller sought in vain during his journey through Siberia.
p.c: Editorial note resting on the late Remezov chronicle (c. 1700), not on Spafarii. The printed dash is shown as a comma.

p.h: Sarai, the khan's great capital
p.g: Returning from Constantinople, Ibn Battuta found the khan had moved to his capital, El Sarai, which he calls very handsome and very large. He met its leading scholar, a Khwarezmian imam whom the khan visited every Friday. The abridged text gives little more about the city itself.
p.q: This city of El Sarai is very handsome and exceedingly large. Of its learned men is the Imam, the learned Nooman Oddin, El Khavarezmi. I met him in this place.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: The full Rihla describes Sarai's quarters and peoples at much greater length; this abridgement cuts it down.

p.h: Kaffa: a walled port of many nations
p.g: The fullest city description in his Tartary chapter is of Kaffa, the Genoese port in Crimea. He counts six thousand houses inside the inner wall and eleven thousand within the outer walls, three bishops (Roman, Greek and Armenian), Muslim and Jewish places of worship, and four thousand houses in the suburbs.
p.q: A city called Kaffa, which lies by the Black Sea, and is surrounded by two walls. Within one wall are six thousand houses, in which are Italians, Greeks, and Armenians; it is a chief city on the Black Sea
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.pe: Genoese colony within Golden Horde territory
p.c: Kaffa was built and run by the Genoese, not by the Tartars, though it lay in lands they claimed.

p.h: The Iron Gate city of Alexander razed by the Tartars
p.g: Sent west with 10,000 horsemen, the Mongol general Jebe ('Gebesagada') took towns before they knew he was coming, killing the armed men but, Sanudo says, sparing the people and leaving gold untouched. At the Caucasus he reached Alexandreta, built by Alexander, later called the Iron Gate, which blocks the way from deep Asia. The Tartars entered it suddenly and 'overthrew both citizens and place from the foundations'.
p.q: peruenitque ad magnum montem Caucasum, vbi Alexandretam Alexander ædificauit, quæ postea Portæ ferreæ dicta est. Hæc transitum prohibet de profunda Asia ad maiorem. Hanc autem inexpugnabilem ciuitatem, intrantes subitò terram Tartari, tam ciues quam locum funditus euerterunt.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: and he came to the great mountain Caucasus, where Alexander built Alexandreta, which was afterwards called the Iron Gates. This blocks the passage from deep Asia to the greater. This impregnable city the Tartars, entering the land suddenly, overthrew from its foundations, both citizens and place.
p.c: Compiled history; the attribution of Derbent's walls to Alexander is medieval tradition (they are Sasanian).
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: derbent iron gate alexander jebe destruction

p.h: 'Kremlin' as a Tartar word for fortress
p.g: In his alphabetical glossary Strahlenberg claims that 'Kremlin' is a Tartar word meaning fortress, and that the Tatars call the Crimea 'Crimm' because of the ancient rampart and ditch at Perekop. He adds that western Tartars and Uzbeks call the Great Wall of China the 'white fortress'. This is his own word-guessing, but it shows how 'Tartar' origins were read into Russian names early on.
p.q: Cremmelin, or Crimmelin; the Name of the Czar's Palace, in the City of Muscow. This is a Tartarian Word, and signifies a Fortress, But not a Flint, as Kremm does in the Sclavonian Language. Thus the Precopensian Tartary is call'd, by the Tartars, Crimm or Cremm, on Account of a Rampart and a Mote, which was there in ancient Times,
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: An etymology offered without evidence; it should not be taken as established.

p.h: A Tatar boy prince in an old stone castle at Kasimov
p.g: At Kasimov on the Oka the embassy met its first Muslims. A twelve-year-old Tatar prince lived with his mother and grandfather in an old stone castle that had once been a fort, under the Tsar's protection. He politely refused baptism until he was old enough to choose, and sent the travellers sheep, mead, beer and butter his mother had churned herself.
p.q: This City lies on the right side of the River Occa, in the Principality of Cassinon in Tartary, and there it was we first met with any Mahometans. Not far from the City, in an old stone Castle, which had sometime been a Fort, lived a young Prince of that County
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

p.h: Krasnoyarsk, where twenty horses stood saddled day and night
p.g: The compiler describes Krasnoyarsk as a large town heavily garrisoned with Cossacks and cavalry against raids by the Kirgiz, so that twenty saddled horses had to stand day and night on the market square before the governor's house. The garrison also guarded the western side against the Mongols and 'the Tartars under them', and the town's name is explained as 'red whirling-river town'.
p.q: Krasnajar ist eine grosse Stadt, von dem Czar starck mit Cosaken und Reuterei besetzet, gegen dem Einfall der Kirgisen, um deren willen auf dem Markt vor des Gouverneurs Haus Tag und Nacht 20. Pferde gesattelt stehen müssen
p.s: Anonymous compiler (Der allerneueste Staat von Siberien, Nuremberg 1720)
p.pe: Kirgiz (Yenisei Kyrgyz) raiders; Mongols and their subject 'Tartars'
p.t: Krasnoyarsk is a large town, strongly garrisoned by the tsar with Cossacks and cavalry against the incursions of the Kirgiz, on whose account twenty horses must stand saddled day and night in the market before the governor's house
p.c: Compiled from reports of Swedish prisoners and travellers, not seen by the compiler.

p.h: Hohhot, the Blue City, and its walls
p.g: Under 'walls and moats' the gazetteer describes Guihua cheng, whose Mongol name is Kokekhota (Blue City): two li around, two zhang high, with north and south gates and an outer wall with three gates. It notes that the Ming gave it its Chinese name when Altan Khan submitted. Nearby was the new Qing fortress of Suiyuan, built in 1739. The gazetteer ties the town's Chinese name to Altan Khan's submission to the Ming in the 1570s.
p.q: 歸化城(在殺虎口邊城外二百里蒙古名庫庫河屯周圍二里高二丈南北門各一外郭東西南三面三門明諳逹歸順改賜今名
p.s: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: Guihua city (200 li beyond the frontier wall at Shahukou; its Mongol name is Kuku Hetun [Kokekhota, Blue City]; two li in circuit and two zhang high, with one gate each on the north and south; the outer wall has three gates on its east, west and south sides. When Anda [Altan Khan] of the Ming period submitted, it was given its present name.
p.c: The gazetteer does not say who built the walls; the Ming history (W131) describes Chinese renegades building walled settlements for Altan Khan in this area.
p.tg: hohhot kokekhota walls altan khan gates

p.h: A friar goes to Sarai to learn the language
p.g: Kuun cites the Franciscan Pascal of Vitoria, who in 1337 went to the 'ancient city of Sarai on the bank of the Volga' to learn Turkish among the Cumans and studied it there for a whole year. Sarai was the capital of the Golden Horde, and the story shows missionaries living in the Horde's own city.
p.q: Fra Pascal de Victoria anno 1337 in antiquam urbem Serai ad ripam Volgae, uti ipse ait, linguae turcicae ediscendae causa ad Cumanos contendit et illic per unum annum integrum studiis linguae quam maxime operam navabat.
p.s: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), citing a letter of Pascal of Vitoria
p.pe: Cumans in the Golden Horde capital
p.t: Friar Pascal of Vitoria in 1337, as he himself says, hurried to the Cumans in the ancient city of Sarai on the bank of the Volga in order to learn the Turkish language, and there worked as hard as he could at the study of the language for one whole year.
p.c: Kuun paraphrases Pascal's letter; Pascal was killed in Central Asia in 1340.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: Coins struck at Sarai, capital of the Golden Horde
p.g: Klaproth reads the coins found at Madzhar: nearly all were minted at Sarai or New Sarai, the Golden Horde capitals, under khans from Mengu-Timur to Tokhtamysh and Pulad (1270s to 1408), some with names in Mongol script. One is struck at Astrakhan. The latest coin helps date the town's end to about 1400.
p.q: The great Ssulthan Ghajats Eddunia (the prop of the world) Toktégu-chan, the Just… Coined at Ssarai, the capital, in the year 715; that is, A.D. 1315.
p.s: Julius Klaproth, transcribing coin legends (English translation, 1814)
p.c: The Arabic legends are garbled in the OCR; the translations are Klaproth's.
p.tg: coins sarai tokhtogu numismatics golden horde

p.h: The horses announce that the town has fallen
p.g: Describing how the Tartars stormed Chinese walled towns, Palafox says archers lying or kneeling on the wall top drove the defenders from their guns while others scaled the walls or seized a gate. Once horses got inside, their noise and neighing told everyone the town was taken. On the next page he notes that the Tartars stormed first and only brought up artillery afterwards, the reverse of European practice.
p.q: they quickly discover, that the Town is taken… Thus the Tartarian horses first proclaim the Victory.
p.s: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (English translation, 1676)
p.c: The OCR on this page is garbled; the quote keeps only the readable words.

p.h: Shahbad: 'the abode of the king' in ruins
p.g: Shahbad, once the largest town at the south end of the Kashmir valley and named as a royal seat, had become a ruin by Vigne's visit. The Mughal palace was hardly worth a remark and its grounds were overgrown. Vigne blames much of Kashmir's decay on recent Sikh rule, famine and earthquake rather than on any lost civilization.
p.q: Shahbad, the abode of the king, which was the largest place at the southern end of the valley, is now a ruin ; and the palace of the Moguls is scarcely worth a remark. Its environs are overgrown with nettles and wild hemp.
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)

p.h: Tyumen, a walled town of Tatar traders
p.g: Reaching Tyumen on 25 June 1692, Brand found a large town with a rampart and walls, mostly fallen into decay. Most of its people were born Tatars who had settled there, many baptised into the Russian faith and the rest Muslims, who traded far into the Kalmyk lands and Bukhara and paid tribute to the tsar. He calls them a courteous people.
p.q: gelangten wir in die Stadt Tumeen an, so ein ziemlich groß begriffener Ort, und mit Wall und Mauren umgeben, aber mehrentheils verfallen, die Einwohner dieser Stadt aber sind meistentheils gebohrne Tartarn, so sich allhier gesetzet, wovon ihrer viel den Rußischen Glauben angenommen, die andern aber den Mahometischen Glauben haben, diese Leute treiben in frembde Oerter, als in Kalmucker und Bugarien Lande, grosse Handelung
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.t: we reached the town of Tyumen, a fairly large place surrounded with rampart and walls, but mostly decayed; the inhabitants of this town are mostly born Tartars who have settled here, many of whom have taken the Russian faith, the others the Muslim faith; these people carry on great trade in foreign places, such as the Kalmyk and Bukharan lands

p.h: The ordu: a ring of tents that became a court
p.g: Schott explains the word ordu, the source of European 'horde': in Mongolian and Turkish it first meant an army camp and then, above all, the khan's court camp, and in a footnote he adds that the Mongols also used it for a palace. He derives it from a root meaning a circle, so that an ordu is literally a ring of tents. At the foot of the page he starts on another root, kor, 'to build', which gives kurghan (kurgan), and on the next page he says the word meant a building in general and then a grave monument.
p.q: Erstgenanntes Wort bedeutet im Mongolischen und Türkischen Heerlager, dann insonderheit Hoflager. Wie nun das mongolische kür-dü kreisförmiges Ding, Rad, von kür (das auch kürijen und küren [s. oben] erzeugt hat), so or-du ein Zeltenkreis, von der stärkeren, aber des consonantischen Anlauts entbehrenden Wurzel or.
p.s: Wilhelm Schott
p.t: The first-named word [ordu] means in Mongolian and Turkish an army camp, then in particular a court camp. Just as the Mongolian kür-dü, a circular thing, a wheel, comes from kür (which has also produced kürijen and küren [see above]), so or-du is a circle of tents, from the stronger root or, which lacks the initial consonant.
p.c: The derivation from a root meaning 'circle' is Schott's own etymology.

p.h: Tobolsk: a stone monastery, and Muslim Tartars trading to China
p.g: In the inserted Ides section, Tobolsk is a strong place with a great stone monastery with high towers, standing on a hill where the Irtysh and Tobol meet. The foot of the hill and the Irtysh bank are inhabited by Muslim Tartars and Bukharans who trade along the river among the Kalmyks and go on as far as China.
p.q: il arriva heureusement à Tobol ou Tobolskoi, place forte, où l'on trouve un grand monastere de pierre, garni de hautes tours … Le pied de cette montagne & le rivage de l'Irtis sont habités par des Tartares & des Bachares Mahometans, qui trafiquent beaucoup sur ce fleuve parmi les Kalmuques, & vont même delà jusques à la Chine.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
p.t: he arrived safely at Tobol or Tobolsk, a strong place, where there is a great stone monastery with high towers … The foot of this hill and the bank of the Irtysh are inhabited by Muslim Tartars and Bukharans, who trade a great deal on this river among the Kalmyks, and even go from there as far as China.
p.c: Not seen by de Bruyn; a summary of Ides inserted by the French editors.

p.h: Kazan taken, its khan seized alive
p.g: After the mines blew open the walls, the Russians stormed the city. The author describes the slaughter, the soldiers taking countless riches and leading away princesses, murzas' wives and children 'from the greatest to the simplest', and the capture of Khan Ediger-Mahmet, found on the wall and nearly killed before some Tatars cried out that he was their tsar.
p.q: Во граде же христьянстіи люде взяша неисчетное богатество и въ полонъ многое множество княгинь и мурзиныхъ женъ и детеи, просто рещи, отъ великихъ даждь и до простыхъ всѣхъ плениша.
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Khan Ediger-Mahmet and the people of Kazan; Ivan IV's army
p.t: And in the city the Christian people took uncountable riches, and into captivity a great multitude of princesses and murzas' wives and children; to put it simply, from the great down to the simple, they captured them all.

p.h: A Qing view of Russia: the White Khan took Kazan and Tobolsk
p.g: Klaproth translates the entry on Russia from the official Manchu imperial geography of China. It calls the Tsar the 'Tsagan khan' (White Khan, a Mongol title), places his residence at Moscow, and says the Russians seized the lands of Kazan and Tobolsk about 160 years earlier. It shows how the fall of the Tatar khanates looked from Beijing.
p.q: Le roi des Oros est le Tsakhan khan; il réside dans une ville appelée Moskowa, qui n'est pas trop éloignée de la mer du nord-ouest. … Leurs khans ont régné pendant vingt-trois générations, durant une période de plus de trois cent cinquante ans. Il y a cent soixante ans qu'ils s'emparèrent des territoires de Kazan et de Tobolsk.
p.s: Official Qing (Manchu) geography of the empire, translated by Julius Klaproth
p.pe: Russians as seen by the Qing court; Kazan and Siberian khanates
p.t: The king of the Oros [Russians] is the Tsagan khan; he lives in a town called Moscow, not very far from the north-western sea. … Their khans have reigned for twenty-three generations, over a period of more than three hundred and fifty years. It is a hundred and sixty years since they seized the territories of Kazan and Tobolsk.
p.c: Tobolsk itself was a Russian foundation of 1587 beside the old Tatar capital Sibir; the Chinese text uses it as the name of the region.
p.tg: kazan tobolsk qing white khan russia

p.h: 70,000 Turks and Tatars besiege Astrakhan
p.g: The English merchants Banister and Ducket were held up at Astrakhan for six weeks by a great army of Turks and Tatars sent by the Sultan to take the town from Russia. Winter and news of a Russian relief army made them give up. The editors' note adds that this was the Ottoman campaign that also tried to dig a canal between the Volga and the Don.
p.q: In this towne of Astracan they were somewhat hindered of their iourney, and staied the space of 6. weekes by reason of a great armie of 70,000. Turkes and Tartares, which came thither vpon the instigation of the great Turke, hoping either to haue surprised it suddenly, or by continuance of siege to win the same.
p.s: Narrative written by 'P. I.' from the report of Lionel Plumtree, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.tg: astrakhan siege ottoman crimean tatars volga-don canal

p.h: Walled Muslim towns of Kashgar and Yarkand, unlike the Eleuths
p.g: Amiot explains why the Muslim princes of Yarkand and Kashgar thought they could resist the Qing after the Eleuths fell: unlike the nomad Eleuths they had firearms, walled towns and strongholds, and Muslim neighbours to help them. The Qing generals took both towns; the younger Khoja's head was sent to Peking in a box and displayed over the palace's Wu Men gate.
p.q: Ils avoient par dessus les Eleuths l'avantage des armes à feu, ils avoient des villes murées, quelques places fortes, & ils pouvoient être secourus par les autres Mahométans leurs voisins.
p.s: Joseph-Marie Amiot (note to the Eleuth monument)
p.pe: Muslim townspeople of 'Little Bukharia' under the two Khojas; contrasted with the Eleuths
p.t: They had the advantage over the Eleuths of firearms; they had walled towns and some strongholds, and they could be helped by the other Mahometans, their neighbours.
p.c: These town-dwellers are the Turkic Muslims of the Tarim oases, not Tartars in Amiot's usage; the passage is useful for the contrast.

p.h: The Volga, 'the river on which the city of Sarai stands'
p.g: In his list of rivers al-Umari describes the Athil (Volga) as the river on which the city of al-Sarai is set, flowing through 'the deserts of the Qipchaq' into the Caspian. Sarai was then the capital of the Golden Horde, with which the Mamluks were allied.
p.q: ومن ذلك نهر أثيل . وهو المركب عليه مدينة السراى . ومخرجه من عين تنبع فى ذيل جبل قاقونا ، ثم يقتبل الجنوب آخذا بغرب فى صحارى القبجاق على شمالى معادن الفضة ، حتى يصب فى بحر طبرستان
p.s: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
p.t: Among them is the river Athil. It is the river on which the city of al-Sarai is set. Its source is a spring welling up at the foot of Mount Qaquna; then it turns south, heading west through the deserts of the Qipchaq, north of the silver mines, until it flows into the Sea of Tabaristan [the Caspian].
p.c: Geographical summary; the source and course are partly traditional.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted.

p.h: Could the empty stone city be Karakorum? The editor wonders
p.g: In his notes, the 1882 editor Arsenyev calls the report of an abandoned fortified city on the Tola 'extremely interesting' and suggests it might be the ruins of Karakorum, the old Mongol capital, which the French scholar Abel-Rémusat had placed near where the Tula joins the Orkhon.
p.q: Свѣдѣніе о запустѣвшемъ укрѣпленномъ городѣ (у каменныхъ стѣнъ котораго „починки немного надобно“), стоящемъ близъ рѣки Толы ниже Урги, чрезвычайно интересно и могло бы относиться къ развалинамъ Каракорума, который, по свидѣтельству Абеля Ремюза, … находился, вѣроятно, недалеко отъ сліянія р. Тулы съ Орхономъ.
p.s: Yu. V. Arsenyev (editor's note, 1882)
p.pe: Mongols (ruins of the old Mongol capital, as the editor suggests)
p.t: The report of the deserted fortified city (whose stone walls 'need little repair'), standing near the Tola river below Urga, is extremely interesting and could refer to the ruins of Karakorum, which, according to Abel-Rémusat, … probably lay not far from the confluence of the Tula with the Orkhon.
p.c: The editor's guess, not Spafarii's. The ruins of Karakorum were identified on the Orkhon at Kharkhorin in 1889, some distance from the Tuul, so the identification is doubtful.

p.h: Pest overrun and burned
p.g: After the defeat at the Sajó, crowds gathered in Pest, 'a great township' on the far bank of the Danube, and began to dig a rampart and weave wicker fences, against the advice of Prince Coloman. The Tartars camped around it and shot it to pieces for two or three days, broke in and slaughtered the people; then they set fire to the whole town. Thomas says about ten thousand more burned in the Dominican house where they had taken refuge.
p.q: Igitur Tartarorum acies suis castris circa totam Villam defixis, coeperunt eam undique impugnare … & quia locus non satis erat munitus die quadam uno impetu Tartari irruperunt, nec fuit ultra congressio, nec resistentia ulla.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: So the Tartar battle lines, having fixed their camps around the whole township, began to attack it from every side … and because the place was not well enough fortified, one day the Tartars burst in with a single rush, and there was no more fighting and no resistance at all.
p.c: Thomas's figure of over 100,000 dead in one day, given on the same page, is not credible as a count.

p.h: Yarkand: from Mughal khans to Kalmyks to China
p.g: Izzet Ullah sketches Yarkand's history: once ruled by Moghul khans, it fell to the Kalmaks, whose chief lived at Ili. Then an epidemic killed the Kalmak ruler, his family and vast numbers of his people, rival Khoja factions fought, and China conquered the country about sixty years before his visit. This matches the collapse of the Dzungar state in the 1750s.
p.q: fell into the hands of the Kalmaks. The chief of the Kalmaks, entitled the Tura, resided at Ila, and a deputy on his part was sent to Yarkand. After some time an epidemic occurred amongst the Kalmaks, which carried off the Tura, his children, his chief men, and a vast number of people.
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.c: Local oral history; Wilson's footnote adds dates from other sources.

p.h: Caydon, the city the men of Tartary built
p.g: Mandeville describes the Great Khan's capital: beside an old city of Cathay the Tartars built a new one, Caydon, with twelve gates and a palace with a tree-covered hill, lakes and a bridge. This is almost word for word Friar Odoric's 'Taydo' (Dadu, Beijing), and makes a good exercise in spotting a borrowed passage.
p.q: After go men yet to another old city toward the east. And it is in the province of Cathay. And beside that city the men of Tartary have let make another city that is clept Caydon. And it hath twelve gates, and between the two gates there is always a great mile
p.s: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
p.pe: Men of Tartary (Mongols of the Yuan dynasty)
p.c: Copied from Odoric (see W041, Taydo), not an independent witness.

p.h: Royal palaces and tombs burned, 1635
p.g: In his year-by-year mission history Semedo notes that in 1635 the Tartars raided widely and set fire to royal palaces and the tombs of ancient princes, adding (as a moralist) a second fire to the one in which the princes' souls already burned. Mandarins were punished for negligence. He does not name the place.
p.q: Los Tartaros discurrian con sus assaltos, haziendo varios desperdicios, i llegaron a hazer bolar en humo de horrible incendio los Palacios Reales, i los sepulcros de los antiguos Principes, que alli yazian
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.t: The Tartars roamed about with their assaults, causing various destruction, and went so far as to send up in the smoke of a horrible fire the royal palaces and the tombs of the ancient princes who lay there
p.c: Based on mission letters; the site is not named.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.

p.h: Bukhara, a century after the Tartars
p.g: Bukhara, the chief city beyond the Oxus, had still not recovered, Ibn Battuta says, from being ravaged by the Tartars more than a century earlier. He found nobody there with any learning. Here 'Tartars' means the Mongol armies of Genghis Khan.
p.q: then, after one stage, we came to Bokhara, which is the principal city of the country beyond the Gihon. After it had been ravaged by the Tartars, it almost entirely disappeared : I found no one in it who knew any thing of science.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: Bukhara was sacked again by Ilkhanid Mongol troops in 1273, so not all the damage he saw dated from 1220.

p.h: A city of clay and a citadel on a man-made hill
p.g: Bukhara, three to four versts across, was ringed by a clay wall with loopholes; its streets were so narrow that a laden camel scraped the houses. Most houses were of clay, richer ones partly of brick, one or two storeys high, flat-roofed and windowless to the street. The khan's citadel, the Ark, stood on a clay hill about 60 feet high which Eversmann calls a colossal work of human hands, brick-faced below and clay above, with a palace of glazed brick on top. He does not call Bukhara a Tatar city; it is included here for its plain account of how a great Central Asian city of the time was built.
p.q: Die Wohnhäuser sind grösstentheils von Lehm aufgebaut, reichere auch zum Theil von Ziegelsteinen, von einem und zwei Stockwerken, aber nicht höher. … Die Burg des Chans (Aerk genannt) liegt erhaben auf einem grossen gegen 60 Fuss hohen Lehmhügel, der ein kolossales Menschenwerk ist; man braucht fast eine halbe Stunde dazu, ihn zu umgehen; die untere Hälfte ist, wenigstens ausserhalb, von Ziegelsteinen, die obere von Lehm
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.t: The dwelling houses are mostly built of clay, the richer ones partly of brick too, of one and two storeys, but no higher. … The khan's castle (called the Ark) stands high on a great clay hill about 60 feet high, which is a colossal work of human hands; it takes almost half an hour to walk round it; the lower half is of brick, at least on the outside, the upper of clay
p.c: Bukhara was an Uzbek emirate, not a 'Tatar' state; Eversmann uses 'Tatar' only for the Russian merchants there and for the language.
p.tg: bukhara ark citadel clay brick city walls

p.h: Kazan, the 'cauldron' town of furs
p.g: Barbaro notes the turn of the tide: the Russians once paid tribute to the Tartar emperor, but Moscow had now subdued Kazan on the Volga. He calls Kazan a town of great trade, the source of most furs sent to Moscow, Poland, Prussia and Flanders, and says its name means 'cauldron'.
p.q: nowe they haue subdued a towne called Cassan (which, in our tonge, signifieth a cawldron), that standeth on the ryver Ledil, on the lefte hande as you go towards the Sea of Bachu … This is a towne of great merchaundise. From whense cometh the most parte of the furres that are caried to Musco and into Polonia, Prusia, and Flandres
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.c: Moscow's 1487 capture of Kazan installed a client khan; the city was not annexed until 1552.

p.h: Leh: a town of a thousand houses
p.g: Gerard describes Leh, the capital of Ladakh, standing a few miles from the Indus, as a town of nearly 1,000 houses built like those of Spiti, with Muslim and Hindu shopkeepers but mostly Tartar (Tibetan) people. It holds fairs attended by Punjabis, Yarkandis, Kinnauris and Kashmiris.
p.q: … contains nearly 1,000 houses, built like those in Speetee. There are some Mahommedan and Hindoo shop-keepers, but the greater part of the inhabitants are Tartars.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.c: Gerard does not say he visited Leh; the description reads as gathered from others.

p.h: A trading city drowned by diverting its river
p.g: Carpini tells how the Mongols took the rich, crowded city of Orna, a port full of Christians and Muslim merchants: finding it hard to storm, they dammed the river that ran through it and drowned the city with everything in it. He goes on to the sack of Kiev and the Russian towns.
p.q: Aprés cela ils vindrent deuant la cité d'Orna qui estoit fort peuplée, & là y auoit plusieurs Chrestiens Gazares, Russes, Alans, & autres, & quelques Sarasins … Les Tartares voyans qu'il estoit difficile de la prendre de force, ils s'aduiserent d'arrester la riuiere qui passe par ceste ville, & ainsi la submergerent auec tout ce qui estoit dedans.
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongol armies); Khazar, Russian and Alan Christians; Muslim traders
p.t: After that they came before the city of Orna, which was very populous, and there were many Christians there, Khazars, Russians, Alans and others, and some Saracens … The Tartars, seeing that it was hard to take by force, decided to stop the river that runs through the city, and so they drowned it with everything that was in it.
p.c: Carpini places Orna on the Don, but the story matches the Mongol flooding of Urgench in Khwarazm (1221), and historians have often suspected a confusion; treat the location as uncertain.

p.h: Balkh: slaughtered by Genghis, built of frail brick
p.g: Burnes lists Balkh's fate: its people 'butchered in cold blood by Jenghis Khan', then ruled by the house of Timur, the Mughals, Nadir Shah, the Afghans and Bukhara. In 1832 it had under 2000 people. Looking at its crumbling remains he doubts it was ever a substantial city, since its buildings rested only on brick foundations.
p.q: Its inhabitants were butchered in cold blood by Jenghis Khan; and under the house of Timour it became a province of the Mogul empire. … and from the frail materials of which its buildings are constructed, the foundations being only brick, I doubt if Balkh ever were a substantial city.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.pe: Inhabitants of Balkh; Mongols under Genghis Khan

p.h: Astrakhan, city of a Tartar founder
p.g: Hanway gives the history as he heard it: Astrakhan was named after a Tartar founder, Hadgee Terkan, was ruled by Tartars for ages and taken by Ivan the Terrible in 1554. In his day it had some 70,000 people, including many Armenians and 'Tartars of various denominations', an 'epitome of Asia'. The old brick wall was ruinous and the houses mostly mean wooden ones.
p.q: …and derives its name from Hadgee Terkan a Tartar by whom it was founded. It was for many ages subject to the Tartars, from whom it was taken by Ivan Wassilowitz czar of Muscovy in 1554, … It contains about 70,000 inhabitants, among whom are many Armenians and Tartars of various denominations, with a few Persians and Indians.
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
p.c: The founder story (Hadji Tarkhan) is a traditional etymology repeated by Hanway.

p.h: Beijing's 'Tartar cities' and a wall built by earlier Tartars
p.g: The description of China printed with Lange's journal explains that Beijing is three cities in one: an outer suburb now called the Chinese city, and two 'Tartar cities', inside which lies the emperor's city with its yellow or red wall. The outer earthen rampart, it says, was built about 500 years earlier by the western Tartars when they ruled China for some thirty years, and is now almost fallen.
p.q: Die Stadt Pekin ist dreyfach: erstlich die Vorstadt, die man heut zu Tage die Sineser-Stadt nennet: die andern zwo sind der Tartaren Städte, und innerhalb dieser, des Kaysers Stadt oder die Stadt mit der gelben oder rothen Mauer, in welcher des Kaysers Pallast ist. Die Vorstadt hat einen Wall, denn die Chineser Tuchin oder die erdene Mauer nennen, ist ohngefehr vor 500. Jahren gemacht worden, von denen Westwerts gelegenen Tartaren
p.s: Description of China printed with Lange's journal in Weber
p.pe: Manchus (the ruling 'Tartars') and the earlier Mongol (Yuan) rulers
p.t: The city of Peking is threefold: first the suburb, which is nowadays called the Chinese city; the other two are the cities of the Tartars, and within these the emperor's city, or the city with the yellow or red wall, in which the emperor's palace stands. The suburb has a rampart, which the Chinese call Tuchin or the earthen wall, made about 500 years ago by the Tartars living to the west
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. The history of the rampart is garbled: Mongol rule of China lasted about ninety years, not thirty.
p.tg: beijing tartar city walls manchus yuan

p.h: Karasubazar's trading khans and the ruins of old Krim
p.g: At the market town of Karasubazar he counts twenty-three mosques and describes the merchants' khans (warehouses) that look like old Gothic palaces. Eski-Krym, the old Tatar capital that gave the whole peninsula its name, now lies in ruins in a fertile plain, its gardens abandoned.
p.q: They reckon in Carasubasar, twenty-three mosques, and three Greek or Armenian churches. The khans, or houses of depôt for commerce, resemble old Gothic palaces… Eski-krym, anciently Krim, which, under the Tatars, gave its name to the whole peninsula, is situated, with its extensive ruins, in a fertile plain at the foot of the mountain
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

p.h: Tobolsk after the great fire
p.g: Lesseps reached Tobolsk, the Siberian capital between the Irtysh and the Tobol, soon after a fire had burned most of it. The lower town had only wooden houses, which went first; the upper town on its hilltop had several fine stone buildings, but the fire reached them too and left only walls. On the next page he describes silent townspeople already rebuilding houses and shops in stone.
p.q: Cette capitale, située entre ces deux fleuves, doit avoir été une des plus belles villes de Sibérie, mais elle venoit d'être la proie d'un incendie qui en avoit réduit en cendres la plus grande partie. Précédemment elle étoit divisée en deux, la ville basse & la ville haute: l'une bâtie sur la plate-forme d'une montagne, présentoit plusieurs beaux édifices en pierre; l'autre n'avoit que des maisons de bois
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: This capital, situated between these two rivers, must have been one of the finest towns in Siberia, but it had just fallen prey to a fire that had reduced most of it to ashes. Formerly it was divided in two, the lower town and the upper town: the one, built on the flat top of a hill, had several fine stone buildings; the other had only wooden houses
p.tg: tobolsk fire stone buildings wooden houses

p.h: Chinese in the suburbs, Tartars in the city
p.g: Shut in covered carts, the soldiers saw little of Beijing except high brick walls and low, rather shabby brick houses. Holmes notes the division of the capital: the Chinese lived in the suburbs, the Tartars in the city proper. He found the suburb's buildings and shops elegant.
p.q: we then entered the suburbs, which the Chinese inhabit, as the Tartars do the city. The buildings here were truly elegant, and the shops of the tradesmen well stocked with all kinds of goods.
p.s: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)

p.h: A brick bell tower and brick monastery near the half-ruined city of Taimingtschin
p.g: From reports, Pallas lists the temples of eastern Mongolia: a remarkable brick tower called Chonchotu with many idol figures and iron bells, and on the Locho a monastery of many brick temples, less than thirty versts from the half-deserted city of Taimingtschin and forty from an old earth fortress. A footnote sends the reader to Ides's and Witsen's accounts of this ruined 'city of the gods' (Burchan-Chotton) and its idol tower, the same ruins Adam Brand described.
p.q: ordentliche Tempel und an lezteren Bach auch ein merkwürdiger Thurn von Ziegeln, mit vielen Götzenfiguren und eisernen Glocken, Chonchotu genant, am Flusse Locho selbst aber, unterhalb dem Bach Elbingol, ein mit vielen Tempeln aus Ziegeln erbautes Kloster … nicht dreißig Werste von der halbwüsten Stadt Taimingtschin und etwan vierzig von einer am Locho vorhandnen alten Erdfestung
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (Naun, Locho and Sharamurin rivers)
p.t: proper temples, and on the latter stream also a remarkable tower of bricks with many idol figures and iron bells, called Chonchotu; but on the Locho river itself, below the stream Elbingol, a monastery built with many temples of brick … not thirty versts from the half-deserted city of Taimingtschin and about forty from an old earth fortress on the Locho
p.c: Pallas says he had only imperfect reports of these distant places.
p.tg: brick pagoda bells ruined city monastery

p.h: Kokotan (Hohhot): earth walls, brick towers, glazed temple roofs
p.g: The first Chinese-ruled town Baikov reached was Kokotan, today's Hohhot in Inner Mongolia. He says its people spoke Mongol and its governors were sent from Beijing. The wall was of earth with towers of burnt brick and iron-bound oak gates, but no cannon; inside and outside were many brick temples with green-glazed tile roofs, and a big market of stone shops.
p.q: а городъ Кококотанъ земляной: башни кирпичные: кирпичь жженой; проѣзжіе башни велики: по двои ворота въ башнѣ; … а ворота дубовые, окованы желѣзомъ; … а огненного бою, пушекъ и пищалей нѣтъ, а кумирницъ въ городѣ и за городомъ много: кумирницы кирпичные, а верьхи у нихъ дѣланы по Руски, а крышы черепицею муравленою.
p.s: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
p.t: and the town of Kokotan is of earth, with towers of brick, burnt brick; the gate towers are large, with two gates in each tower; … the gates are of oak, bound with iron; … there are no firearms, cannon or muskets; and there are many idol-temples in the town and outside it: the temples are of brick, their tops made as in Russia, and the roofs of glazed tile.
p.tg: hohhot brick towers temples glazed tile market

p.h: Almaliq: a Muslim ruler beside a Mongol governor
p.g: At Almaliq in the Ili valley the local Muslim ruler and the Mongol governor (darughachi, Bretschneider explains) rode out together to greet the sage, a glimpse of how the Mongols ruled a town through its old prince. The city was named for its apples (alma in Turkic). The travellers bought cloth woven from 'vegetable wool', cotton, then little known in China, saw people carrying water in jars on their heads, and heard the locals praise the Chinese as 'very able men' when they saw a Chinese well-bucket (pp.70-71).
p.q: The ruler of the realm of P'u-su-man came out of the city, together with the Mongol ta-lu-hua-chi, to meet the master. We stopped at a fruit orchard west (of the city). The people here call a fruit a-li-ma; and as the place is famed for its fruits, the city received the above name.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Muslim ruler of the P'u-su-man; Mongol darughachi
p.c: P'u-su-man (Muslims) and darughachi are Bretschneider's readings of the Chinese transcriptions; he places Almaliq near modern Kuldja.

p.h: Omsk, once a Tatar stronghold
p.g: Cochrane says Omsk was 'one of the strong places of the Tartars' and held out against Yermak. Across the Irtysh lay the land of the wandering Kazakhs (whom he calls Kirgeese), with no fields or houses, and he says Kazakh and Kalmyk children could be seen in Omsk as slaves, sold by their parents for tobacco or spirits.
p.q: Omsk was one of the strong places of the Tartars, and successfully withstood the attacks of the great Yermak. The country round is fertile as to its soil, though not extensively cultivated: it is one vast plane as level as a floor.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: Doubtful: the Russian fortress of Omsk was founded in 1716, long after Yermak, and no Tatar fortress there is known to have resisted him.

p.h: Kashgar, the 'many-coloured brick' city
p.g: The Qing gazetteer describes Kashgar as one of the great cities of Turkestan, so famous that foreigners called all East Turkestanis 'Kashgarians'. It lists its Manchu and Chinese garrison, taxes paid in cash, grain and cotton cloth, silk and gold-thread products, and skilled jade polishers and goldsmiths. A note explains the name as 'many-coloured brick building', because the city had many buildings of coloured brick.
p.q: Кашб значитъ разноцвѣтный, гаръ кирпичное зданіе. Здѣсь много разноцвѣтныхъ кирпичныхъ зданій, отъ чего и названіе дано. Еще говорятъ, что слово Кашгаръ означаетъ богатый.
p.s: Note in the Chinese original ('Author's note'), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
p.t: Kash means many-coloured, gar a brick building. There are many buildings of coloured brick here, which is where the name comes from. It is also said that the word Kashgar means rich.
p.c: A folk etymology from the Chinese compiler; the true origin of the name Kashgar is uncertain.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.
p.tg: kashgar brick oasis city qing etymology

p.h: Derbent's stone towers, cut down by the Tartars
p.g: Rubruck passed through the Iron Gate (Derbent) on the Caspian. He credits Alexander the Great with building it, following medieval legend, and describes a narrow town with strong walls and towers of dressed stone. The Tartars had levelled the tops of the towers and the parapets, making them even with the walls. Rockhill's note says Muslim geographers credited the Persian king Khosrow Anushirvan.
p.q: The next day we came to the Iron Gate, which Alexander the Macedonian made … It has very strong walls without moats, and towers of great dressed (politis) stones ; but the Tartars have destroyed the tops of the towers and the parapets of the walls, making the towers even with the walls.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.c: The Alexander attribution is legend; the walls are Sasanian Persian work.
p.tg: derbent iron gate walls alexander destruction

p.h: Rey, 'the Market of the Universe', brought to nothing
p.g: Near Saveh Chardin passed the scattered traces of Rey, once, the Persian histories said, the greatest city in Asia, with incredible numbers of streets, baths and mosques. He blames its fall on sectarian wars together with Tartar incursions, and notes that a later prince tried to rebuild it after making peace with 'Cazan-Can, King of Persia, of the Race of the Tartars' (the Ilkhan Ghazan), but failed.
p.q: These Wars, together with the Incursions of the Tartars, destroy'd the Potent Rey, and reduc'd it to nothing before the end of the sixth Age of the Mahumetan Epoche.
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.c: Taken from Persian and Arabic histories; the huge figures for Rey on the previous page Chardin himself doubts.

p.h: The brick ruins of Saraichik on the Ural River
p.g: At the Cossack outpost of Saraichik on the Yaik (Ural) River, Pallas walked the ruins of what he calls a Nogai city, whose people were said to have migrated to Khiva. Inside a rampart four to five versts round he saw foundations and vaults of brick houses, fragments of glazed, porcelain-like pottery in white, blue and yellow, and small copper and silver coins ruined by the salty soil.
p.q: Innerhalb dem Wall befinden sich viele Spuren, Grundlagen und Gewölber von gemauerten Gebäuden, nach welchen mitten in der Stadt einige sehr ansehnliche Wohnungen müssen gestanden haben. Die Ziegel, deren man sich bedient hat, sind länglicht und ziemlich groß gestrichen… Von altem Geschirr findet man itzt fast nichts mehr, als Stücke von zerbrochenem Porcellanartigen Irdenzeug, welches eine starke und schöne Glasur hat
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: Within the rampart there are many traces, foundations and vaults of masonry buildings, from which it appears that some very handsome dwellings must have stood in the middle of the town. The bricks used are oblong and moulded fairly large… Of old vessels one now finds almost nothing but pieces of broken porcelain-like earthenware with a strong and fine glaze.
p.tg: saraichik nogai brick glazed pottery coins

p.h: Balkh, 'mother of cities', a mass of ruins and dust
p.g: Mohan Lal found the ancient city of Balkh reduced to ruins and dust among orchards, with a broad bazaar roofed crudely with rafters, hay and mud, whose shops opened only on Tuesdays. An Uzbek customs officer searched their baggage. Locals called Balkh the mother of cities, founded by a son of Noah.
p.q: This was formerly a very large and populous city, but at present nothing is to be seen except a mass of ruins and dust. Orchards are scattered in every spot … The bazar of Balk, though broad, is irregularly roofed with rafters, hay, and mud.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)

p.h: Ningxia, a Tartar capital ruined by Genghis Khan
p.g: Passing through the half-deserted city of Ning-Hia, Huc gives its history: a prince 'of Tartar race' from Tou-Pa founded a small state near the Yellow River in the tenth century with Ning-Hia as its capital (the Tangut Xi Xia kingdom). It flourished for two centuries until 1227, when it was ruined by Genghis Khan. Here 'Tartar' covers the Tanguts too.
p.q: In the tenth century, a prince of Tartar race, a native of Tou-Pa, … having induced a few hordes to follow him, came, and formed, despite the Chinese, a small state not far from the banks of the Yellow River. He chose for his capital, Hia-Tcheou, which afterwards came to be called Ning-Hia. … in 1227, it was involved in the common ruin, by the victories of Tchinggiskhan
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.tg: xi xia tangut ningxia genghis khan

p.h: Khwarezm, largest city of the Turks, where skipping prayers meant a whipping
p.g: After forty days across the steppe by camel cart, by way of Saraichuk with its bridge, Ibn Battuta reached Khwarezm (Urgench), which he calls the largest and most crowded city of the Turks, ruled by an emir for Uzbek Khan. He praises its people as the best-mannered he had met, and describes a whip hung in every mosque to punish those who missed prayers.
p.q: This is the largest city the Turks have, and is very much crowded, on account of the multitude of its inhabitants. It is subject to the sultan Uzbek Khan, and is governed on his part by a great Emir, who resides within it.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

p.h: Tarki, capital of 'Dagestan Tartary'
p.g: Peter the Great's army camped below Tarki, seat of the shamkhal. Bruce describes a town of over 3,000 houses on a hillside, without walls, with two-storey flat-roofed houses where women walked in the evening, each with its own garden and spring.
p.q: This city of Tarku, being the metropolis of Dagestan, contains above three thousand houses, and is very full of inhabitants ; the houses all two stories high, platformed at top, standing close to each other : the women walk upon them in the cool of the evenings, as the men do in the streets. Every house has a garden stored with all kinds of delicious fruits
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.tg: tarki dagestan flat roofs houses kumyks

p.h: Repairing a Mongol khan's palace at Karshi
p.g: Before marching on Samarkand, Timur orders the palace of 'Kepee Khan' at Karshi repaired, a fortress built at the town gate and other buildings put up. The translator's note explains that the old town of Nakhsheb took the name Karshi (Turkic for 'palace') from a palace built there by a Mongol prince, the Chaghatayid khan Kebek.
p.q: I prepared for marching to Samerkund, but first gave orders to repair the palace of Kepee Khan, whose name in the Turky language, was Karshy ; and I commanded that a fortress should be erected at the gate of the town, and some other buildings constructed.
p.s: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
p.c: The wording makes 'Karshy' the palace's Turkic name; the footnote is by the translator.
p.tg: karshi palace fortress kebek khan building

p.h: Yarkand, a magnificent city 'under the Chinese'
p.g: Gerard passes on what he was told about Yarkand, forty days north of Leh. It is described as a large, magnificent city of lofty buildings, ruled by China, where the people are 'Moguls' who speak Turkish and Russian merchants often come. He had not seen it himself.
p.q: Yarkund is described as being a large and magnificent city, containing many splendid and lofty buildings ; it is under the Chinese, and the inhabitants are Moguls, and speak the Turkish language. It is said that Russian merchants often visit Yarkund.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.c: Pure hearsay; Gerard never went north of the Himalaya.

p.h: A city surrendered by treaty, but its towers pulled down
p.g: Passing through Zwanjefoe (Quanzhou), the Dutch envoys learned that the city had never been taken by the sword: its commander handed it over to the Tartars by agreement, keeping his office. Even so, as a sign of victory, the Tartar had all the city's towers torn down except three. A small, precise record of what conquest meant for a Chinese city's skyline.
p.q: Noit is de Stadt door het zwaert, by de Tarters overwonnen, maer wierd, door den Krijgs-overste … met verdrag overgegeven … Ten teken evenwel der overwinning, liet de Tarter al de torens, behalve de voorzeide drie, afbreken en ten gronde slopen
p.s: Olfert Dapper, from the journals of the second Dutch embassy (Jan van Kampen and Constantijn Nobel)
p.t: The city was never conquered by the sword by the Tartars, but was handed over by its military commander … by treaty … As a sign of victory, however, the Tartar had all the towers, except the three mentioned before, torn down and razed to the ground
p.c: The envoys saw the city but the story of its surrender was told to them.
p.n: OCR normalized; the two printed columns, interleaved in the OCR, are read in order.

p.h: Crimean Tatar towns: Perekop, Bakhchysarai and ruined Caffa
p.g: Bergeron sketches the Crimean khanate of his own day. The Tatars' chief fortress is Perekop on the canal across the isthmus, the khans' royal seat is at Bakhchysarai, and they hold other towns such as Crim, from which they are called Crimeans. The Turks hold Mangup and Caffa (ancient Theodosia), the old Genoese trading port, which he says now lies half deserted, with ruins of a very great city.
p.q: Or la principale ville ou forteresse de ces Precopites, située sur ce canal pour la garde du pays, est Precop, ou Perecop; le siege royal des Chans, ou Cans est à Bacasaray, ou Almasaray; & y a plusieurs autres villes de leur partage, comme Crim, dont ils sont surnommez Crimenses, ou Krimski
p.s: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634)
p.t: Now the chief town or fortress of these Precopites, set on this canal to guard the country, is Precop or Perekop; the royal seat of the Khans is at Bacasaray or Almasaray; and they have several other towns in their share, such as Crim, from which they are called Crimenses or Krimski
p.c: Compiled from other writers, not observed.

p.h: Sarra, capital of Comania, 'almost all laid waste'
p.g: In his geography of Comania (the Kipchak steppe, the Golden Horde's land) Hayton names its chief city Sarra, 'once a very good city', which the Tartars have almost entirely ruined. The editor identifies Sarra with Sarai on the Volga, and later in the book Hayton says the Tartar king Toqta holds his seat in a city called 'Sera'.
p.q: La maistre cité du roiaume de Comaine est apellée Sarra, laquele fu ancienement molt bone cité, mès les Tartars l'ont presque toute gastée.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: The chief city of the kingdom of Comania is called Sarra, which was once a very good city, but the Tartars have laid it almost entirely waste.
p.c: Sarai is usually credited to the Golden Horde itself (founded under Batu in the 1240s to 1250s), so Hayton's 'once good, now wasted' is puzzling; he may mean another Kipchak town or be confused.

p.h: Maimachin: a wooden frontier town guarded by Mongols
p.g: Following Pallas, Coxe describes the Chinese trading town of Maimachin facing Russian Kiakhta, with frontier posts inscribed in Russian and Manchu. Its only defence was a wooden wall and a small ditch dug in 1756 during the Qing wars with the Kalmyks (Dzungars), and its gates were watched by a garrison of Mongols in tattered clothes armed with clubs.
p.q: Maimatschin has no other fortification than a wooden wall, and a small ditch of about three feet broad; the latter was dug in the year 1756, during the war between the Chinese and the Calmucs … over each of these gates there is a wooden guard-house for the Chinese garrison, which consists of Mongols in tattered clothes, and armed with clubs.
p.s: William Coxe (from P. S. Pallas's travels)
p.pe: Chinese merchants; Mongol garrison of the Qing
p.c: The following pages describe the town's one-storey wooden, plastered Chinese houses; those are Chinese, not Tartar, buildings.

p.h: How Siberia's Tatar khanate fell
p.g: Opening his description of Tobolsk, Chappe tells how Siberia, ruled by a Tatar prince of the Uzbek line, was conquered by the Cossack brigand Yermak. Helped by the Stroganov family, Yermak sailed down the Tagil and Tura rivers, took Tiumen, surprised 'Tobolsk', captured the twelve-year-old son of Khan Kuchum and sent him to Moscow, buying the tsar's pardon with the gift of Siberia.
p.q: Elle étoit gouvernée par un Prince Tartare de la Famille des Usbeks. … Il s'embarqua avec sa troupe sur la riviere Tagil, qu'il descendit jusqu'à son embouchure dans la riviere Tura. Continuant ensuite sa route sur cette derniere riviere, il s'empara de la Ville de Tumen, surprit celle de Tobolsk, fit prisonnier le fils du Kan Zutchuin, âgé de douze ans, & l'envoya à Moscou
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.pe: Siberian Tatars under Khan Kuchum; Yermak's Cossacks
p.t: It was ruled by a Tartar prince of the family of the Uzbeks. … He embarked with his band on the river Tagil, which he descended to its mouth in the river Tura. Continuing down that river, he seized the town of Tiumen, surprised that of Tobolsk, took prisoner the twelve-year-old son of Khan Kuchum, and sent him to Moscow
p.c: Second-hand history with a slip: Yermak took the Tatar capital Isker (Sibir) in 1582, and Tobolsk was built nearby by the Russians only in 1587. 'Zutchuin' is Khan Kuchum.

p.h: Lodging in the 'Tartar's town' of Peking
p.g: Entering Peking with the Russian embassy, Bell's party rides for two hours through crowded streets to lodgings in the part of the city called the 'Tartar's town', near its centre. This is the inner walled city where the Manchu garrison families lived, so called because Europeans called the Manchu rulers of China 'Tartars'.
p.q: After a march of two hours from the gate where we entered, we, at last, came to our lodgings, in that part of the city called the Tartar's town; which is near the center of Pekin,
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: Wooden houses burned, stone palaces stormed
p.g: Seeing they could not hold the town, the Hungarian, French and Lombard citizens who ran Esztergom burned the suburbs and the many wooden houses right up to the stone palaces, destroyed their cloth and goods, buried their gold and retreated into the palaces. Enraged at losing the plunder, the Tartars stormed the palaces; Roger doubts fifteen people survived. The castle itself, held by a Spanish count with crossbowmen, was not taken.
p.q: Hungari vero et Francigenae ac Lombardi, qui quasi erant domini ciuitatis, se non posse defendere aduertentes combusserunt suburbia et domos ligneas, quae multa erant, usque ad palatia ciuitatis. … coeperunt postmodum palatia expugnare. Quibus velociter expugnatis, non credo ut verum fatear quod XV de tota remanserunt ciuitate
