p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.pe: Mongol army; Hungarian, French and Lombard defenders
p.t: But the Hungarians, the French and the Lombards, who were as it were the masters of the city, seeing that they could not defend themselves, burned the suburbs and the wooden houses, of which there were many, right up to the palaces of the city. … Afterwards they began to storm the palaces. These were quickly taken, and I do not believe, to tell the truth, that fifteen people of the whole city survived
p.c: Roger adds that the Tartars 'roasted men alive like pigs'; like other atrocity details it is reported, not witnessed.

p.h: How Yermak took the Tatar prince's town
p.g: Ides retells the conquest of Siberia about a century after it happened. The Cossack outlaw Yermak, backed by the Stroganov family, sailed up the rivers, razed Tyumen and took the town where a twelve-year-old 'Tartarian Prince' lived, sending him captive to Moscow. The prince's grandson, Ides says, still lived in Moscow with the title 'Siberian Czarevitz'. Yermak later drowned in his heavy armour during a Tatar night attack.
p.q: advanced up the River Tobol to Tobolska, where then resided a Tartarian Prince, aged about twelve Years, whose Name was Altanai Kutzjumowitz (whose Grandson at present lives at Muscow, and is honoured with the Title of the Siberian Czarewitz.) This City he likewise attacqued and took with small loss, after which he carried the Prince Prisoner to Muscow
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Hearsay a century after the events. The Tatar capital Yermak took in 1582 was Isker (Sibir); Tobolsk itself was founded by the Russians nearby in 1587, so Ides compresses the story.
p.tg: yermak conquest khanate of sibir kuchum

p.h: Hyemo, a city a day's ride across
p.g: Jordanus heard from people who had seen them that the Great Tartar's empire has very great cities, one called Hyemo which takes a full day on horseback to cross by a straight road through the middle. On the next page he adds that the emperor rules two hundred cities bigger than Toulouse. Yule guessed Hyemo might be Emil, a Mongol town built by Ögedei, but thought it more likely a vast Chinese city like Hangzhou.
p.q: In isto imperio, sunt civitates permaximæ, prout ab hiis qui viderunt audivi; nam est una quæ Hyemo vocatur quæ per quadrum, rectâ viâ, habet dietam unam cum equo transeundo per medium, rectâ viâ.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.pe: Subjects of the Great Tartar (Yuan China)
p.t: In this empire there are very great cities, as I have heard from those who have seen them; for there is one called Hyemo which, square as it is, takes a day's journey on horseback to cross through the middle by a straight road.
p.c: The city is unidentified; the identification offered is Yule's guess.

p.h: Coins of the Khans dug from the ruins
p.g: Zwick picked up antiquities at the site: an inscribed alabaster, a copper amulet, a seal, inscribed gems including one bearing the Muslim creed 'There is no God but God', and silver and copper coins of the Khans dated from 710 to 766 of the Hijra, which he converts as 1310 to 1364 AD, from 'Tochtocho-Chan' (Tokhta Khan) to 'Asis Chan' (Aziz Khan). The finds tie the city to the Muslim Golden Horde of the fourteenth century.
p.q: I here procured several antiques; amongst others, an alabaster with an inscription, a copper amulet with magical characters, a seal with a name upon it ; a number of ring-jewels, and jewels with inscriptions, … also a quantity of silver and copper coins of the old Chans, from 1310 A.D. (or 710 of the Hegira) to 1364 (or 766.)
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.c: The OCR reads the last date as '1864'; 766 of the Hijra is 1364 to 1365.

p.h: Hovels and palaces at the emperor's summer town
p.g: Zhe-hol (Jehol, modern Chengde), beyond the Great Wall, was the Qing emperors' summer capital in Tartary. Staunton contrasts the poor, crooked town with the grandeur of the imperial palaces, gardens and temples just beyond it. He adds that the principal buildings 'in this part of Tartary' differed little from those of China.
p.q: The town of Zhe-hol, excepting the houses of mandarines, consisted of miserable hovels full of people. The streets also were crooked, unpaved, and dusty. Immediately beyond it, the imperial garden, the palaces, the temples displayed much grandeur; and magnificence and wretchedness knew no medium.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton

p.h: Beijing made capital to face the Tartars
p.g: Semedo explains that Beijing, called Cambalu by the Muslims, became the court when Yongle ('Yunlo'), who lived in that region, seized the throne after Hongwu's death and moved the court from Nanjing, both to be among his own supporters and to stand up better to the neighbouring Tartars. The Mongol name Khanbaliq survives in 'Cambalud'.
p.q: tiene aora la soberania de gozar de la Corte en la ciudad del mismo nombre: el propio es Xunthienfu: Cambalud la llaman los Moros … un nieto suyo llamado Yunlo … como para poder mejor hazer rostro a los Tartaros confinantes, sacò la Corte de NamKim, i plantòla acà.
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Ming emperors; Tartars on the northern border
p.t: it now has the sovereign privilege of enjoying the Court, in the city of the same name; its proper name is Xunthienfu; the Moors call it Cambalu … a grandson of his named Yunlo … [both to trust those he had always dealt with] and to be better able to face the neighbouring Tartars, took the Court out of Nanjing and planted it here.
p.c: Yongle was Hongwu's son, not his grandson ('nieto') as the Spanish says.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.

p.h: Peking's inner city belongs to the Tartars
p.g: During the New Year festival Ides noticed that women rode openly through the streets on donkeys and in carts, some ladies smoking pipes in public. He explains this by the fact that the walled inner city of Peking was lived in by 'Tartars', meaning the conquering Manchus, while the Chinese had to live around the walls and in the suburbs, where the markets were.
p.q: The Women never appear in publick in all China, except the Province of Peking only, and more especially the City, which is inhabited by Tartars; the Chinese being obliged to live all about the City Wall, and the Suburbs, where all the chief Markets, and publick Places of Sale, are.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

p.h: Tobolsk: churches on the bluff, Russians and Tatars below
p.g: Spafarii set out from Tobolsk, then the capital of Russian Siberia, in May 1675. He describes a town in two levels: churches, houses and people in the upper town on the high bluff over the Irtysh, and a large trading quarter under the hill where many Russians and Tatars lived. From here, he adds, roads ran to Bukhara, to Kazan and to other states.
p.q: А городъ Тоболескъ построенъ на рѣкѣ Иртышѣ на высокомъ мѣстѣ, на яру, и мѣсто зѣло красивое, и множество церквей Божіихъ, и дворовъ, и людей живутъ въ верхнемъ городѣ; такъ же и подъ горою посадъ великой, въ которомъ живутъ множество Рускихъ людей и Татаръ.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Siberian (Tobolsk) Tatars living beside Russian settlers
p.t: And the town of Tobolsk is built on the Irtysh river on a high place, on a bluff, and the place is very beautiful, and there are many churches of God, and houses, and people live in the upper town; and below the hill there is also a great trading quarter (posad), in which live many Russian people and Tatars.

p.h: A lama builds a new wall against the conquerors
p.g: Describing 'Giegazze' (Shigatse), seat of the lama second only to the Dalai Lama, Desideri praises the lama's courage in 1717. When the conquerors of Lhasa, the Dzungar Tartars, marched on the town to plunder its rich temple and monastery, he quickly fortified both with a new wall, armed his people and drove them off. On the next page Desideri adds that the damage from the siege was repaired and the town enlarged in 1720.
p.q: Every one admired his firmness and courage when he offered heroic resistance to the conquerors of Lhasa, who after the sack of this town marched on Giegazze to make the fabulously rich temple and the monastery share the same fate. In a short time he fortified both with a new wall, armed his people and forced the enemy to retreat.
p.s: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924)
p.c: Desideri was at Sera near Lhasa during the invasion, so the defence of Shigatse is reported, not seen.

p.h: Kazan and Astrakhan fall to Ivan IV
p.g: Possevino sums up how Ivan IV took the two Tatar khanates on the Volga. The king of Poland told him the Kazan Tatars were easy to storm because they were unused to bronze cannon. Astrakhan, 'no mean emporium of the East' on the Caspian, is called the capital of another Tartar Horde or kingdom, and its fall carried Muscovite rule to the Circassians.
p.q: vlcisci Tartarorum iniurias, & pedem figere in Liuonia statuit. Casanenses adortus, admotis æneis tormẽtis, facilè fuit ei (vt Stephanus Poloniæ Rex mihi narrauit) siue armorum, seu machinarum generi insuetos expugnare. Inde Astracanum ad ostia fluuij Volgæ situm cœpit, non ignobile Orientis emporium ad mare Caspium. Id cùm alterius Tartarorum Hordæ (seu Regni) esset caput; protulit ditionis suæ fines vsq; ad Circassos
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
p.pe: Tartars of Kazan and Astrakhan (the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates)
p.t: He resolved to avenge the wrongs done by the Tartars and to set foot in Livonia. Attacking the people of Kazan with bronze cannon brought up, it was easy for him (as Stephen, King of Poland, told me) to storm men unused to that kind of arms or engines. Then he took Astrakhan, set at the mouths of the Volga, no mean emporium of the East on the Caspian Sea. Since it was the capital of another Horde (or kingdom) of the Tartars, he pushed the bounds of his realm as far as the Circassians.
p.c: Possevino arrived 30 years after these conquests; the Kazan detail is second-hand from Stephen Bathory.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.

p.h: Andijan: a stone-faced moat and three gates
p.g: Babur begins his memoirs with his own kingdom of Fergana. Its capital Andijan was, he says, the largest fortress in Transoxiana after Samarkand and Kesh, with three gates, a citadel on the south, a stone-faced moat circled by a pebbled road, and suburbs all round. Its people were all Turks and spoke the same Turki that poets wrote in.
p.q: In Maweralnaher, after the fortresses of Samarkand and Kesh, none is equal in size to Andejan. It has three gates. The citadel is situated on the south of the city. … Around the fortress, on the edge of the stone-faced moat, is a broad highway covered with pebbles. All round the fort are the suburbs
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

p.h: Sarai, once the Horde's capital, now a heap of stones
p.g: A footnote to Nikitin's route explains that Sarai, on the Akhtuba branch of the Volga, had been the capital of the Golden Horde, where Russian grand dukes went for two centuries to pay tribute. By the nineteenth century it was reduced to ruins. The note is a useful reminder that the Horde did have a real capital city, and that it was well known to Russian historians.
p.q: Sarai, now a heap of stones and the abode of loathsome reptiles, still observable on the borders of the Akhtouba, an arm of the Volga, forty-six miles from the sea, was at that time the capital of the great or Golden Orda, the famous residence of the great conqueror Baty, the place where, during two centuries, the Grand-Dukes of Russia had to pay their allegiance and their tribute
p.s: Editorial footnote in the 1857 Hakluyt Society edition (translator Count Wielhorski or editor R. H. Major)
p.c: Nineteenth-century editorial comment, not Nikitin. The neighbouring note on Kazan reads '1052' in this OCR, evidently for 1552.
p.tg: sarai golden horde ruins tribute batu

p.h: Samarkand: every trade in its own bazaar
p.g: Babur calls Samarkand 'a wonderfully elegant city'. Its markets were arranged so each trade had its own bazaar, its bakers and cooks were excellent, and it made the best paper in the world and a crimson velvet exported everywhere. He also measured the city walls himself at 10,600 paces round.
p.q: Samarkand is a wonderfully elegant city. One of its distinguishing peculiarities is, that each trade has its own bazar ; so that different trades are not mixed together in the same place. The established customs and regulations are good. The bakers' shops are excellent, and the cooks are skilful. The best paper in the world comes from Samarkand.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

p.h: The Great Kouren: a monastery city of 30,000 lamas
p.g: Huc describes the Great Kouren (Urga, today's Ulaanbaatar) on the Tula river: temples with gilded roofs, 30,000 lamas, and a plain always covered with pilgrims' tents from every people of the Qing north, including 'Fish-skin Tartars' from the Amur and Torghuts. The next page adds a fortified Chinese trading post of wooden and mud huts, where everything was priced in bricks of tea.
p.q: Thirty thousand Lamas dwell in the Lamasery itself, or in smaller Lamaseries erected about it. The plain adjoining it is always covered with the tents of the pilgrims who resort hither from all parts to worship Buddha. Here you find the U-Pi-Ta-Dze, or "Fish-skin Tartars," encamped beside the Torgot Tartars
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols and pilgrims of many peoples

p.h: Tatar Khan's realm by the powerful town of Dsurdsut
p.g: When Oghuz Khan forced his neighbours to accept the true faith, a few refugees fled to Tatar Khan, who lived near 'Dsurdsut'. Abu'l Ghazi calls it a very powerful town ruling several smaller ones, near China's frontier. Dsurdsut is most likely the Jurchen, the people of Manchuria, so here the early Tatars are placed beside a town-dwelling kingdom.
p.q: a very few who retir'd into the Dominions of Tatar Chan, who resided in the Neighbourhood of Dsurdsut. The Town of Dsurdsut is very powerful, having several small Towns under its Jurisdiction: 'Tis situate towards the Frontiers of Kitay, being called Zinu in the Indian and Persian Language.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pl: Borders of northern China and Manchuria
p.pe: Tatars under the legendary Tatar Khan; the Jurchen (Dsurdsut)
p.c: Part of the Oghuz Khan legend; identifying Dsurdsut with the Jurchen is a modern reading, not the text's.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.

p.h: Sarai in 1666: nine thousand reed-roofed houses under Moscow
p.g: Evliya says the Sarai of his day was a city full of all kinds of Tatars, now in Muscovite hands. Half the subjects and soldiers were Muslim Kazan Tatars ('Hashdek') and half Muscovite Christians. The town had about nine thousand wretched houses of planks, rushes and reeds and seven monasteries. He names Nogay, Yaman, Teb and Yishdak Tatars living there as subjects of Moscow since its conquest.
p.q: ( دربیان عمارت شهر سرای ) جمله طقوز بیك تخته وساز وقامش ایله مستور خانهٔ منحوسلردر جمله یدی عدد دیر معظملر واردر ... حالا بو سرای شهری قوم تاتارك اجناسیله مملو بر شهردر
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pe: Tatars of Sarai under Muscovite rule
p.t: (On the buildings of the city of Sarai.) In all there are nine thousand wretched houses covered with planks, rushes and reeds, and there are seven great monasteries in all … Today this city of Sarai is a city filled with every kind of Tatar people.
p.c: Evliya's Volga itinerary is doubted by modern scholars; which town he calls Sarai is unclear, since the Golden Horde capital had long been in ruins.

p.h: Astrakhan once belonged to the Nogai Tartars
p.g: Struys explains that Astrakhan used to belong to the Nogai Tartars under a king, allied with the Cheremis and Kazan Tatars. After taking Kazan the Tsar marched on Astrakhan, took it just as easily and drove out the Tartars. The town, he adds, was then neither as fine nor as large as it later became under Russian rule.
p.q: Cette ville étoit autrefois aux Tartares du Nagai, qui obeïssoient à un Roi … La prise de Cazan ayant rendu le chemin libre, le Vainqueur alla devant Astracan qu'il emporta avec la même facilité, & dont il chassa les Tartares
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: This town formerly belonged to the Tartars of the Nogai, who obeyed a king … The capture of Kazan having opened the way, the victor went before Astrakhan, which he took with the same ease, and from which he drove out the Tartars
p.c: History from books; the Astrakhan khanate was ruled by a Chinggisid khan and conquered in 1556.

p.h: Once the rulers, now pushed to the suburbs
p.g: Haxthausen notes that the Tatars, who ruled Kazan before the Russian conquest of 1552, now live in their own quarter outside the Russian town proper. They are mostly traders, and he met rich merchant families among them.
p.q: The Tatars in Kazan live mostly together, in a separate quarter of the town. Formerly the ruling people, they have been driven into the suburbs, whilst the town proper is inhabited by Russians. They are traders rather than artisans ; among them are merchants of all the guilds.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

p.h: Bakhchysarai: founded 1501, partly burned by the Russians
p.g: An editor's note, citing a writer it calls Brzhinski, gives a short history of the khans' capital: its story begins in 1501, Greeks ('Rum') lived there before the Tatars came into Crimea, a Russian army burned about a quarter of it in a war, and the khans' first palace was at Salacik nearby. The note goes on to say that the one old monument left there is the tomb by the monastery gate, rebuilt in 1510 by Mengli Giray in his father's name. So the town is presented as a dated foundation of the Giray khans on a site with earlier Greek inhabitants.
p.q: باغچه سرای تاریخی ( ١٥٠١ ) سنه سندن باشلار . تاتار قریمه کیرمه دن اول اوراده ( روم ) لر واردی . باغچه سرایک ( ١٧٨٦ ) ده روسلرله اولان محاربه ده ، همان ربعی یانمشدر . قریم خانلرینک ایلک سرایی صلاجقده در .
p.s: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan, quoting a writer it names as Brzhinski
p.t: The history of Bakhchysarai begins in the year 1501. Before the Tatars entered Crimea, there were Greeks (Rum) there. In the war with the Russians in (1786), about a quarter of Bakhchysarai burned. The first palace of the Crimean khans is at Salacik.
p.c: The printed '1786' is very likely a misprint for 1736, when a Russian army under Munnich burned Bakhchysarai; Crimea was already Russian in 1786. This is the 1911 editor's note, not Halim Giray.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled).

p.h: Marco Polo's lost city of Campion
p.g: Strahlenberg says he asked every nation in Tartary about Marco Polo's city of Campion, shown on old maps, and found no one who had heard of it. He concludes the name was mispronounced and that it must be the city at the western entrance of the Chinese Wall, which the Tatars call Camtzi, where all caravans must stop and wait for permission to enter China.
p.q: ob gleich bey allen Nationen in der Tatarey von dem Nahmen der Stadt Campion, wie eben uns Marcus Paulus und andere alte Mappen darlegen, ziemliche Nachfrage gethan, ich dennoch keine einzige gefunden, die mir weder aus alter noch neuer Zeit, davon Unterricht geben können … welche im Gebürge und beym Eingange der Chinaeischen Mauer Westlicher Seiten lieget, die von den Tatern in Stelle vor Campion, Camtzi … genant wird
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.pl: Gansu corridor (western end of the Great Wall)
p.t: although I made considerable inquiry among all the nations of Tartary about the name of the city of Campion, as Marco Polo and other old maps set it before us, I nevertheless found not a single one who could inform me about it from old or recent times … [the city] which lies in the mountains at the entrance of the Chinese Wall on the western side, which the Tatars call Camtzi instead of Campion

p.h: Two villages for every village: summer and winter
p.g: Sailing up the Irtysh, Gmelin passed Uttus aul, which was really three villages: two for summer and one for winter. This, he says, was the general custom of the local Tatars, who moved into the winter village when the cold set in. He adds that 'aul' is the Tatar word for village, and that Russians call every Tatar village 'yurty', a Tatar word that simply means 'house'.
p.q: Dieses ist unter den hiesigen Tataren eine allgemeine Gewohnheit, daß sie ein anderes Dorf für den Sommer, ein anderes für den Winter haben. Sobald die Kälte einfällt, ziehen sie in ihr Winterdorf, und sobald die Wärme kommt, in das Sommerdorf.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: It is a general custom among the Tatars here that they have one village for the summer and another for the winter. As soon as the cold sets in they move into their winter village, and as soon as the warm weather comes, into the summer village.

p.h: Jehol: wretched huts beside imperial palaces
p.g: Hüttner contrasts the emperor's summer seat with the town that served it: apart from the palaces, the magnificent park and the rich lama temples, the town offered only miserable huts, crooked streets and great dirt. He praises the fertile valley ringed by mountains, which he thought could carry vineyards and orchards. A useful corrective to any idea of Jehol as a grand 'Tartar' city: the splendour was the court's, not the town's.
p.q: findet man in der Stadt nichts, als elende Hütten, krumme Strassen und grosse Unsauberkeit. Die Kaiserlichen Palläste, der prächtige Park und die reichen Lama-Tempel machen damit einen grossen Abstich!
p.s: Johann Christian Hüttner (1797)
p.t: one finds nothing in the town but wretched huts, crooked streets and great filth. The imperial palaces, the magnificent park and the rich lama temples make a great contrast with it!
p.c: The start of the sentence is on the previous, badly scanned page.

p.h: A 'Tartarian or Circassian' village of four hundred houses
p.g: Marching south from the Terek, the embassy reached a large village of 300 to 400 houses called Andreofske Derevna, ruled by a prince named Alish under Russian protection. Cook is unsure whether to call it Tartar or Circassian. The prince, drunk from celebrating, showed the scars of many raids and boasted of horses stolen from Turkey and Georgia.
p.q: at seven o'clock at night we arrived, very cold, in a large Tartarian or Circassian village, called Andreofske Derevna, consisting of between three and four hundred houses. The prince of this village is called Alish, and is under the protection of Russia.
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.pe: Kumyks or Kabardians (called Tartars or Circassians)

p.h: The Tatar caravanserai of Bukhara
p.g: Eversmann entered Bukhara through the gate as a merchant and lodged in the Tatar caravanserai (p. 65). He explains that each trading nation kept to its own serai: Indians in the Indian serais, Tatars in the Tatar one, merchants of Kokand and Kashgar in the 'Chinese' one. Caravans from Troitsk, Orsk, Orenburg and from Astrakhan by way of Khiva brought English and Russian cloth, calico and metalware, handled mostly by Bukharans, Russian Tatars and Armenians.
p.q: Meistentheils halten sich diese verschiedene Nationen so viel wie möglich beisammen; so wohnen z. B. in den sogenannten indischen Seraien fast nur Indier, im tatarischen Serai, Tataren, im chinesischen, Kaufleute aus Kokan und Kaschkar, etc. … Die handelnden Personen sind grösstentheils Bucharen, dann (russische) Tataren, und von Astrachan, Armenier
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.pe: Russian Tatars as merchants; Indians, Kokandis, Kashgaris, Armenians
p.t: For the most part these various nations keep together as much as possible; so, for example, in the so-called Indian serais live almost only Indians, in the Tatar serai Tatars, in the Chinese one merchants from Kokand and Kashgar, and so on. … The people trading are mostly Bukharans, then (Russian) Tatars, and from Astrakhan, Armenians
p.tg: caravanserai trade russian tatars merchants bukhara

p.h: Empty cities of an old kingdom in the desert
p.g: Crossing the drifting sands east of Niya, travellers piled up bones to mark the way, and people heard singing or wailing that led them astray, which Xuanzang blames on demons. After 400 li he reached the 'old country of Tukhara', long empty, its cities all desolate. He credits the ruins to a vanished kingdom, not to any Turks or Tartars.
p.q: 是以往來者聚遺骸以記之乏水草多熱風…時聞歌嘯或聞號哭視聽之間怳然不知所至由此屢有喪亾蓋鬼魅之所致也行四百餘里至覩貨邏故國國久空曠城皆荒蕪
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 12 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
p.pl: Southern Tarim Basin, between Niya and Cherchen, Xinjiang
p.t: So those who come and go pile up the bones of the dead to mark the way. Water and grass are lacking and hot winds are frequent... At times one hears singing and whistling, or wailing and crying, and between what is seen and heard one is bewildered and does not know where one is going; many die this way, which is the work of demons and goblins. Going 400 li or so one reaches the old country of Tukhara. The country has long been empty and its cities are all in ruins.
p.c: Beal's English (page 325) is badly garbled in this OCR, so the Chinese is quoted.

p.h: Stone houses burned by the Tartars, heads on stakes
p.g: Going ashore with Bort's fleet after the joint Dutch and Qing attack on the island bases of the Zheng (Koxinga) regime, the Dutch found a walled town and its suburb packed with fine stone houses, all wrecked and burned by the Tartars. In a square lay stakes and human heads, which the enemies of the Tartars had displayed six years before, after a great Tartar defeat at sea, and which had now been thrown down and burned 'after the manner of the Tartars'.
p.q: Zoowel de voor als de bemuurde stad, was zeer dicht met ontelbare redelijke schoone steene huizen betimmert, welke alle door de Tartaren verwoest, en door den brant in d'assche gelegt wierden. Men zag aldaer op zeker plein eenige staken, en daer by verscheide menschen hoofden leggen
p.s: Olfert Dapper, from the journals of Balthasar Bort's fleet
p.pe: Tartars (Qing army), fighting the Zheng regime
p.t: Both the suburb and the walled town were very densely built with countless fairly handsome stone houses, all of which were destroyed by the Tartars and laid in ashes by fire. On a certain square one saw some stakes, and beside them several human heads lying

p.h: Shaoxing, the cleanest city in China, surrenders
p.g: Martini, who knew Zhejiang well, pauses as the Tartars cross the Qiantang to praise Shaoxing: not the largest city but the cleanest and most comely in China, circled by fresh water, with wide streets paved in white square stone, a navigable canal down the middle, stone bridges and arches. On the next page he says its houses are built of the same square stone, 'which I observe no where else in China'. It submitted without resistance.
p.q: This City in bigness yields to many others, but in cleaness and comeliness it surpasses all: it is so invironed with sweet waters as a man may contemplate its beauty by rounding it in a Boat ; it hath large and fair Streets paved on both sides with white square stones, and in the middle of them all runs a Navigable Chanel,
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: A Chinese city, not a Tartar one; it matters here as a city the Tartars took.

p.h: Genghis Khan takes Bukhara
p.g: In a later addition to the book Wolff notes that Genghis Khan besieged Bukhara in 1219 and took it in 1220, and repeats a tradition that thousands of Jews then fled to China. He adds that the city's houses were mostly of mud.
p.q: The town of Bokhara is situated one day's journey to the north of the river Jehoon or Amoo ; Ghengis Khan besieged it in 1219, and took it in 1220. Thousands of Jews emigrated at that time to China. The houses are mostly built of mud.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.pe: Mongols under Genghis Khan; Jews of Bukhara
p.c: The Jewish migration to China is Wolff's claim, probably from Bukharan Jewish tradition, not a documented event.
p.tg: bukhara genghis khan siege jews mud

p.h: Karakorum explained as 'the circle of the common people'
p.g: In a footnote Zwick explains that kura means a circle, especially the ring of priests' huts around a Kalmyk temple tent, which served as the centre of a horde without a prince. He then derives the name of Genghis Khan's capital from the same word. It is a striking attempt to read an old imperial capital as a camp word.
p.q: Thus, the capital of the famous Genghis Khan, which is known in history under the name of Karakorum, was originally Chara Kura, or, in the Tartar dialect, Kara Kura, the circle of the Blacks, or common people.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (footnote, English edition, 1831)
p.c: This is Zwick's own etymology; the name is usually explained as Turkic qara qorum, 'black rocks'.

p.h: Storming a city behind a wooden wall
p.g: Martini describes how the Tartars, armed only with sabres and bows against Chinese muskets, took 'Leaotung', which he calls the chief city of the province of Liaodong. The front ranks carried thick boards as a moving 'wooden wall' to soak up the musket fire, ladder-men followed, and cavalry came behind. Before the Chinese could reload, the Tartars were over the walls. He credits their speed and nimbleness, 'in which they excel all Nations'.
p.q: the scaling ladders being applied, before they could charge again, they were upon the Walls and enterd the City ; for such is the quickness and nimbleness of the Tartars (in which they excel all Nations, and in which also they place their chief art) that in a trice, they either prevail in their Designs, or retire :
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: An event before Martini reached China, told from report; he runs several Liaodong campaigns together.

p.h: Yakutsk: a decaying wooden fort and ice windows
p.g: Sarychev describes Yakutsk as the oldest town in the region, grown up around a wooden ostrog of 1647 whose towers still stood but were falling into decay. There were a few stone churches, but all the houses were wooden, 'in the old Russian taste', with Yakut huts scattered between them. For windows they used mica or bladders in summer and slabs of ice in winter.
p.q: The ostrog, or wooden fortress, was erected in the year 1647, and soon afterwards the building of the town commenced. This old edifice, with its towers, is still standing, but in some places is fallen very much to decay. … All the dwelling-houses are built of wood, in the old Russian taste, with here and there Jakutish huts interspersed between them.
p.s: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)
p.pe: Russians, with Yakut (Sakha) huts among them
p.c: Sarychev's date of 1647 differs from Sauer's (W008) story of a first fort in 1632 that was later moved.

p.h: Akmetshet: stone houses and three mosques
p.g: Simferopol, the Russian capital of the Crimea, still went by its Tatar name Akmetshet ('white mosque'). Alexander lists three Tatar mosques alongside the new cathedral and government buildings, and notes that the houses were of stone with tiled roofs, while in the Tatar quarter houses stood behind courtyards and high walls. His guide was the governor's Tatar interpreter.
p.q: The public buildings of Akmetshet, besides three Tartar mosques, are a very handsome cathedral, the halls of justice, residences of the civil officers, &c. The houses are built of stone, and roofed in the ancient Greek style with tiles: in the Tartar quarter courts surround the houses and high walls
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and the Russian administration

p.h: Kozlov, a stone town, and Tatar villages with dug wells
p.g: Coming from Perekop, the book notes on the right, by the sea, the stone town of Kozlov (the 1838 editor adds: now Yevpatoria). Between the Alma, Bakhchysarai and Kozlov, Tatar villages lined both sides of the road, watered by dug wells because there were no rivers. Crimea appears as a settled country of towns and villages as well as nomads.
p.q: Да отъ Перекопи ѣдучи, на правѣ, у моря на берегу, городъ Козлевъ каменной. … А отъ Алмы до Бакчисарая, и до Козлева, по обѣ стороны дороги, деревни Татарскія, а воды копаные колодези, а рѣкъ нѣтъ.
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.t: And travelling from Perekop, on the right, on the seashore, is the stone town of Kozlov. … And from the Alma to Bakhchysarai and to Kozlov, on both sides of the road, are Tatar villages, and the water is from dug wells, and there are no rivers.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Tobolsk, capital of the Siberian cities
p.g: Tobolsk, founded by the Russians in 1587, is described as the capital of the Siberian towns, seat of the Tsar's viceroy, where tribute from both sides of the Ob is collected and sent to Moscow. Tartars come from the south from far inside Tartary to trade. Massa adds a pointed comparison: would that the 'cruel Spaniards' had taken America as peacefully.
p.q: From Tinnen one reaches Tobolsca, the capital of the Siberian cities; there is the seat of Siberia and the supreme Viceroy of the Muscovites … Also Tartars from the south come at a great distance from Tartary, and many other nations who gradually arrive there, in proportion as the fame of the country spreads wider.
p.s: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars and traders from further south
p.c: Massa's picture of a peaceful conquest reflects his Russian informants' view.

p.h: Khoy, 'the Turkestan of Persia'
p.g: Jaubert describes Khoy in Persian Azerbaijan as a fairly new town with regular fortifications, few mosques or large houses, tree-shaded streets and a good caravanserai for merchants. Its 25,000 inhabitants said they were of Tartar origin, which earned the district the nickname 'the Turkestan of Persia'.
p.q: La ville de Khoï, qui n'est pas fort ancienne, a des fortifications régulières. On n'y voit pas un grand nombre de mosquées ni de maisons considérables; mais les rues sont ombragées d'arbres, et l'on y trouve un assez beau caravanséraï spécialement réservé pour les marchands. On peut évaluer à vingt-cinq mille âmes la population de cette ville, dont les habitans se disent aussi d'origine tartare
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
p.t: The town of Khoy, which is not very old, has regular fortifications. One does not see many mosques or large houses there; but the streets are shaded with trees, and there is a rather fine caravanserai reserved especially for merchants. The population of this town may be put at twenty-five thousand souls, whose inhabitants also say they are of Tartar origin
p.c: The nickname comes from the Ottoman geographer Katib Celebi (Jihannuma), whom Jaubert cites.

p.h: The Great City of the Volga Bulgars burned
p.g: A year before they reached Rus, the Tatars came 'from the eastern lands' and took the 'glorious Great City' of the Volga Bulgars, a Muslim trading state on the middle Volga. The chronicler says they killed everyone, took a great quantity of goods and burned the city. The Great City is usually identified by historians with Bilyar.
p.q: Тое же осени придоша отъ всточныя страны въ Болгарьскую землю безбожніи Татари, и взяша славный Великый городъ Болгарьскый, и избиша оружьемъ отъ старца и до унаго и до сущаго младенца, и взяша товара множство, а городъ ихъ пожгоша огнемъ, и всю землю ихъ плѣниша.
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.t: That same autumn the godless Tatars came from the eastern lands into the Bulgar land, and took the glorious Great City of the Bulgars, and slew them with weapons from old man to youth to the infant at the breast, and took a great quantity of goods, and burned their city with fire, and captured all their land.
p.c: Reported from Suzdal at a distance; 'from old man to infant' is a stock phrase for a massacre.

p.h: The first city after the Flood, sacked by the 'Emperor of Tartary'
p.g: In Armenia the envoys reached Calmarin, a strong city in sight of Mount Ararat, which locals said was the first city built after Noah's flood. Its people told them that eight years earlier an 'Emperor of Tartary' had besieged it, broken the terms of surrender, and sacked and burned it. A few days later Clavijo passed Cusacana, 'half destroyed', which he says Toktamish, Emperor of Tartary, had ruined.
p.q: This city of Calmarin was the first city that was built in the world, after the flood, and it was built by the lineage of Noah. The people of the city said that, eight years ago, Tetani, Emperor of Tartary, besieged
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Golden Horde army ('Tetani, Emperor of Tartary')
p.c: The Noah origin is local legend; the siege story continues on the next page.
p.tg: armenia siege golden horde noah legend

p.h: A tent bazaar between two princes
p.g: Arriving at the 'place of heroes' whips', where two Torgut princes were camped, the missionaries found a market that had grown up in the gap between the two princely tents. Russian, Armenian and Tatar merchants lived there in their own tents and carts, forming the travelling bazaar of the horde.
p.q: Their tents were about a quarter of a mile asunder, and between them was a multitude of tents and cars belonging to the Russian, Armenian, and Tartar merchants, forming the market, or rather bazaar, of the horde.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)
p.pe: Kalmyks; Russian, Armenian and Tatar traders

p.h: A Tartar general storms Quansy and burns it to the ground
p.g: Pinto describes the Tartars setting more than two thousand scaling ladders against the walls of the city where he was held, breaking the four gates with iron-bound beams, killing the governor and, he says, more than sixty thousand people, then burning every house and temple and carrying off gold and silver. He presents himself as a captive eyewitness.
p.q: arremeteraõ a elles com hũa grita taõ espantosa que parecia que se ajuntaua o Ceo com a terra, & aruorando mais de duas mil escadas que para isso trazião, lhe deraõ o assalto a toda em roda, por todas as partes que puderaõ, subindo pelas escadas acima muyto determinadamente, & sem nenhum medo
p.s: Fernão Mendes Pinto (Peregrinaçam, Lisbon 1614)
p.pe: Tartar army of the 'Nauticor of Lançame'
p.t: they rushed at them with so terrible a shout that it seemed heaven and earth were coming together, and setting up more than two thousand ladders which they had brought for the purpose, they assaulted it all around, on every side they could, climbing up the ladders very resolutely and without any fear
p.c: Pinto's Tartar episodes are widely regarded as fictional or built from hearsay; treat as claimed travel. The city and general cannot be identified.
p.n: OCR normalized (checked in part against the page image).
p.tg: siege ladders massacre destruction claimed travel

p.h: The Tanguts cannot carry off their walled towns
p.g: When Chinggis fell from his horse on his last campaign against the Tangut kingdom, a commander advised going home to recover, arguing that the Tanguts, unlike steppe people, were tied to their pounded-earth towns and fixed camps and would still be there later. Chinggis refused to withdraw. The passage shows how the Mongols saw walled towns: as something that cannot run away.
p.q: The Tang’ut people Are ones who have towns with pounded-earth walls, Are ones who live in permanent camps. They won’t leave, carrying off their towns with pounded-earth walls; They won’t leave, abandoning their permanent camps. Let us withdraw.
p.s: Anonymous author of the Secret History, words given to Tolun Cerbi (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)
p.tg: tangut walled towns pounded earth campaign

p.h: Bela warns that the Tartars are building forts in Hungary
p.g: In the same letter Bela urges the German princes to march with crossbowmen and supplies, warning that a Tartar hold on Hungary would be a heavy threat to the Empire 'because they are raising many fortifications there'. He also says he knows their strength from personal experience of battle, and that their wealth from forty conquered kingdoms could enrich twenty kingdoms if they were destroyed.
p.q: cum eorum ibidem receptio, Tartarorum videlicet, esset imperio plurimum honerosa, eo quod munitiones ibidem plurimas erigant
p.s: King Bela IV of Hungary, letter to Conrad IV, Vienna, June 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
p.t: since their being received there, that is of the Tartars, would be most burdensome to the Empire, because they are raising very many fortifications there
p.c: A king pleading for help; 'many fortifications' may be an alarm rather than a survey. The Mongols withdrew from Hungary in 1242.

p.h: Batu's campaign west and his capital, Coc-orda
p.g: Abu'l Ghazi tells how Ögedei gave Batu an army to conquer the Russians ('Uresses'), Circassians and Bulgars. After a forty-day feast Batu set out, 'filled all the West' with his exploits, returned to the Kipchak steppe and died in his capital, which Abu'l Ghazi calls Coc-orda (probably Kök Orda, the 'Blue Horde'). The name shows the royal camp, the orda, serving as the capital.
p.q: gave him a numerous Army to go and subdue the Uresses, the Zerkass, the Bulgars, and other neighbouring Nations … Batu-sagin Chan after he had filled all the West with the Glory of the great Exploits which he atchieved upon that Occasion, at length return'd happily into his own Country of Dasht Kipzak, where he died some time after in the Capital of the Country called Coc-orda.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pe: Batu Khan and the Mongols of the Golden Horde
p.c: Written four centuries after Batu; he does not describe the capital or mention Sarai here.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.
p.tg: batu golden horde orda capital russia bulgars

p.h: Lhasa, a trading capital with a Chinese garrison
p.g: Stewart describes Lhasa as populous and flourishing, home to Chinese mandarins, Chinese and Kashmiri merchants and craftsmen, and a daily stream of caravans. Just before this he notes that while Bogle was with the Lama, 'several Mongols and Calmucs arrived from Siberia'. Neither Bogle nor Stewart saw Lhasa: the city is 'represented' to them.
p.q: The city of Lahassa, which is the capital, is of no inconsiderable size, and is represented as populous and flourishing. It is the residence of the chief officers of government, and of the Chinese mandarins and their suite. It is also inhabited by Chinese and Cassemirian merchants and artificers, and is the daily resort of numberless traders from all quarters,
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.c: Hearsay about a city no Briton had then visited.

p.h: Peking's Tartar city and Chinese city
p.g: Davis describes Peking as two walled cities: the northern 'Tartarian, or City of Nine Gates', holding the palace and under strict military police, and the southern Chinese city, whose walls are weaker, 'like the ordinary Chinese towns', and which holds the Temples of Heaven and Agriculture. On an earlier page he notes that Amherst's party pulled bricks out of holes in the neglected north-east wall. 'Tartar city' names who lived in it under the Qing.
p.q: The Chinese town, which lies to the south of the Tartarian, or "City of Nine Gates," is not subject to the same rigid system of military police as that which contains the abode of the Emperor; and its walls and defences are inferior to those of the other, being, in fact, like the ordinary Chinese towns.
p.s: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
p.pe: Manchu Tartars (the imperial garrison) and Chinese
p.c: Davis saw Peking only briefly in 1816; much of his description comes from Barrow and Father Hyacinth.
p.tg: beijing tartar city walls temple of heaven

p.h: Anapa: mud cabins and a medley of peoples
p.g: Anapa, the first Russian fortress on the Circassian coast, is described from notes by the expedition's historiographer: most houses were cabins of wood and mud thatched with maize leaves or reeds, and its 2,000 people included Circassians, Nogai Tatars, Kalmyks, Kumyks, Kabardians, 'Kazannes', Dagestanis and Bukharans. Spencer admits he did not land there himself.
p.q: The greater number of the houses of the town are mere cabins, constructed of wood and mud, thatched with the leaves of Indian corn or reeds. The inhabitants, consisting of Circassians, Nogay Tartars, Kalmucks, Komouks, Kabartis, Kazannes, Demikarponis, Daghistanes, Boukhares, with a few Greeks, Armenians, and Russians, speaking a medley of tongues
p.s: Edmund Spencer, from the expedition historiographer's notes
p.pe: Nogai Tatars, Kalmyks, Kumyks, Kazan Tatars and others
p.c: Second-hand, as Spencer says.
p.tg: anapa mud houses nogai population fortress

p.h: Timur's 'Tartars' slip into Delhi and sack it
p.g: After taking Delhi, Timur's wives wanted to see the city and its palace of a thousand columns; when a gate was opened for them, fifteen thousand 'Tartars' slipped in unnoticed. Fighting with the inhabitants, fires and looting followed, and Delhi was given over to plunder; Deguignes says some soldiers ended up with a hundred and fifty slaves each.
p.q: les Sulthanes, femmes de Tamerlan, ayant envie de voir cette belle ville & principalement un superbe palais qui étoit orné de mille colonnes, elles entrèrent avec toute leur cour, la porte de la ville fut ouverte, & quinze mille Tartares y pénétrèrent sans qu'on s'en apperçût. … Dehli fut entièrement livrée au pillage.
p.s: Joseph de Guignes
p.t: the Sultanas, Tamerlane's wives, wishing to see this fine city and above all a superb palace adorned with a thousand columns, went in with their whole court; the city gate was opened, and fifteen thousand Tartars got in without anyone noticing. … Delhi was given over entirely to pillage.
p.c: The page presents the sack as a disorder the Tartar officers could not stop, which is the version given by Timur's own court historians.

p.h: Astrakhan, the great emporium of the Tartars
p.g: Herberstein calls Astrakhan a wealthy city and the Tartars' main trading hub near the Volga delta, which he pictures splitting into some seventy branches. On the same page he lists forest-dwelling Siberian Tartars and says the Kalmyks are called that because they alone let their hair grow.
p.q: Astrachan is a wealthy city, and the great emporium of the Tartars, which gives its name to all the surrounding country. It lies on this side of the Volga, near to its mouth, ten days' journey below Kazan.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

p.h: Moscow in panic as the Crimean khan approaches
p.g: In 1521 the Crimean khan Mehmed Giray and his brother, the khan of Kazan, raided up to Moscow. Herberstein, drawing on witnesses including German gunners, describes the Grand Duke fleeing (reportedly hiding under a haystack) and crowds crushing each other at the fortress gates. The city bought off the khan with gifts, above all mead, and a written promise of tribute.
p.q: On the 29th of July the Tartars made a farther advance, and devastated the country with fire in all directions ; and such was the terror which they inspired amongst the people of Moscow, that they had little confidence in their security even in the city and the fortress.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.pe: Crimean Tartars under Mehmed Giray; Kazan Tartars

p.h: A ruined earth fort on the Mongol frontier
p.g: Near the end of the desert crossing the mission sheltered at Tsagan balgassou, the 'white walled town', a small square fort of rammed earth, now in ruins and used to shelter cattle. Timkovsky describes its bastions and a stone circle he took for the site of a khan's tent, and reports that people credited such forts to the Kangxi emperor's campaigns of the late 1600s.
p.q: The ramparts, which are in ruins, are five toises high, and have small bastions at the four corners. In the interior, in the north-west angle, there is a circular space enclosed with unhewn stones: it was probably the site of the Khan's tent. … Some persons affirm that this fort, as well as those situated farther to the south, served as encampments during the expeditions of the celebrated Emperor Kanghi
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.pl: Inner Mongolia (Tsagan Balgas, north of Kalgan)
p.c: The attribution to Kangxi is hearsay, which Timkovsky reports without endorsing.

p.h: Nurhaci pulls down unlucky walls and builds new ones
p.g: After taking 'Leaotung' and then Guangning, Martini says, the Tartar king returned to Liaodong rich with plunder. His soothsayers told him the old walls were unlucky, so he pulled them down, built new ones, and proclaimed himself emperor of China though he held only its edge. A page earlier Martini explains that Chinese soldiers and citizens fled their houses because the Tartars destroyed any city that resisted but only plundered those that surrendered.
p.q: And because his Southsayers had perswaded him that the standing of the old Walls were unfortunate, he beat them down, and compassed them about with new, fortifying them with new Munitions, and there proclamed himself Emperour of China:
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: Martini's report; historically Nurhaci moved his capital to Liaoyang in 1621 and to Shenyang in 1625.

p.h: Kazan, 'capital of the Khan of the Dasht Kipchaks'
p.g: Describing the lands north of Ferghana, Izzet Ullah says the Kazakhs and Karakalpaks there depend on Russia, and that the capital of the Khan of the Dasht-i Kipchak, 'Bulghar, now known by the name of Kazan', lies in Russian territory. He runs together two different Volga cities (old Bulghar and Kazan), but the line shows how the Tatar khanates were remembered in Central Asia.
p.q: To the north of the mountains of Andejan the country is a barren plain ; to the north of which are the tribes of Kazzaks and Kara Kalpaks, dependant on Russia. The capital of the Khan of the Dast Kapchaks, Bulghar, now known by the name of Kazan, is in the Russian territory.
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.pe: Kazakhs, Karakalpaks; the old khans of the Kipchak steppe
p.c: Bulghar and Kazan were separate cities; the identification is his, and it is wrong.
p.tg: kazan bulghar dasht-i kipchak kazakhs russia

p.h: Bakhchysarai kept for the Tatars by imperial decree
p.g: The old Tatar capital, the authors explain, kept its eastern look because Catherine II granted the Tatars sole possession of the town. Walking its narrow streets of mosques, shops and cemeteries felt like the old quarters of Constantinople. On the same page they give a potted history: Batu Khan's Tatars founded the kingdom in the 1200s, and Bakhchysarai became the capital in the early 1500s.
p.q: Bagtche Serai has completely retained its national character in consequence of an ukase of Catherine II., empowering the Tatars to retain exclusive possession of their own capital. You would fancy yourself in the heart of the East, in walking through the narrow streets of the town, the mosques, shops, and cemeteries of which so much resemble those of the old quarters of Constantinople.
p.s: Xavier and Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: Ferghana: walled cities, rice, wine and blood-sweating horses
p.g: In contrast to the Xiongnu, Zhang Qian reported that the people of Dayuan (Ferghana) were settled farmers growing rice and wheat, made grape wine, and bred fine 'blood-sweating' horses descended from 'heavenly horses'. They had walled cities and houses, some seventy towns large and small, and several hundred thousand people. The same chapter labels the Wusun, Kangju and Yuezhi as 'moving nations' (行國).
p.q: 其俗土著，耕田，田稻麥。有蒲陶酒。多善馬，馬汗血，其先天馬子也。有城郭屋室。其屬邑大小七十餘城，眾可數十萬。
p.s: Sima Qian, Shiji ch. 123, from Zhang Qian's report (Kanseki Repository text)
p.pe: Dayuan (people of Ferghana, reported by Zhang Qian)
p.t: Their custom is to stay settled on the land; they plough fields and grow rice and wheat. They have grape wine. They have many fine horses; the horses sweat blood, and their ancestors were the offspring of heavenly horses. They have walled cities and houses; the towns under them, large and small, number over seventy, and the people several hundred thousand.
p.c: Zhang Qian's report as edited by the court historian; 'heavenly horses' is a legend he passes on.
p.tg: ferghana dayuan walled cities horses zhang qian

p.h: Astrakhan, a city of many Asian peoples
p.g: Rose found Astrakhan smaller than Kazan but more mixed than almost any city he knew, drawn together by trade from the far ends of Asia and Europe. Russians were slightly under half the population; besides Cossacks and Europeans there were Armenians, Tatars, Georgians, Bukharans, Khivans, Turkmens, Persians, Hindus, Kazakhs and Kalmyks. Delegations of many of them called on Humboldt.
p.q: …man wird selten eine Stadt finden, in welcher wie hier eine so gemischte Bevölkerung lebt, die das merkantilische Interesse aus den entferntesten Enden von Asien und Europa zusammengeführt hat. Denn ausser den Russen, die etwa die kleinere Hälfte der Bewohner Astrachans ausmachen, den Kosaken und den übrigen hier ansässigen Europäern, finden sich hier noch Armenier, Tataren, Georgier, Bucharen, Chiwensen, Truchmenen, Perser, Hindus, Kirgisen und Kalmücken
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.pe: Tatars, Kalmyks, Kazakhs, Armenians, Persians, Indians and others
p.t: …one will rarely find a city in which, as here, such a mixed population lives, brought together by commercial interest from the farthest ends of Asia and Europe. For besides the Russians, who make up somewhat less than half of Astrakhan's inhabitants, the Cossacks and the other Europeans settled here, there are also Armenians, Tatars, Georgians, Bukharans, Khivans, Turkmens, Persians, Hindus, Kirghiz and Kalmyks

p.h: Mamai flees to Kaffa, and the Genoese mock him with Batu's memory
p.g: In the poem Mamai escapes from his army 'howling like a grey wolf' and runs to the city of Kaffa, the Genoese colony in Crimea. The Fryazi (Italians) jeer that he is no Batu: Batu had 400,000 armoured men and warred over the whole Russian land, while Mamai came with nine hordes and seventy princes and now flees with eight companions. Historically Mamai did flee to the Crimea and was killed near Kaffa.
p.q: А не бывати тебѣ въ Батыя царя, у Батыя царя было четыреста тысячъ кованные рати, а воевалъ всю Русскую землю отъ востока и до запада … И ты пришелъ на Рускую землю, царь Мамай, съ многими силами, съ девятью ордами и семидесятью князьями, а нынѣ ты поганый бѣжишь самъ-девятъ въ лукоморье.
p.s: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), words the poet gives to the Genoese of Kaffa, ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
p.pe: Mamai and the Golden Horde; Genoese (Fryazi) of Kaffa
p.t: You will never be like Tsar Batu: Tsar Batu had four hundred thousand armoured men, and he made war on the whole Russian land from east to west … And you came to the Russian land, Tsar Mamai, with great forces, with nine hordes and seventy princes, and now, pagan, you flee with eight companions to the sea-shore.
p.c: The flight to 'Khafesta grad' (Kaffa) is on the previous page, n31. The figures are poetic, not a muster roll.

p.h: Peking: the Tartar kings' city becomes the Northern Court
p.g: Ricci explains why China had two capitals. The Ming founder ruled from Nanjing, but his son Yongle, who had guarded the northern frontier against the recently expelled Tartars, seized the throne and moved his seat north, fearing the Tartars would break out again to win back the empire. He chose the very city where the Tartar kings had lived and renamed it Peking, 'Northern Court'. The Mongol capital (Dadu, Khanbaliq) thus became Ming Beijing.
p.q: Et quoniam in aquilonaribus provinciis plus habebat virium ac fidei, & Tartaros inde ad recuperandam regni tyrannidem credibile erat erupturos, iis in partibus considere statuit; & quidem ea in Urbe, in qua Reges Tartari, cum Sinis imperitabant, morabantur. Eam Urbem ipse Pequim, id est, Borealem Curiam, ad similitudinem australis, quae dicitur Nanquim nominavit.
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.pe: The Tartar (Yuan) kings and the Ming emperor Yongle
p.t: And since he had more strength and loyalty in the northern provinces, and it was likely that the Tartars would break out from there to recover their tyranny over the kingdom, he decided to settle in those parts, and indeed in the very city where the Tartar kings lived when they ruled the Chinese. He named that city Pequim, that is, Northern Court, on the model of the southern one called Nanquim.

p.h: Tarku, an unwalled capital of a thousand houses
p.g: On the way home the embassy spent five weeks at Tarku (Tarki), capital of Dagestan, whose people Olearius calls Tartars. The town had no walls and about a thousand houses built in the Persian manner, set among rocks full of fossil shells. He found the local lords frightening: over dinner, he says, they talked only of robbing and selling people.
p.q: The City is not wall'd. It may contain a thousand houses, built according to the Persian way, but not so well. These Tartars, as also those of … and the others who live more Northerly, are called Kaitacks
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)

p.h: A Nogai town outside Astrakhan's walls
p.g: Wintering at Astrakhan, Christopher Burrough's party saw half of the Nogai Tatar settlement beside the Russian castle burn by accident. He notes that these Nogais were the Tsar's vassals, some seven thousand men, women and children. Weeks later other Nogais and Crimeans camped around Astrakhan with 1,400 horsemen but did not attack.
p.q: The Nagayes that inhabit that towne are the Emperour of Russia his vassals. It is supposed there are of them inhabiting that place, of men, women, and children, the number of seuen thousand. … The seuenth of March 1580. the Nagayes and Crims came before Astracan to the number of one thousand foure hundred horsemen, which incamped round about
p.s: Christopher Burrough's reports, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Nogai Tatars (vassals of the Tsar) and raiding Crimeans
p.c: The town's name (given on the previous page as the 'Yurt') is badly garbled in this OCR.

p.h: Suzdal, great Christian city, taken by trickery
p.g: Thomas sketches the Mongol advance before Hungary: they had been held back by the Russians, circled the northern lands for twenty years, then returned with Cumans and other subject peoples. Their first great prize was 'a very great city of the Christians called Suzdal', which they besieged and took more by guile than force, killing its king George and many of his people. (Grand Prince Yuri of Vladimir-Suzdal died in 1238.)
p.q: Et primo quidem Civ. maximam Christianorum nomine Susdaliam circumdantes obsederunt, & obsessam, diu, non tam vi, quam fraude ceperunt, & destruxerunt, Regemque ipsius nomine Georgium cum magna multitudine sui populi neci dederunt.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: And first they surrounded and besieged a very great city of the Christians named Suzdal, and having besieged it for a long time they took it, not so much by force as by fraud, and destroyed it, and put to death its king, named George, with a great multitude of his people.
p.c: Thomas's chronology is loose; the capture of Vladimir and Suzdal and Yuri's death were in 1238.

p.h: The Bulgar towns dug up to their foundations
p.g: The first Russian capture of Kazan: Prince Iurii, sent by his brother Vasilii I, took the Bulgar towns on the Volga (Kazan, Bolgar, Zhukotin, Kermenchuk), raided the Golden Horde and 'dug all those towns up to their foundations', killing the Kazan tsar. The author says Kazan then stood empty for forty years. The passage lists real Volga towns of the Golden Horde era.
p.q: Тои шедъ взя грады Болгарскія, по Волзе стояща, Казань, и Болгары, Жюкотинъ, Керменчюкъ, и Златую Орду повоева, по совету Крымского царя Азигерея, и вся тѣ грады до основанія раскопа
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Prince Iurii Dmitrievich of Moscow; the Bulgar-Tatar towns of the middle Volga
p.t: He went and took the Bulgar towns standing along the Volga, Kazan, and Bolgar, Zhukotin, Kermenchuk, and ravaged the Golden Horde, on the advice of the Crimean tsar Azigerei, and dug all those towns up to their foundations
p.c: The alliance with the Crimean khan Hacı Giray is an anachronism (he ruled in the 1440s to 1460s).

p.h: Khiva's mud walls and towns
p.g: In the extract from Muraviev's journal that Monteith appended, Khiva appears as a walled capital of 10,000 to 15,000 people with mud walls 20 feet high, a palace and a fine mosque. The other towns of the khanate were of flat-roofed mud with a few brick mosques, and lasted well because the climate was so dry.
p.q: The walls of the city are built of mud and 20 feet in height … The buildings in all these towns are only of mud with flat roofs, some few mosques are of brick and mortar. They are however very permanent from the dryness of the climate.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev, in William Monteith's English extract
p.c: Not Meyendorff's text: Muraviev's journal as extracted by the translator. The full Muraviev translation is record W027.

p.h: Merv abandoned when its dam broke
p.g: Abbott gives a short history of Merv: founded, he says, by fire-worshippers, long Persian, and fought over by Turkic tribes. He explains that the old city emptied when the dam on the Murghab river was neglected and swept away during decades of disorder, leaving a deserted ruin beside a new village of mud huts.
p.q: Merv was one of the most ancient cities of Asia. … Merv has probably changed masters as often as any city in the world. … During the misrule and anarchy of the last sixty years the ancient dam of the Moorghaub was neglected and carried away. The city in consequence became uninhabitable, and was utterly abandoned.
p.s: James Abbott
p.pe: Turkmens under the Khan of Khiva
p.c: The founding by fire-worshippers is local tradition that Abbott repeats; the abandonment story is what he learned on the spot.

p.h: Kazan, old capital of a Tartar kingdom
p.g: Bell wintered at Kazan. He describes the Russian brick citadel with its cathedral and palaces, and then the Muslim Tatars who live in a street or two of the suburbs as 'posterity of the ancient natives', free to practise their religion and some of them rich from trade with Turkey and Persia. He recalls that the city was the capital of a Tartar kingdom until Ivan the Terrible took it in 1552.
p.q: The suburbs are inhabited chiefly by mechanics, except a street or two possessed by Mahometan Tartars, the posterity of the ancient natives. … Cazan was anciently the capital of a part of Tartary, and the seat of government, where the royal family resided. It was taken from the Tartars by Czar Ivan Vasiloviz, in the year fifteen hundred and fifty two,
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.tg: kazan khanate ivan iv suburbs islam

p.h: Kasimov: a Tatar town of wood with a mosque tower
p.g: Sailing down the Oka, de Bruyn passed Kasimov, which had been the seat of a small Tatar khanate under Moscow. He found a fair-sized town with no walls, where every house and all four churches were of wood, and a mosque with a tower used by 'Turks and Tartars'.
p.q: Elle n'a point de murailles quoi qu'elle soit assez grande, toutes les maisons en sont de bois, aussi-bien que les quatre églises. Il y a une tour à une mosquée, qui sert aux Turcs & aux Tartares
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: It has no walls, although it is fairly large; all the houses are of wood, as are the four churches. There is a tower at a mosque, which serves the Turks and the Tartars

p.h: A Nogai prince in a little clay town
p.g: An Italian merchant told her he had crossed the Nogai steppe and was welcomed by the Nogai chief Beyazet Beg, who lived in a small clay-built town and ate mostly milk, koumis and mutton. Trying to please a European, the prince served an 'Italian' feast so strange that the guest slipped out to be sick, and promised a French one next day.
p.q: He said, he found their chief named Beyazet Beg, i. e. Prince Bajazet, dwelling in a little town built with clay, on the lake and rivulet Bolotchik… This Tartar prince, who lives like his Scythian ancestors… principally on milk and its preparation koumis (which constitutes the food, wine, and brandy of the Tartars), with occasionally the flesh of his flocks
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802), reporting an Italian merchant of Kherson
p.c: Second-hand story from a merchant.

p.h: The Qipchaq steppe: pasture, nomads and few towns
p.g: Mustawfi's short entry on the Dasht-i Qipchaq, the Golden Horde's steppe, says it has rich pasture but few houses, towns or villages, and that most people are nomads. He then lists its towns, including 'Saray Batu', the Horde capital on the Volga. Le Strange's footnote places the ruins of Saray above Astrakhan.
p.q: Dasht-i-Qipchaq. This is of the Sixth Clime, its plains bear excellent pasturage, stretching to the north of the Caspian Sea, but there are here few houses or towns or villages. Most of the inhabitants are nomads of the plain. Its most celebrated town is Khazar … then there is Burtas, also Suvar, Muhtal, Saray Batu and Sarir
p.s: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)
p.pe: Nomads of the Qipchaq steppe (Golden Horde lands)
p.c: Compiled at second hand: several of the 'towns' (Khazar, Burtas, Suvar) are names from much older Arabic geographies.

p.h: Tobolsk: Russian brick above, Tartar streets below
p.g: Bell notes that the Tartar princes of Siberia once lived about thirty versts from Tobolsk at a place now 'neglected and ruinous' (he does not name it; it is probably the old khanate capital Isker, or Kashlyk). The Russian town on the hill has a brick wall, the governor's palace and brick churches, while the Tatars, descendants of the old inhabitants, live in several 'Tartar-streets' in the lower suburb along the river, with freedom of religion and trade.
p.q: Formerly the Tartar princes had their abode at a place about thirty verst south from Tobolsky, which is now neglected and ruinous. … Under the hill in the suburbs, along the banks of the river, are several large streets, called the Tartar-streets, occupied by the remains of the ancient inhabitants of these parts.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.tg: tobolsk siberian khanate tatar quarter ruins

p.h: A Tartar town with whitewashed clay walls
p.g: The Russian embassy of 1746 passed a Tartar town under Russian protection, ruled by a prince called Alt Sheff, on a high river bank on the road north of Derbent. It had about 300 houses with clay walls whitened with lime. The diarist grumbles that its people were the most skilful thieves in the world.
p.q: …arrived at a tartar town under the Russian protection; though otherwise a kind of independent state. The prince of it was called Alt Sheff: it stands on a high bank on the north side of the river …, and contains about 300 houses; the walls of which are of clay whitened with lime. The inhabitants are the most acute thieves in the world,
p.s: Anonymous journal of the Russian embassy to Persia of 1746, extract printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.pl: North Caucasus lowlands north of Derbent (Dagestan)

p.h: Entering walled Khiva
p.g: Abbott rode to his first audience through a suburb, a bazaar and a fortified gateway, with women crowding the rooftops to stare. The royal citadel itself he found to be a modest brick building set into a corner of the town walls.
p.q: On approaching the town, we entered a considerable suburb, and afterwards passed through a miserable bazaar to the gateway ; for Khiva is fortified. … It was not long before we reached, through some very poor streets, the citadel, within which resides the "Father of Victories," the king of Khaurism. It is a poor, brick building, forming an angle of the city defences.
p.s: James Abbott

p.h: The baskak's two settlements empty overnight
p.g: Akhmat had founded two 'slobodas' (tax-free trading settlements) in the Kursk land and left two brothers to guard and fortify them. After a Rus prince ambushed their men, the brothers fled to Kursk and on the next day the whole of both settlements scattered. It is a rare glimpse of settlements founded under Horde protection inside Rus, and of how fragile they were.
p.q: Того же лѣта, по Велицѣ дни въ недѣлю Фомину, побѣгоста 2 братеника та бесерменина къ Курьску, а на заутрѣи въ понедѣльникъ побѣже вся свобода та, и другая; и тако розоидошася обѣ свободѣ бесерменьскиѣ.
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Akhmat's 'besermen' (Muslim) settlers; Rus princes of Rylsk and Lipovichsk
p.t: That same year, after Easter on St Thomas Sunday, those two besermen brothers fled to Kursk, and on the morrow, Monday, all that sloboda ran away, and the other one too; and so both besermen slobodas dispersed.
p.c: The manuscript spells sloboda as 'svoboda'.

p.h: Bulghar, summer seat of the Golden Horde khans
p.g: Rose summarises the history of Bulghar on the Volga: it suffered from 'Mongol-Tatar' raids, was conquered by Batu Khan in 1236, and then served the Golden Horde khans as their summer residence, with Sarai on the lower Volga as their winter seat. The next page adds that Marco Polo's father and uncle stayed there in 1261.
p.q: …von Batü Chan, dem Enkel von Dschingis Chan, 1236 völlig unterworfen und dem Kaptschakischen Reiche einverleibt wurde. Die Nachkommen Dschingis Chans in diesem Reiche, die von den Russen die Chane der Goldnen Horde genannt wurden, erwählten Bulghar zu ihrer Sommer-Residenz, und Serai an der untern Wolga zu ihrer Winter-Residenz.
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.pe: Volga Bulghars; Mongols of the Golden Horde
p.t: …was completely subdued in 1236 by Batu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, and incorporated into the Kipchak empire. The descendants of Genghis Khan in this empire, whom the Russians called the khans of the Golden Horde, chose Bulghar as their summer residence and Sarai on the lower Volga as their winter residence.
p.c: Background history compiled from Klaproth, Frähn and Erdmann, not observation.
p.tg: bulghar golden horde sarai batu capital

p.h: Samarkand: an earth-walled city a little bigger than Seville
p.g: Clavijo compares Samarkand to his own Seville: an earthen wall, a city a little larger, but with suburbs and gardens stretching for leagues and more people outside the walls than within. Timur's palaces stood among the gardens. Elsewhere he watches Timur drive a vaulted market street through the city in twenty days, pulling down houses in its path.
p.q: The city of Samarcand is situated in a plain, and surrounded by an earthen wall. It is a little larger than the city of Seville, but, outside the city, there are a great number of houses, joined together in many parts, so as to form suburbs.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.tg: samarkand earthen wall suburbs gardens seville

p.h: Nobody yet knew where Karakorum lay
p.g: In a footnote Humboldt lists the rival guesses for the ruins of Karakorum, Mongke Khan's capital: Klaproth put it at one set of coordinates, Abel-Remusat at one of two named ruins, and d'Anville had it two degrees too far south-east. He adds that Wilhelm Schott thought the name meant 'black town' or 'black residence'. The site was still unidentified in his day.
p.q: Klaproth place les ruines de Kara-Khorum lat. 46° 41', long. 100° 24'. … Abel-Rémusat croit Kara-Khorum identique ou avec Talarho-kara-balgasoun (long. 100° 44', lat. 47° 32') ou avec Baisiri-bouritou (long. 100° 36', lat. 48° 24'). … M. Schott, auquel on doit d'ingénieuses et savantes recherches sur les langues tartares, pense que Kara-Koroum signifie ville ou résidence noire.
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt (footnote)
p.t: Klaproth places the ruins of Karakorum at latitude 46° 41', longitude 100° 24'. … Abel-Remusat believes Karakorum identical either with Talarho-kara-balgasun (long. 100° 44', lat. 47° 32') or with Baisiri-buritu (long. 100° 36', lat. 48° 24'). … Mr Schott, to whom we owe ingenious and learned research on the Tartar languages, thinks that Karakorum means black town or black residence.
p.c: Longitudes are reckoned from Paris. The ruins of Karakorum were identified beside Erdene Zuu monastery only in 1889.

p.h: A Turkmen camp of 150 black 'beehives'
p.g: On the desert road Burnes halted at a Turkmen oba (camp) of about 150 conical, movable huts called khirgahs, scattered on a rise with no order, like giant beehives with black roofs, with the children swarming like bees. A Turkmen settlement of this size was a whole mobile town.
p.q: It consisted of about 150 conical moveable huts, called "khirgahs," which were perched on a rising ground. There was no order in the distribution, and they stood like so many gigantic beehives
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.pl: Turkmen desert (between the Murghab and the Oxus)

p.h: Kazan, Astrakhan and Siberia conquered
p.g: In his summing up of Ivan the Terrible's reign, Horsey lists the conquest of the Tatar 'kingdoms' of Kazan and Astrakhan and the peoples along the Volga to the Caspian, the end of tribute to the Crimean khan, and the conquest of the 'kingdom of Siberia'.
p.q: he conquered the kingdom of Casan and the kingdom of Astracan, and all the regions and great people of the Nagaie and Chercas Tartors, and many other of that kinde, inhabitinge above two thowsand miells of each side that famous river of Volga, sowthward eaven to the Mare Caspian Sea.
p.s: Sir Jerome Horsey (memoir; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.pe: Kazan, Astrakhan, Nogai and Circassian Tartars
p.c: Horsey overstates: the Nogais and Circassians were never fully conquered in Ivan's lifetime.

p.h: Ili: the old Kalmyk capital becomes a Chinese garrison
p.g: In the route copied from a Kashgar man's journal, the note on Ili says the old city by the river, once the Kalmaks' capital, is deserted, and that the name now covers two towns: Gulja, mostly Muslim, and Kura, the Chinese garrison and seat of the governor-general. It also mentions the grave of Tughluk Timur, the first Chaghatai khan to become Muslim, and a burning stone (coal) found nearby.
p.q: Ila is properly the name of the river on the borders of which stood the city, thence so called, and which is now deserted. There is the grave of Tughluk Timor, the first of the Chaghatai Sultans who adopted Mohammedanism.
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah, from Mullah Nazr of Kashgar's route notes (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.c: Not seen by Izzet Ullah; copied from another traveller's journal and oral notes.
p.tg: ili gulja chaghatai qing garrison kalmyks

p.h: Chufut-Kale, the 'Castle of Miscreants'
p.g: Contrasting the Jews of Constantinople with the Karaite Jews of the Crimea, Clarke praises the Karaites' character. He notes that their town was known by a Turkish insult, Tchufut-kaleh, the 'Castle of Miscreants' (his footnote glosses Tchifuit as 'a vile miscreant'), and says their good name had turned it into an honourable title.
p.q: How different from the character borne by the Karaite Jews of the Crimea! whose virtues have rendered even the opprobrious name, derived from their Turkish brethren, an honourable title ; for their place of residence is called Tchufut-kaleh, the "Castle of Miscreants."
p.s: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)
p.c: A passing remark; Clarke's full description of Chufut-Kale is in Part I, not in this volume.

p.h: Tomsk's Tatar suburb of slender minarets
p.g: At Tomsk Erman found the Tatar and Bukharan quarter south of the main streets, its low but regular wooden houses broken by 'the slender towers of several mosques'. The richer Russian town stood on the hill above the river.
p.q: The suburb inhabited by the Tatarian and Bukharian part of the population lies upon the south of the main line of streets, displaying from between its low but regular wooden houses, the slender towers of several mosques.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

p.h: Balkh: a great ruin with one corner lived in
p.g: Balkh, the old capital of the Uzbek-populated province south of the Oxus, is called by Asians the oldest city in the world and the 'mother of towns' (the scan is garbled here). By Elphinstone's day it had shrunk to a small inhabited corner inside a vast walled ruin, with a citadel held by the Afghan governor. The rich countryside was still watered by eighteen canals.
p.q: Its ruins still cover a great extent, and are surrounded with a wall, but only one corner is inhabited.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: The page does not say who ruined Balkh; the surrounding text is badly garbled.

p.h: Mukden, the emperor's hunting capital
p.g: An official mentions Mukden (Shenyang), the old Manchu capital in Manchuria, where the emperor goes to hunt; Ellis records its Chinese name. The official feared being summoned to the imperial hunt.
p.q: Chang called Moukden, Moulin; but the latter may be the Chinese pronunciation of the name. The Emperor goes there to hunt.
p.s: Henry Ellis

p.h: The ruined city of Taiminzin
p.g: Discussing old silver mines on the Argun, Strahlenberg quotes the Dutch envoy Isbrand Ides that the Jurchens and Mongols once mined silver there. He then identifies the 'large and ancient city' of Alackzin in Abulghazi's Tartar history with the ruined city of Taiminzin that Ides described, once the seat of 'Chan Utay'.
p.q: But that large and ancient City, which this Tartarian Author calls Alackzin, is the now ruin'd City of Taiminzin; … See the Description which Isbrand Ides gives of the ancient City of Taiminzin, (p. 75.) formerly the Residence of Chan Utay:
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)
p.c: An identification made from books (Ides and Abulghazi), not from a visit.
p.tg: ruins silver mines dauria isbrand ides abulghazi
